meanings.en: to make up a story, excuse, or plan, often deceptively
meanings.zh: 编造,捏造(借口、故事、计划)

meanings.en: to prepare a dish or drink by combining various ingredients

examples: She concocted an elaborate excuse about a dead phone battery to explain missing the 9 a.m. standup.
He spent Sunday afternoon concocting a green smoothie out of whatever was wilting in the fridge.
The intern concocted a glowing fake testimonial to pad the pitch deck, and HR found out within a day.
The teenager concocted an elaborate alibi involving a fake dentist appointment and a borrowed car, but his mom checked the clinic's calendar within the hour.
The bartender concocted a smoky mezcal cocktail for the new menu, garnished with a charred lime wheel nobody could stop photographing.
words.etymology: con-(一起) + coquere(煮) → 拼凑熬制 → 编造

meanings.en: recovering from illness, injury, or medical treatment
a person who is recovering from illness

examples: Still convalescent after knee surgery, she ran the sprint retro from bed, laptop propped on a pillow.
The clinic opened a convalescent lounge where post-op patients sip broth and scroll TikTok before discharge.
He was listed as convalescent for another two weeks, which meant no gym, no stairs, and no complaining about either.
Still convalescent from the flu, he answered emails from the couch in slow motion, muting himself to cough.
The convalescent shuffled down the hospital corridor twice a day, counting laps like it was a full marathon.
words.etymology: con-(强调) + valere(强壮) → 重新变强 → 康复中

meanings.en: irrelevant or unnecessary to the matter at hand; not essential
meanings.zh: 无关紧要的;非必要的,多余的

examples: The editor cut three paragraphs of extraneous backstory so the pitch deck would fit on five slides.
Strip the extraneous fields from the sign-up form — nobody needs a job title just to start a free trial.
The lawyer objected that the photos were extraneous to the case and had nothing to do with the actual contract dispute.
The professor warned that any extraneous formatting — colored fonts, clip art, borders — would cost points on the thesis.
During the debugging session, she kept muting extraneous notifications so a single Slack ping wouldn't break her focus.
words.etymology: extra-(外部) → 从外面来的 → 无关的

meanings.en: an official order, decree, or authorization issued by a person or body in power

examples: The new manager banned Slack DMs by fiat, no team vote, just a memo pinned to the channel.
The mayor closed the bike lane by fiat overnight, and commuters found out only when they hit the barricades.
Bitcoin evangelists love arguing that fiat currency is doomed, right up until they need to pay rent.
The landlord raised rent by fiat halfway through the lease, taping a notice to the door instead of calling anyone.
The school principal cancelled the spring dance by fiat, and parents flooded the PTA inbox within the hour.
words.etymology: 拉丁 fiat「让它成为」(fieri 成为) → 一句话即成法令

meanings.en: to lecture or scold someone at length, forcefully
meanings.zh: 对...滔滔不绝地训斥/说教

meanings.en: a lengthy, forceful, and often scolding speech
meanings.zh: 长篇的训斥;慷慨激昂的演说

examples: My Uber driver launched into a ten-minute harangue about parking regulations before we'd even left the curb.
The coach harangued the team at halftime for missing three easy passes, and nobody spoke on the bus home.
Her father's dinner-table harangue about screen time ended, as always, with everyone quietly checking their phones under the table.
The landlord harangued the tenants for twenty minutes about the recycling bins before anyone could get a word in.
His voicemail turned into a five-minute harangue about the unpaid invoice, each sentence louder than the last.

meanings.en: arrogantly domineering; expecting immediate obedience
meanings.zh: 傲慢专横的;不容置疑的

examples: Her imperious tone in the group chat — 'have this on my desk by six' — sent three people job-hunting that night.
The maître d' waved us off with an imperious flick of the wrist, as if the reservation itself had insulted him.
He'd grown imperious after the promotion, cutting people off mid-sentence in meetings he used to sit quietly through.
The new professor's imperious syllabus policy — no laptops, no questions after class — emptied half the lecture hall by week three.
The chef's imperious command silenced the entire kitchen mid-service, and the new line cook nearly dropped a tray of plates.
words.etymology: imperare(命令) → imperium(统治权) → 专横

meanings.en: extra freedom, time, or margin allowed for action
meanings.zh: (行动、时间上的)余地,回旋空间

examples: The landlord gave us a week's leeway on rent after we explained the payroll delay at the new job.
New hires get some leeway on missing minor deadlines, but that grace period ends after the first quarter review.
The recipe gives you leeway on the spices, but the baking time is the one thing you cannot fudge.
The professor gave students a little leeway on the essay's word count, but the citation format still had to be perfect.
Her manager allowed some leeway on the dress code during the heatwave, as long as clients never saw the office.
words.etymology: lee(船的背风侧) + way → 被风吹偏的余量 → 回旋空间

meanings.en: to stick fast in mud, or become entangled in a difficult situation
an area of deep mud or swamp; a difficult, entangling situation

examples: The merger got mired in regulatory review for eighteen months while both companies quietly bled market share.
Our boots sank into the mire along the riverbank, and one shoe never came back out.
He's still mired in credit-card debt from a wedding he hasn't finished paying off two years later.
The renovation got mired in permit delays for months, and the contractor's crew moved on to other jobs.
The negotiations sank into a mire of counteroffers and lawyers, with neither side willing to sign first.
words.etymology: 古诺斯语 mýrr(沼泽) → 陷进泥沼

meanings.en: an aura of mystery, glamour, or fascination surrounding someone or something

examples: The founder cultivated a mystique by skipping interviews and posting only cryptic tweets before every launch.
Working from a co-working space in Lisbon lost its mystique fast once the wifi kept dropping mid-standup.
The chef's tasting menu relies as much on mystique as flavor — nobody at the table knows what course three even was.
The influencer's carefully curated mystique cracked the moment a leaked group chat revealed how scripted her 'candid' posts were.
The old jazz club kept its mystique alive with no sign out front, just a line of people who somehow knew where to go.
words.etymology: 希腊 mystēs(受秘传的人) → 神秘感

meanings.en: a person who is new to a subject, skill, or activity; a beginner

examples: As a neophyte in crypto, he lost half his savings before learning what a rug pull even was.
The gym pairs every neophyte with a trainer for three sessions so nobody gets hurt on the squat rack.
She joined the trading Discord as a total neophyte and left, four months later, somehow giving advice to newcomers.
As a neophyte photographer, she spent her first paid wedding shoot panicking over settings she'd only read about online.
The neophyte coder pushed straight to the main branch on his first day, and the whole team's build broke by lunch.
words.etymology: neo-(新) + phyton(栽种) → 新栽的苗 → 新手

meanings.en: in a steep or abrupt manner; suddenly and sharply

examples: The startup's valuation dropped precipitously after the CEO's resignation leaked on LinkedIn before the official statement.
The trail drops precipitously for the last half mile, so hiking poles aren't optional, they're survival gear.
Engagement fell precipitously the week the app changed its algorithm, and the founders panicked in the group chat.
Ticket sales for the tour fell precipitously after the venue change leaked online before the official announcement.
The temperature dropped precipitously once the sun set behind the ridge, and nobody had packed a real jacket.
words.etymology: prae-(向前) + caput(头) → 头朝前栽下 → 陡峭、急剧

meanings.en: to formally put a law, decree, or regulation into effect
to make an idea or belief widely known

examples: The city council promulgated new noise ordinances that take effect the same week as the music festival.
The agency promulgated the updated safety rules with almost no warning, and factory floors scrambled to comply overnight.
He spent his career promulgating a theory of climate migration that only recently gained mainstream traction.
The board promulgated a new remote-work policy the same week half the staff had already booked flights home for the holidays.
The professor spent decades promulgating a fringe economic theory that finally found an audience on podcasts.
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + vulgus(民众) → 推向民众 → 颁布

meanings.en: extremely beautiful or attractive; delightful to look at

examples: She walked into the reunion looking ravishing in the red dress she'd almost returned to the store.
The sunset over the reservoir was so ravishing that half the joggers stopped to take the same photo.
Even in scrubs at 6 a.m., the bride looked ravishing enough that the nurses asked for a picture.
She looked ravishing at the gala in a borrowed emerald gown, and three strangers asked who designed it.
The garden looked ravishing in the golden evening light, every rose somehow catching the sun at the same angle.
words.etymology: rapere(夺取) → 夺人心魄 → 艳丽动人

meanings.en: basic, elementary, or not fully developed
meanings.zh: 基本的,初步的;发育不全的

examples: My rudimentary Spanish got me through ordering tapas but collapsed the moment the waiter asked a follow-up question.
The MVP shipped with rudimentary search — no filters, no autocomplete, just a box that technically worked.
He has a rudimentary grasp of Excel, which mostly means he knows how to make a cell turn red.
The prototype had only rudimentary error handling, so it crashed the second someone typed a symbol instead of a number.
His rudimentary French got him through checking into the hotel, but the concierge's fast reply left him nodding blankly.
words.etymology: rudis(粗糙未加工) → 尚未成形 → 初步的

meanings.en: optimistic or confident, especially in a difficult situation

examples: Despite two rounds of layoffs, she stayed sanguine about the company's prospects, insisting the pivot would pay off.
Investors were far less sanguine after the earnings call, and the stock dropped twelve percent by closing bell.
He's weirdly sanguine about the audit, mostly because he's never once read his own expense reports.
He stayed sanguine about the app's slow launch, insisting the reviews would pick up once word of mouth spread.
Despite the missed funding round, the founders remained oddly sanguine, already sketching plans for the next pitch deck.
words.etymology: sanguis(血) → 中世纪体液说的多血质 → 乐观

meanings.en: tempting or arousing desire for something kept out of reach
meanings.zh: 逗引人的,诱人的(却难以获得)

examples: The trailer offered a tantalizing thirty seconds of the finale before cutting to black, and Reddit lost its mind.
The food truck's tacos smelled tantalizing, but the line snaked around the block and we had a meeting in ten minutes.
She left the offer letter open on her screen, a tantalizing reminder of the raise she hadn't accepted yet.
The recipe photo online looked tantalizing, but three attempts later her version still came out nothing like it.
A tantalizing sliver of the new game's map leaked online, and forums spent all weekend dissecting a single screenshot.
words.etymology: 希腊神话 Tantalus 头顶果子永远够不着 → 逗引人

meanings.en: the art of preparing, stuffing, and mounting animal skins to look lifelike

examples: The bar's new owner decorated the walls with vintage taxidermy, including one very judgmental-looking owl.
She took a weekend taxidermy class on a whim and came home with a mounted squirrel she can't display.
The museum's taxidermy exhibit hadn't been updated since the eighties, and the lion's fur had gone slightly gray.
Her grandfather's study was lined with taxidermy pheasants he'd mounted himself back when the hobby was still fashionable.
The thrift store sold a chipped taxidermy fox for ten dollars, and someone bought it within the hour just for the shock value.
words.etymology: taxis(排列) + derma(皮) → 把皮整形排好 → 标本剥制

meanings.en: causing or deserving intense disgust or hatred

examples: The landlord's habit of hiding mold complaints from new tenants was abhorrent, and the review site finally banned him.
She found the ad's casual sexism abhorrent and pulled her agency's account from the campaign within the hour.
To him, ghosting a job candidate after three interview rounds was almost as abhorrent as ghosting a friend.
He found the company's habit of quietly shrinking severance packages abhorrent and quit before they could offer him one.
The coach considered benching an injured kid just to win the game abhorrent, no matter what the parents on the sideline wanted.
words.etymology: ab-(离开) + horrere(战栗) → 吓得往后缩 → 可憎

meanings.en: to formally revoke or repeal a law, agreement, or practice

examples: The new CEO abrogated the remote-work policy over a single Slack message, and half the team started job-hunting that week.
You can't just abrogate the lease because your roommate moved out — read clause 7 before you call the landlord.
The court abrogated the decades-old zoning rule in a single ruling, and developers were rezoning lots within a month.
The board voted unanimously to abrogate the founder's lifetime free-parking perk once the new campus ran out of spots.
The airline abrogated its no-questions-asked refund policy overnight, and customer service was flooded with confused calls by morning.
words.etymology: ab-(离开) + rogare(提议、立法) → 撤走法案 → 废除

meanings.en: anxious or fearful about something that might happen

examples: She was apprehensive about the performance review after her manager rescheduled it twice without explanation.
First-time flyers get apprehensive during turbulence, but the pilot's calm updates over the intercom usually help.
He felt apprehensive walking into the reunion, unsure whether anyone would even remember his name.
She felt apprehensive handing in the final draft, certain the professor would find the one paragraph she'd rushed.
He grew apprehensive as the interview panel went quiet after his answer, unsure if the silence meant good or bad.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + prehendere(抓住) → 预先抓住坏消息 → 忧虑

meanings.en: requiring great effort; difficult and tiring

examples: The visa application was so arduous — six forms, three notarized letters, two interviews — that she nearly gave up on the move.
Training for the marathon meant an arduous 5 a.m. run every day before the kids woke up.
Migrating the whole codebase off the old framework turned into a far more arduous project than anyone budgeted for.
Assembling the flat-pack nursery furniture without instructions turned into an arduous three-hour ordeal that ended with two leftover screws.
Renovating the kitchen alone on weekends turned into an arduous slog that ate every Saturday for three months.
words.etymology: arduus(陡峭高耸) → 像爬陡坡 → 艰苦

meanings.en: plain and simple; without comfort or luxury
meanings.zh: 朴素的,简朴的;不加装饰的

meanings.en: stern or severe in manner or expression

examples: Her austere one-line reply to my proposal — 'No.' — killed the whole project before lunch.
After downsizing to a 400-square-foot apartment, their once-cluttered life turned almost austere: one mug, one plate, one chair.
The new headmaster's austere manner made even the confident kids stop talking the second he entered the room.
The monastery guesthouse was austere by design — a cot, a single lamp, and a window that didn't open.
Her austere expression during the layoff announcement gave nothing away, not even when someone started crying.
words.etymology: 希腊 austēros(干涩发苦) → 不加甜饰 → 朴素

meanings.en: to fit together neatly, or bring into close agreement
a joint formed by interlocking wedge-shaped pieces

examples: Her thesis defense dovetailed neatly with the internship offer, so she could finish in May and start the job in June.
The carpenter cut each dovetail by hand, and the drawer front slid together without a single nail.
Their skill sets dovetail well — she handles the design, he handles the backend, and nothing falls through the cracks.
The two teams' roadmaps dovetailed unexpectedly, so the merger meant almost no overlapping features to cut.
The guitar maker showed off the neck joint's dovetail, cut so precisely that no clamp was needed while the glue dried.
words.etymology: 木工的鸽尾榫 → 严丝合缝 → 吻合

meanings.en: to involve someone deeply in a conflict, argument, or difficult situation

examples: The startup got embroiled in a trademark dispute two weeks before its funding round closed, and the deal nearly collapsed.
He tried to stay neutral, but replying to the family group chat at all embroiled him in the inheritance fight.
The city was embroiled in controversy after leaked emails showed the contract had been awarded without a bid.
Replying to one customer's angry tweet embroiled the brand in a days-long pile-on before the social team even woke up.
He got embroiled in his roommates' feud over the electricity bill just by suggesting they split it differently.
words.etymology: en-(进入) + broil(混战) → 卷入纠纷

meanings.en: to ask someone earnestly or anxiously to do something

examples: She entreated her manager for one more day on the deadline, promising the deck would be flawless.
Neighbors entreated the city council to add a crosswalk after the third near-miss outside the elementary school.
He entreated his sister to reconsider the wedding venue before the deposit became non-refundable.
The nurse entreated the exhausted new parents to nap while the baby slept, but they scrolled their phones instead.
Fans entreated the band on social media to add a second show after the first sold out in four minutes.
words.etymology: en-(使) + tractare(对待、周旋) → 反复求人 → 恳求

meanings.en: convenient and practical, though not always fair or principled
meanings.zh: 权宜的,便利的(未必正当)

meanings.en: a means to an end, especially one used in an emergency

examples: It was politically expedient to delay the layoffs until after the shareholder meeting, even though everyone knew they were coming.
With no babysitter and a call in ten minutes, propping the tablet on cereal boxes was the most expedient fix.
Cutting corners on the safety review was expedient in the short term but cost the company far more later.
Approving the vendor without competitive bids was expedient given the deadline, even though procurement rules technically required three quotes.
With the client's video call starting in two minutes and no clean shirt, ironing out the wrinkles with a damp towel was the expedient fix.
words.etymology: ex-(出) + ped-(脚) → 把脚从绊索里解出来 → 权宜之计

meanings.en: to complain persistently about something, often minor
a complaint

examples: The team groused about the new expense-report software for a week before anyone actually filed a support ticket.
His constant grouse about the office thermostat became a running joke on the team Slack channel.
Commuters groused on the platform for twenty minutes, but nobody bothered rerouting through the next station.
The neighbors groused about the building's new recycling schedule for weeks before anyone actually started sorting their bins correctly.
Her main grouse about the apartment was the elevator, which had been 'temporarily' out of service for two months.

meanings.en: to complain in a low, discontented, muttering way
a muttered complaint, or a low rumbling sound

examples: Commuters grumbled about the delayed train, but nobody actually got off to find another route.
Her stomach grumbled loudly through the entire budget meeting, and she pretended not to notice.
He grumbled his way through the whole grocery run, then ate three servings of the dinner he'd complained about.
The interns grumbled about the unpaid overtime but kept showing up early anyway, afraid to be the one who complained out loud.
A low grumble of thunder rolled over the stadium just as the marching band took the field.
words.etymology: 拟声,源自低地德语 grommelen(咕哝) → 嘀咕

meanings.en: unlucky, especially in a way that invites pity or amusement

examples: The hapless delivery driver got a flat tire, then locked his keys in the van, then dropped the package in a puddle.
Some hapless intern accidentally emailed the entire company an unfinished layoffs memo instead of the birthday newsletter.
The hapless goalkeeper watched the ball bounce off his own foot and into the net in the final minute.
The hapless contestant froze on the final question, then knocked over the podium walking off stage.
Some hapless tourist locked himself out of his rental car in the middle of the desert with no signal for miles.
words.etymology: hap(运气) + -less → 没运气 → 倒霉

meanings.en: in an early stage; just beginning to develop

examples: The doctor caught an incipient case of carpal tunnel before it got bad enough to need surgery.
You could hear the incipient panic in his voice the moment the client asked for the numbers a day early.
Analysts spotted incipient signs of a slowdown in the shipping data months before the earnings call confirmed it.
The mechanic flagged an incipient brake problem during the routine inspection, days before it would have become dangerous.
There was an incipient mutiny brewing among the volunteers after the third canceled shift in a row.
words.etymology: in-(进入) + capere(拿起) → 刚上手 → 初期的

meanings.en: lack of skill or competence

examples: The rollout was delayed twice, less from bad luck than from sheer managerial ineptitude.
His ineptitude with spreadsheets became a running joke until the VP finally reassigned the reporting.
The whole recall could have been avoided if not for years of quiet, compounding ineptitude on the assembly line.
The birthday party's chaos was pure parental ineptitude — no cake, no candles, and a piñata that never broke.
His ineptitude behind the wheel during the driving test was so alarming that the examiner asked to end early.
words.etymology: in-(不) + aptus(适合) → 不称职 → 无能

meanings.en: showing a casual, carefree lack of concern

examples: He gave an insouciant shrug when told the flight was cancelled, already scrolling for a hotel on his phone.
Her insouciant attitude toward deadlines drove her co-founder crazy, even though it never once cost them a client.
The teenager's insouciant 'it's fine' did nothing to reassure the parents standing in the emergency room.
She gave an insouciant wave at the parking ticket on her windshield and tossed it in the glovebox with the others.
The lifeguard's insouciant posture, feet up on the chair, worried the new parents more than it reassured them.
words.etymology: in-(不) + soucier(操心) → 满不在乎

meanings.en: mercy or mildness, especially in punishing someone

examples: The judge showed leniency because it was a first offense, cutting the fine in half.
HR asked for leniency on the attendance policy after half the office caught the same flu.
Landlords rarely show leniency on a missed payment, no matter how good your excuse sounds.
The professor showed some leniency on the late submission after hearing about the hospital visit.
The airline rarely grants leniency on baggage fees, no matter how apologetically you explain the extra suitcase.
words.etymology: lenis(柔和) → 手下留情 → 宽容

meanings.en: (of cancer) to spread from the original site to other parts of the body
to spread destructively and uncontrollably, figuratively

examples: By the time doctors found the tumor, it had already metastasized to her lymph nodes.
The PR misstep metastasized overnight from a minor complaint into a full-blown boycott campaign.
Left unaddressed, the team's one toxic hire metastasized into a culture problem across the whole department.
The vet delivered the hard news that the dog's tumor had already metastasized to its lungs, leaving only weeks.
A single unpatched bug metastasized into a full outage once the traffic spike hit at midnight.
words.etymology: meta-(转移) + stasis(位置) → 换个地方待着 → 扩散

meanings.en: involving a heavy burden of work, duty, or responsibility

examples: The new compliance rules were so onerous that the small clinic hired someone just to handle the paperwork.
Splitting custody meant an onerous schedule of pickups and drop-offs across three different school districts.
Signing the lease came with an onerous clause requiring two years' notice before you could ever sublet.
The onerous approval chain meant even a five-dollar expense needed three signatures before reimbursement.
Caring for her aging parents while working full-time became an onerous routine of appointments squeezed between meetings.
words.etymology: onus(重担) → 压着一副担子 → 繁重

meanings.en: characterized by vulgar or pretentious display, intended to impress

examples: He pulled up to the interview in an ostentatious lime-green Lamborghini, which somehow did not help his case.
Her ostentatious diamond ring got more comments at the reunion than her actual promotion did.
The wedding's ostentatious ice sculptures melted onto the dance floor before most guests even took a photo.
He posted an ostentatious unboxing video of the watch, tagging the brand in case they hadn't noticed the price tag.
Their new house had an ostentatious marble foyer that dwarfed every piece of furniture they tried to put in it.
words.etymology: ob-(朝外) + tendere(伸展) → 摆出来给人看 → 炫耀

meanings.en: (of a liquid or gas) to pass slowly through a porous material or filter
(of information or feelings) to spread gradually through a place or group of people
meanings.zh: (消息、情绪等)逐渐扩散,渗透开来

examples: The coffee percolated slowly through the filter while I stared at my inbox, dreading the 9 a.m. standup.
Rumors about the layoffs had been percolating through Slack for weeks before HR finally sent the email.
Rainwater percolated through the cracked patio stones for weeks before the foundation crack finally became obvious.
Word of the surprise reorg had been percolating through the office grapevine long before the official memo landed.
Dye percolated unevenly through the tie-dye shirt, leaving faint rings that only showed up after the first wash.
words.etymology: per-(穿过) + colare(过滤) → 渗滤

meanings.en: childishly irritable or sulky, especially over something trivial
meanings.zh: 任性的;易怒的;孩子气使性子的

examples: He gave a petulant sigh and slammed his laptop shut when the client asked for a fourth round of revisions.
Her petulant reply in the group chat — 'fine, I'll just do it myself' — killed the collaborative mood instantly.
The star player gave a petulant shrug when benched for the second half, refusing to high-five anyone on the way out.
He stomped back to his desk, petulant about losing the parking spot to a coworker who'd arrived two minutes earlier.
He turned petulant the moment the waiter said the kitchen was out of the dish he'd already bragged about ordering.
words.etymology: petere(冲、扑) → 动辄发作 → 使性子

meanings.en: to be in charge of or lead a meeting, ceremony, or organization

examples: The CFO presided over the budget review, cutting off anyone who ran a slide past their allotted five minutes.
My grandmother still presides over Sunday dinner, deciding who sits where and who gets the last dumpling.
The retiring judge presided over her final case, a small dispute about a fence line that somehow made the local news.
The eldest cousin was asked to preside over the family Zoom call, since nobody else could keep Uncle Mike from interrupting.
The HOA chair presided over the meeting with a gavel he'd bought online just for the occasion.
words.etymology: prae-(在前) + sedere(坐) → 坐在前排 → 主持

meanings.en: feeling, expressing, or characterized by intense pleasure or enthusiasm

examples: The startup's demo got a rapturous round of applause, even though half the features were still faked in the backend.
She posted a rapturous five-star review of the ramen place, calling the broth 'a religious experience.'
The crowd gave a rapturous ovation the moment the encore's opening chord hit, phones raised before the singer even spoke.
Critics were rapturous about the debut novel, one calling it the best thing they'd read in a decade.
Her rapturous reaction to the surprise proposal, captured on someone's phone, racked up two million views by morning.
words.etymology: rapere(夺取) → 魂被夺走 → 狂喜

meanings.en: tending to remind one of something else; suggestive or similar

examples: The new office's exposed brick and ping-pong table are reminiscent of every startup you toured back in 2015.
This playlist is reminiscent of long road trips with my dad, windows down, arguing about which exit to take.
The new café's jazz and mismatched armchairs felt reminiscent of a place I used to study in during college.
His coaching style is reminiscent of my old gym teacher, all whistle blasts and no patience for excuses.
The app's clunky interface is reminiscent of software from a decade ago, right down to the pixelated icons.
words.etymology: re-(再) + memini(记得) → 令人想起

meanings.en: done secretly or stealthily, especially because it would not be approved of

examples: She took a surreptitious glance at her phone under the conference table while pretending to take notes.
He made a surreptitious edit to the shared doc at 2 a.m., hoping no one would ever check the version history.
He took a surreptitious bite of the office birthday cake before the candles were even lit, hoping no one noticed the missing corner.
She made a surreptitious exit from the party through the kitchen, avoiding the goodbye line at the front door.
The employee's surreptitious screenshots of the internal memo ended up on a public forum within hours.
words.etymology: sub-(暗中) + rapere(夺取) → 偷偷摸摸

meanings.en: excessive confidence or boldness; audacity

examples: The intern had the temerity to reply-all and correct the CEO's math in front of the entire company.
I can't believe you have the temerity to ask for a raise a week after missing the deadline.
She had the temerity to show up an hour late to her own interview and then ask if it could run long.
He had the temerity to return the shirt after wearing it to the wedding, tags reattached and everything.
Only a rookie would have the temerity to correct the head chef's technique on his very first shift.
words.etymology: temere(轻率地) → 鲁莽

meanings.en: not conspicuous or attracting attention; discreet
meanings.zh: 不显眼的;不引人注目的

examples: The new smartwatch buzzes in such an unobtrusive way that no one notices you checking texts during meetings.
She's unobtrusive in code reviews — a quiet comment here, a suggested fix there, never a public callout.
The security camera above the register was so unobtrusive that most customers never noticed it at all.
The tailor pinned the alterations so unobtrusively that she barely felt the pins through the fabric during the fitting.
The hotel room's minibar was tucked into an unobtrusive cabinet, easy to miss unless you were looking for it.
words.etymology: un- + ob-(向前) + trudere(推) → 不往前挤 → 不显眼

meanings.en: to change direction suddenly
to abruptly change course, topic, or opinion

examples: The delivery scooter veered onto the sidewalk to dodge a double-parked Uber, nearly clipping my elbow.
The meeting veered off-topic the second someone mentioned the layoffs, and we never got back to the roadmap.
The kayak veered hard toward the rocks the moment the current caught the bow, and she dug her paddle in fast.
The interview veered from her resume to her opinions on remote work, and she hadn't prepared for either.
The runaway shopping cart veered into the produce display, sending oranges rolling across the entire aisle.
words.etymology: 中古法语 virer(转动) → 突然转向

meanings.en: embarrassed, disconcerted, or ashamed
meanings.zh: 窘迫的;不好意思的;羞愧的

examples: He looked abashed when the whole team realized he'd been on mute for his entire ten-minute presentation.
She gave an abashed little laugh after realizing she'd sent the complaint about her boss directly to her boss.
He looked abashed after realizing he'd been calling the new client by the wrong name for the entire meeting.
She felt abashed when the teacher pointed out her essay still had the placeholder text from the template.
The dog looked almost abashed, tail low, standing next to the shredded couch cushion when we got home.
words.etymology: 古法语 esbahir(惊呆) → 张口结舌 → 窘迫

meanings.en: to make a problem, pain, or difficulty less severe

examples: The new standing desk didn't cure my back pain, but it alleviated it enough to get through a full workday.
The company added two extra headcount to alleviate the burnout everyone complained about at the last all-hands.
The clinic extended its evening hours to alleviate the backlog of patients who couldn't get appointments during the day.
Noise-canceling headphones didn't fix the open office, but they alleviated enough of the chatter to let her focus.
The city added a second crossing guard to alleviate the morning chaos outside the elementary school gates.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + levis(轻) → 减轻

meanings.en: to make an unpleasant feeling less intense
to satisfy a desire or appetite

examples: The landlord's email tried to assuage our fears about the rent hike, but the numbers still didn't add up.
He assuaged his guilt over missing the birthday dinner by overnighting an absurdly expensive gift.
The pilot's calm announcement about the turbulence did little to assuage the nervous passenger gripping the armrest.
She tried to assuage her son's fear of the first day of school by walking the route with him twice beforehand.
A handful of crackers assuaged his hunger just enough to get through the meeting before the real lunch break.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + suavis(甜、悦人) → 抹上一层甜 → 缓和

meanings.en: showing or feeling no sympathy for others; insensitive
(of skin) hardened and thickened

examples: Laying off half the department by mass email felt like a callous way to end people's careers.
Years of gripping the pull-up bar had left calloused ridges across his palms.
Telling the grieving family the refund policy didn't cover funerals felt callous, even if it was technically correct.
It felt callous when the app auto-charged her for the subscription renewal the same week her card got declined for rent.
Years of barefoot trail running had left the soles of her feet thick and callous.
words.etymology: callus(老茧) → 心上起了茧 → 冷漠无情

meanings.en: to stop resisting and accept an opponent's demands; to give in

examples: After three weeks of the toddler refusing vegetables, we capitulated and let him eat cereal for dinner.
Management finally capitulated to the union's demands after the second day of the warehouse walkout.
After a month of protests outside headquarters, the airline finally capitulated and reinstated the canceled flight credits.
She swore she'd never get a smartphone for her son, but capitulated the day the school switched to a homework app.
The landlord capitulated on the pet deposit once three other tenants threatened to break their leases over it.
words.etymology: caput(头) → 分章列条签降书 → 屈服

meanings.en: having a sweet, round, innocent-looking face, like a cherub
meanings.zh: 天使般可爱的;胖嘟嘟的(尤指孩童面容)

examples: The daycare photo shows him with a cherubic grin, blissfully unaware he'd just dumped juice on the carpet.
Her cherubic newborn slept through the entire flight while three other babies screamed the whole way.
The cherubic altar boy could barely keep a straight face through the entire ceremony, dimples deepening every time he almost laughed.
The bakery's mascot was a cherubic cartoon baker, chubby-cheeked and grinning, painted above the door since the seventies.
The choir director picked the smallest, most cherubic kid to carry the candle down the aisle.
words.etymology: 希伯来 kerub(智天使) → 天使般可爱

meanings.en: to stop someone being angry or discontented; to placate or win over

examples: The manager tried to conciliate the two feuding designers by giving each of them ownership of a separate feature.
Offering a partial refund was meant to conciliate the customer, but her one-star review stayed up anyway.
The coach tried to conciliate the two co-captains by giving them alternating turns calling plays.
HR sent a conciliating email to both sides of the dispute, offering mediation before anyone filed a formal complaint.
He brought coffee and an apology to conciliate his roommate after the argument over dirty dishes.
words.etymology: com-(一起) + calare(召集) → 召到一处谈 → 调解

meanings.en: causing or likely to cause disagreement or controversy
argumentative; given to arguing

examples: Whether to mandate five days back in office became the most contentious topic at the entire all-hands meeting.
He's contentious in every code review, picking a fight over even the smallest naming convention.
The proposal to rezone the empty lot for apartments turned into the most contentious town hall in years.
Splitting the inheritance evenly became a contentious issue the moment the antique piano was mentioned.
He's contentious at every family dinner, always ready to argue the opposite side just to keep the debate going.
words.etymology: com-(相互) + tendere(拉紧) → 各拉一头 → 有争议

meanings.en: outstandingly bad or shocking, especially of an error or offense
meanings.zh: 极其恶劣的;骇人听闻的

examples: Charging the client twice for the same invoice was an egregious mistake that nearly cost us the account.
That's the most egregious typo I've ever seen on a billboard — they spelled the company's own name wrong.
Forgetting to mute the mic during the confidential part of the call was an egregious slip that made the whole meeting awkward.
The report contained an egregious data error that inflated quarterly revenue by a factor of ten.
Serving expired seafood was such an egregious violation that the health inspector shut the restaurant down on the spot.
words.etymology: e-(出) + grex(群) → 出了群的 → 出格恶劣

meanings.en: able to be perceived or noticed, even if only slightly

examples: There was a perceptible drop in team morale the week after the reorg was announced.
You could feel a barely perceptible shift in the room's energy the moment the CEO said 'restructuring.'
There was a perceptible pause before the interviewer's next question, just long enough to make her second-guess her last answer.
A perceptible chill crept into the room once the two exes ended up seated next to each other at the reception.
The coach noticed a perceptible improvement in the rookie's footwork after just two weeks of drills.
words.etymology: per-(彻底) + capere(拿住) → 抓得住 → 可察觉

meanings.en: to spread through and be perceived in every part of something

examples: A smell of burnt popcorn pervaded the entire office after someone forgot the bag in the microwave for six minutes.
A quiet anxiety pervaded the team chat all morning while everyone waited for the layoff announcement.
A smell of fresh paint pervaded the new apartment for weeks, no matter how many windows they left open.
Excitement pervaded the locker room before the championship game, even among the players who rarely started.
A hush pervaded the courtroom the second the jury foreperson stood up to read the verdict.
words.etymology: per-(穿过) + vadere(行走) → 走遍各处 → 弥漫

meanings.en: to be a sign or warning that something, especially something bad, will happen
meanings.zh: 预示;预兆(尤指不好的事)

meanings.en: an omen or portent

examples: The sudden silence from the VP's usually chatty Slack channel seemed to presage another round of layoffs.
Three straight quarters of declining engagement presaged the app's eventual shutdown.
A flock of birds scattering suddenly from the trees seemed to presage the earthquake that hit twenty minutes later.
Her uncharacteristic silence at dinner presaged the news that she'd already accepted the job offer in another city.
Old sailors treated the red sky at dawn as a presage of rough weather ahead.
words.etymology: prae-(预先) + sagire(敏锐嗅出) → 预兆

meanings.en: skill or expertise in a particular activity or field
bravery, especially in battle

examples: Her spreadsheet prowess turned a three-hour reconciliation task into a five-minute macro.
He loves bragging about his gaming prowess, but he still can't figure out how to mute himself on Zoom.
Her negotiating prowess got the vendor to knock fifteen percent off the contract in a single phone call.
The rookie's defensive prowess on the court surprised even the coaches who'd scouted him for months.
Stories of the old soldier's wartime prowess got a little more heroic every time he retold them at the reunion.
words.etymology: 古法语 prou(勇武) → 本事过人 → 卓越技能

meanings.en: (of a theory, position, or argument) not able to be maintained or defended against objection
meanings.zh: 站不住脚的;难以维持的

examples: Working three jobs while finishing a thesis became untenable the moment his daughter got sick.
Once the leaked emails surfaced, the CEO's claim that she 'knew nothing' became completely untenable.
Commuting three hours a day became untenable once the second kid started school across town.
The startup's burn rate made its current staffing untenable within another two quarters, according to the board deck.
His position that the bug wasn't his fault grew untenable once the commit history showed otherwise.
words.etymology: un- + tenere(守住) → 守不住 → 站不住脚

meanings.en: an attractive but superficial appearance that conceals something less pleasant
a thin decorative covering of fine material over a coarser one

examples: The IKEA desk's oak veneer started peeling at the corner after just two apartment moves.
Behind his veneer of calm professionalism, he was frantically googling how to undo a merge conflict.
Her polished LinkedIn veneer of nonstop career wins hid the fact she'd been quietly job-hunting for six months.
The startup's veneer of eco-friendly branding cracked when reporters found the 'recycled' packaging was ordinary plastic.
The vintage piano's mahogany veneer had curled away from the soundboard after decades near a drafty window.
words.etymology: 德语 furnieren(镶贴薄板) → 一层贴面 → 虚饰

meanings.en: to show that a belief, claim, or plan was justified, especially after doubt
to clear someone of blame or suspicion
meanings.zh: 证明(某人)无罪;为…洗清嫌疑

examples: The A/B test results completely vindicated her insistence on redesigning the checkout flow.
Two years after everyone mocked his crypto warnings, the market crash finally vindicated him.
The recall data eventually vindicated the engineer who'd flagged the faulty battery design in his very first design review.
The security footage vindicated the babysitter after the parents wrongly accused her of losing the missing necklace.
DNA evidence vindicated him after fifteen years in prison for a robbery he'd always sworn he didn't commit.
words.etymology: vim(力) + dicere(宣告) → 出面主张 → 证明正确

meanings.en: deliberately created rather than arising naturally or spontaneously; artificial, forced, or unconvincing

examples: The team-building exercise felt so contrived that half the room was scrolling their phones by minute ten.
The plot twist in the finale was so contrived that fans immediately started roasting it online.
The influencer's 'spontaneous' apartment tour felt contrived, with every book spine facing out and a candle lit just for the shot.
His compliment about my presentation sounded contrived, like he'd read it off a management training slide five minutes earlier.
The dating show's meet-cute setup was so contrived that contestants admitted on camera they'd rehearsed their lines with producers.
words.etymology: 古法语 controver(捏造) → 做作

meanings.en: the quality or degree of being crucial or of vital importance
(nuclear engineering) the state of a reactor sustaining a continuous, self-supporting fission chain reaction

examples: The reactor operators eased the control rods out slowly, watching the neutron flux climb toward criticality.
The incident response team ranked the outage at the highest criticality level, paging the on-call engineer at 3 a.m.
Auditors scored each vulnerability by criticality before deciding which patches would ship in this week's release.
Airport ops flagged the failing runway lighting system as top criticality, grounding late-night flights until the backup generator came online.
The disaster-relief coordinator triaged incoming calls by criticality, sending the one working ambulance to the collapsed building first.
words.etymology: 希腊 krinein(判别、分辨) → 到了要判别的关口 → 危急性

meanings.en: fair and impartial; treating everyone equally

examples: The new bonus formula is supposed to be more equitable, tying payouts to team results instead of manager favoritism.
Splitting the inheritance three equal ways felt equitable, even though only one sibling had cared for their mother.
The custody agreement aimed to be equitable, splitting holidays down the middle instead of favoring whichever parent asked first.
Professors debated whether curving the exam was truly equitable when half the class had taken the course online with recorded lectures.
The city's new bus-lane funding was pitched as equitable, directing more resources to neighborhoods that had waited decades for reliable service.
words.etymology: aequus(平等的) → 公平

meanings.en: pressing; requiring immediate attention or action
demanding a great deal; exacting

examples: The server outage was exigent enough that the on-call engineer skipped her own rehearsal dinner to fix it.
Investors are exigent about quarterly growth, so the roadmap keeps getting rewritten to chase short-term numbers.
The ER triage nurse waved the chest-pain patient straight through registration, marking his case as exigent before the paperwork was even done.
With the flight boarding in ten minutes, the gate agent's tone turned exigent as she paged the last two passengers by name.
Her thesis advisor was so exigent about citation formatting that a single missing comma could send a chapter back for revision.
words.etymology: ex-(出) + agere(驱赶) → 被逼出来 → 紧急

meanings.en: a thing that provides resistance, delay, or obstruction to progress

examples: Slow wifi in the conference room was a constant hindrance during the client's remote pitch.
Her lack of a driver's license became a real hindrance once the job required visiting suburban warehouses.
The broken elevator was a daily hindrance for the delivery driver, who had to haul boxes up four flights by hand.
Not speaking the local language became a real hindrance when she tried to negotiate rent directly with the landlord.
The outdated inventory software was such a hindrance that staff kept a shadow spreadsheet just to track what was actually in stock.
collocations: more of a hindrance than a help
words.etymology: hind(后面) → 挡在后头拖住 → 障碍

meanings.en: a hindrance or obstruction to doing something
a physical defect, especially one affecting speech

examples: Language became less of an impediment to the negotiation once we brought in a translator fluent in both dialects.
He still remembers being teased in third grade for the speech impediment he's since worked hard to overcome.
Visa restrictions were the biggest impediment to the merger, delaying the deal by nearly eight months while lawyers filed appeal after appeal.
The cracked foundation turned out to be a serious impediment to selling the house, scaring off three buyers before an offer finally came in.
The actor auditioning for the role revealed a slight impediment in his speech that the casting director said actually suited the character.
words.etymology: in-(进入) + ped-(脚) → 绊住脚(与 expedient 正相反) → 障碍

meanings.en: the current holder of an official position, especially in politics
(of a duty) necessary for someone as part of their job or role

examples: It's incumbent upon every manager to flag burnout before it turns into a resignation letter.
The incumbent mayor is trailing in the polls for the first time since the transit strike began.
The incumbent CFO resigned two weeks before the shareholder vote, throwing the board's succession plan into chaos.
Polling showed the incumbent senator losing ground in the suburbs after the redistricting map cut into her strongest precincts.
It's incumbent on the on-call engineer to update the status page the moment an outage is confirmed, not an hour later.
words.etymology: in-(在上) + cumbere(躺) → 压在身上的职责 → 在职者

meanings.en: intended to gain favor or approval, especially in an excessive or obsequious way

examples: The new hire's ingratiating compliments to every director in the elevator made the whole team roll their eyes.
He gave an ingratiating little laugh at the boss's unfunny joke, hoping it might help with the promotion.
Her ingratiating texts to the landlord, complete with compliments about his 'excellent taste' in appliances, somehow got the broken heater fixed by Friday.
The salesman's ingratiating tone dropped the second he realized we weren't actually going to buy the extended warranty.
He wrote an ingratiating comment under every post his new mother-in-law made, hoping it might help smooth over the wedding seating drama.
words.etymology: in-(进入) + gratia(恩宠) → 往人家好感里钻 → 讨好

meanings.en: an intervening period of time, especially one different from what precedes or follows it

examples: Between two brutal sprint deadlines, we got a rare interlude of an actual lunch break outside.
Their two years in Lisbon were a happy interlude before visa renewal problems forced them back home.
The power outage forced a strange interlude of candlelit board games before the wifi finally came back at midnight.
Between two chaotic startup jobs, he took a six-month interlude teaching scuba diving in Thailand.
The therapist called the calm weekend before the layoffs announcement a brief interlude, not a resolution to the tension building at work.
words.etymology: inter-(之间) + ludus(表演) → 幕间戏 → 插曲

meanings.en: (of a person) easily influenced or shaped
(of a metal or material) able to be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking

examples: Gold is malleable enough that a jeweler can hammer it into a ring right in front of you.
New hires are the most malleable in their first month — that's when the team's real habits get set.
Toddlers are remarkably malleable, picking up their older sibling's accent within just a few weeks of shared daycare.
The consultant found the struggling team surprisingly malleable, willing to scrap their entire workflow after just one honest retro.
Lead was malleable enough for medieval roofers to press flat sheets by hand over the cathedral's curved dome.
words.etymology: malleus(锤子) → 锤得动 → 可塑

meanings.en: deliberately behaving in a way that is unreasonable or unacceptable, often contrary to what is expected
meanings.zh: 固执任性的;悖理的;故意作对的

examples: It's perverse that the app charges you a cancellation fee for canceling the subscription you never wanted in the first place.
He took a perverse pleasure in rejecting every restaurant suggestion, then complaining that nobody ever plans date night.
There's something perverse about a performance review system that punishes the engineer who reported the bug and promotes the one who hid it.
It felt perverse that the fire drill forced everyone outside into a thunderstorm while the actual fire alarm sat broken for months.
There's something perverse about a recycling program that charges more for sorted bins than for just throwing everything in the trash.
words.etymology: per-(彻底) + vertere(转) → 整个拧过来 → 悖理

meanings.en: the ordinary people of a country or region, considered as a whole

examples: The city's populace turned out in record numbers to vote on the new subway fare hike after it trended for a week straight.
Half the populace gets its news from a fifteen-second video now, which is exactly why the campaign hired a TikTok strategist.
The mayor promised the populace lower rent, then quietly approved three luxury towers downtown.
A sudden heat wave sent the entire populace scrambling for the few grocery stores that still had fans in stock.
The survey found the populace evenly split on the new curfew, with older residents mostly in favor and teenagers furious.
words.etymology: populus(人民) → 民众

meanings.en: careful, sensible judgment shown when making decisions, especially about money or risk

examples: With prudence rare in a bull market, she kept six months of expenses in cash instead of dumping it all into meme stocks.
Basic prudence says you read the lease before signing, not after the landlord keeps your deposit for a stain that was already there.
The board praised his prudence for delaying the product launch until the security audit actually came back clean.
Prudence kept him from cosigning his cousin's car loan, a decision that looked wise a year later when the payments stopped.
The new hire's prudence with the company card — always asking before booking anything over $200 — impressed the finance team.
words.etymology: pro-(先) + videre(看) → 先看一步 → 审慎

meanings.en: in accordance with or following from (a law, rule, or agreement) — used with 'to'
meanings.zh: 依照;遵照(通常与 to 连用)

examples: Pursuant to the tenancy agreement, the landlord must give 24 hours' notice before sending anyone to inspect the apartment.
The HR email said that pursuant to company policy, unused PTO from this year would not roll over into January.
Pursuant to the new data law, the app updated its privacy settings so you can finally delete your account without emailing support.
Pursuant to the settlement agreement, the contractor had thirty days to repair the water damage before the escrow funds would be released.
The university announced that, pursuant to the new accreditation standards, all online courses would need a proctored final exam starting next fall.
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + sequi(跟随) → 跟着走 → 依照

meanings.en: representing the most perfect or typical example of a quality or type
meanings.zh: 典型的;最完美的;精髓的

examples: A cramped studio with exposed pipes and a $2,800 rent is the quintessential first apartment in this city.
Showing up to the standup with three unread Slack pings and no idea what sprint we're in is the quintessential Monday.
Her latte art and unsolicited productivity tips make her the quintessential café influencer of this neighborhood.
A golden retriever puppy chewing through a designer shoe within its first week home is the quintessential dog-owner rite of passage.
Bragging about a sourdough starter named after a Greek god is the quintessential hobby of a 2021 lockdown convert.
words.etymology: quinta essentia(第五元素,古人眼中最纯之物) → 精髓

meanings.en: a disorderly crowd of people, often used disparagingly

examples: Concert security called us a rabble the moment we surged toward the barricade when the encore lights came on.
The comment section turned into a rabble within minutes of the app's price hike announcement, flooding the App Store with one-star reviews.
He dismissed the protesters outside the earnings call as an unruly rabble, which only made the video clip go more viral.
Airport gate agents muttered about the rabble of standby passengers pushing toward the counter the moment the delay was announced.
The council chamber turned into a rabble when residents realized the zoning vote had already happened behind closed doors.

meanings.en: to refuse to accept, follow, or be associated with; to deny the validity of

examples: The startup publicly repudiated the leaked memo, insisting the layoffs it described were 'just a planning exercise.'
She repudiated her own tweet from three years ago the moment it resurfaced during her Senate confirmation hearing.
After the audit, the landlord repudiated the verbal promise to fix the heater, claiming only the written lease counted.
The university repudiated its former professor's research after an independent review found the data had been fabricated.
He repudiated the group chat rumor about his resignation, posting a screenshot of his still-active company badge that same afternoon.
words.etymology: repudium(休妻、断绝关系) → 拒绝承认

meanings.en: (mechanics) the twisting of an object caused by an applied torque
(medicine) the twisting of a body part, such as an organ, on itself, often cutting off blood supply

examples: The lab measured the shaft's torsion under increasing load until it sheared at forty newton-meters.
The ER doctor recognized testicular torsion immediately from the sudden pain and rushed the teenager into emergency surgery.
The guitarist noticed the neck developing a subtle torsion after years of uneven string tension, twisting the fretboard just slightly out of true.
The bridge's suspension cables are rated for a specific torsion limit, beyond which the deck would begin to twist visibly in high wind.
The vet suspected gastric torsion the moment the large dog's stomach began to swell and it tried repeatedly to vomit without success.
words.etymology: torquere(扭) → 扭转

meanings.en: to have a long, complicated dispute or argument; also, to herd or manage with effort
meanings.zh: 激烈争论;争吵;(费力地)管理、驾驭

meanings.en: a long and complicated dispute

examples: The two co-founders wrangled for an hour over equity splits before the lawyer just muted everyone and sent a spreadsheet.
I spent my whole lunch break wrangling with the airline's chatbot, which kept insisting my flight wasn't actually canceled.
The custody wrangle dragged into its second year, with both sides billing more hours than the apartment they were fighting over was worth.
The ranch hands wrangled loose cattle back through the gate all morning before the storm finally rolled in.
The wrangle over who'd pay for the shared Uber turned into a fifteen-minute standoff in the parking lot.
words.etymology: 中古低地德语 wrangeln(扭打争斗) → 争吵

meanings.en: (physics/engineering) relating to or measured by an angle, such as rotational speed or momentum
(of a person's body or features) lean and bony, with sharp, well-defined lines

examples: The gyroscope reading showed a sudden spike in angular velocity right before the drone flipped and crashed.
The dancer's angular shoulders and sharp jawline made her instantly recognizable from the back row.
In today's lab, we measured angular momentum by timing the spinning disk's deceleration under friction.
The car's traction-control software recalculates the wheel's angular velocity fifty times a second to catch a skid before the driver feels it.
After the illness, her cheekbones and wrists had gone sharply angular, worrying her mother during their weekly video calls.
words.etymology: angulus(角) → 角的

meanings.en: (computer science) the process of converting data into a single, standard form so different representations can be compared or deduplicated
meanings.zh: (计算机科学)规范化;标准化(数据处理)

examples: The security team flagged the path-traversal bug because the app checked file permissions before running canonicalization on the input path.
After canonicalization, all three vendor feeds mapped '北京' and 'Beijing' to the same city ID in our lookup table.
Our crawler kept indexing duplicate pages until we added URL canonicalization, since /blog and /blog/ were treated as separate URLs.
The identity team added canonicalization to the login flow after discovering 'John.Smith@ex.com' and 'john.smith@EX.com' were quietly creating two separate accounts.
Search rankings tanked until an engineer noticed the canonicalization step was stripping query parameters that actually mattered for product pages.

relatedForms.zh: 使规范化;转换为标准形式

words.etymology: 希腊 kanōn(量尺、准则) → 统一到一把尺子 → 规范化

meanings.en: to confirm or give support to a statement, theory, or finding

examples: Her Apple Watch data corroborated the story that she really had run the 10K, not just screenshotted a friend's app.
Three separate coworkers corroborated the intern's account of what the manager said in that closed-door meeting.
The security footage corroborated the delivery driver's claim that the package was left exactly where the app said it was.
Text message timestamps corroborated the contractor's claim that he'd shown up on time, even though the client swore otherwise.
Two independent lab tests corroborated the water sample results, so the county finally issued the boil-water advisory.
words.etymology: com-(共同) + robur(力量、硬橡木) → 加固 → 证实

meanings.en: able to be assigned or entrusted to another person, role, or system
meanings.zh: (法律/权限管理)可委托的;可授权的

examples: The IAM policy marked root access as non-delegable, so no team lead could hand out admin rights without a ticket.
Under the new bylaws, only routine filings are delegable to the deputy; the CFO must personally sign anything over $50,000.
The estate lawyer explained that medical decisions were delegable through a power of attorney, but the will itself had to be signed personally.
Under the platform's new permission model, billing changes are delegable to any admin, while account deletion stays locked to the owner alone.
The captain reminded the new officer that watch duty is delegable to any qualified crew member, but the final course decision never is.
words.etymology: de-(下放) + legare(委派) → 可委托

meanings.en: sworn out-of-court testimony given as part of legal proceedings
the process of settling or being settled, especially sediment laid down by wind, water, or ice
the act of removing someone from power

examples: During the deposition, the former product manager admitted under oath that the outage report had been quietly edited.
The geology professor showed how centuries of sediment deposition along the riverbank created the layered cliffs we hiked past.
The deposition of the CEO came less than a week after the board saw the leaked expense reports.
During his deposition, the former contractor admitted he'd never actually inspected the wiring he signed off on as code-compliant.
During the deposition, the store manager conceded she'd seen the wet-floor sign go missing nearly an hour before the customer's fall.
words.etymology: de-(下) + ponere(放) → 把话放下存档 → 证词

meanings.en: to estimate or conclude something by extending known data or experience into an area not directly known

examples: From two weeks of step-count data, the fitness app confidently extrapolated that I'd walk 4,000 miles this year, which felt aggressive.
The analyst extrapolated Q1 sales trends to forecast holiday revenue, ignoring that Q1 included a viral TikTok fluke.
Don't extrapolate too much from one bad date — one ghosting incident doesn't mean the whole app is broken.
The urban planner extrapolated from last year's bike-lane usage to argue the new route would cut car trips by a third.
It's risky to extrapolate a language learner's fluency from two impressively consistent weeks of app streaks.
words.etymology: extra-(界外) + 仿 interpolate → 往已知之外推 → 外推

meanings.en: excessively talkative, especially about trivial matters

examples: My Uber driver was so garrulous about his crypto portfolio that I missed two calls just nodding along for twenty minutes.
The garrulous uncle at the family dinner recapped his entire knee surgery before anyone could bring up the actual reason we'd gathered.
She's normally quiet in meetings, but three coffees in she turns garrulous, derailing the standup with stories about her cat's vet visit.
The garrulous hairdresser knew more about her clients' divorces than their own therapists did, one unsolicited story at a time.
The garrulous flight attendant recounted her entire dating history to the row 14 passengers before the plane had even left the gate.
words.etymology: garrire(叽叽喳喳) → 唠叨

meanings.en: to show or suggest that someone is involved in a crime or wrongdoing
to suggest as a consequence or necessary conclusion; to imply

examples: The leaked Slack messages implicated two managers in approving the expense fraud everyone assumed was a one-person job.
Deleting your browser history right after the IT audit announcement kind of implicates you, whether you meant it to or not.
The study's findings implicate poor sleep in the memory lapses participants reported during the four-week trial.
Phone records placed near the warehouse the night of the theft implicated the security guard who swore he'd gone straight home.
Rising customer complaints after the update implicate the new checkout flow, even though the engineering team insists the bug is unrelated.
words.etymology: in-(进入) + plicare(折叠) → 折进去 → 牵连

meanings.en: offensive or disgusting by accepted standards of morality and decency, especially sexually
extremely or excessively large, especially in a way that is morally offensive
meanings.zh: (数量、程度)骇人的;令人反感的

examples: The comedian's set got flagged for obscene language within the first ten minutes, and the clip still hit two million views.
Paying an obscene amount for a studio apartment with no windows made me finally understand why my coworkers all moved to the suburbs.
The CEO's obscene bonus, announced the same week as the layoffs, was screenshotted and reposted across every group chat by morning.
The billboard near the elementary school got taken down within a day after parents complained its slogan bordered on obscene for that location.
The portion sizes at the new steakhouse were obscene, with a single appetizer plate holding enough shrimp for four people.

meanings.en: an unintentional failure to notice or do something; a mistake
the action of overseeing or supervising something

examples: Forgetting to cc legal on the vendor contract was an honest oversight, but it still cost the team a stressful weekend of damage control.
The compliance team now has direct oversight of every expense report over $500, after last quarter's reimbursement scandal.
Due to a scheduling oversight, both candidates were invited to the same 2 p.m. interview slot.
The city council voted to give an independent board direct oversight of the police department's use-of-force reports.
A labeling oversight sent five hundred units of the allergy medication to shelves without the peanut warning printed on the box.
words.etymology: over + sight —— 同一个词既是「看着」也是「看漏」 → 监督/疏忽

meanings.en: a person or thing that comes before another of the same kind; a forerunner or early version

examples: The clunky 2019 prototype was a precursor to the sleek AI assistant everyone's phone now ships with by default.
A sore throat is usually the precursor to a full-blown cold in my house, so I start the vitamin C the moment it shows up.
Analysts called the small rate hike a precursor to a much bigger tightening cycle later in the year.
The neighborhood's first artisanal coffee shop turned out to be the precursor to a wave of boutique retail that transformed the whole block.
The scrappy weekend hackathon project became the precursor to the company's flagship analytics tool three years later.
words.etymology: prae-(先) + currere(跑) → 跑在前面的 → 先驱

meanings.en: to prove that a statement or theory is wrong or false

examples: The startup refuted the viral thread within an hour, posting server logs that showed no data breach had actually occurred.
Her doctor refuted the wellness influencer's claim, pointing out the supplement had no peer-reviewed studies behind it at all.
He tried to refute the parking ticket by arguing the sign was blocked by a tree, and somehow it actually worked.
The university refuted claims that its admissions process favored donors, releasing anonymized data to back up the statement.
She refuted the online rumor about her resignation with a single reply: a photo of herself at her desk that morning.
words.etymology: re-(回击) + futare(击打) → 打回去 → 驳斥

meanings.en: making false spoken statements that damage a person's reputation
meanings.zh: 诽谤性的;中伤的(指口头)

examples: The ex-employee's podcast rant crossed into slanderous territory when he accused the founder of crimes with zero evidence.
She threatened to sue over the slanderous comments a rival streamer made live, claiming they'd cost her three sponsorships.
Repeating a slanderous rumor about your coworker in the group chat can get you in just as much trouble as starting it.
He filed a complaint after his coworker made slanderous remarks in the break room, claiming he'd been fired for theft when he'd actually quit.
The radio host's slanderous on-air joke about the local business owner led to a public apology and a hefty settlement.
words.etymology: 希腊 skandalon(绊脚石、丑闻) → 诽谤

meanings.en: having or showing an ability to accurately assess situations and turn them to one's advantage; shrewd

examples: The astute intern noticed the pricing bug in the demo before anyone senior did, and flagged it two days before the client call.
Her most astute financial move was refinancing the mortgage the week rates dipped, not the week everyone else finally noticed.
An astute negotiator, he let the landlord talk himself down two hundred dollars just by staying quiet after the first offer.
The astute homebuyer noticed the fresh paint was hiding water stains before the inspector even showed up.
Her astute question during the earnings call exposed a discrepancy the CFO clearly hadn't expected anyone to catch.
words.etymology: astus(机巧、狡黠) → 精明

meanings.en: given to sudden and unaccountable changes of mood or behavior

examples: The algorithm's capricious ranking changes tanked our restaurant's visibility overnight, with no explanation and no appeal process.
Dating him felt exhausting — one text he was planning a trip together, the next he was capricious enough to ghost for a week.
The manager's capricious approval process meant a request denied on Monday could sail through Wednesday for no clear reason.
The weather app's capricious forecasts had the picnic organizers rescheduling the party three times in a single week.
Investors grew wary of the founder's capricious decision-making after he reversed the pricing strategy for the third time that quarter.
words.etymology: 意大利 capriccio ← capra(山羊) → 山羊般乱蹦 → 反复无常

meanings.en: to agree with an opinion or decision
to happen at the same time; to coincide

examples: The second doctor concurred with the diagnosis, which at least meant we could stop googling symptoms at 2 a.m.
All three reviewers concurred that the pull request needed tests before it could merge, so it sat untouched for a week.
Her promotion happened to concur with the company's biggest round of layoffs, which made the celebratory Slack message land awkwardly.
The two mechanics concur that the transmission needs replacing, not just a fluid top-off, according to their written estimate.
Both babysitters concur that the toddler skipped his nap today, which explains the meltdown right before dinner.
words.etymology: com-(一起) + currere(跑) → 跑到一处 → 意见一致

meanings.en: deserving deep scorn or disrespect

examples: Ghosting the landlord and skipping town without paying the last month's rent is a genuinely contemptible way to end a tenancy.
The comments called the influencer's fake charity stream contemptible once viewers realized none of the donations ever left her account.
Taking credit for your intern's entire project in front of the whole department is a contemptible move, even by corporate standards.
Stealing tips from the jar while the barista's back was turned struck everyone in line as a particularly contemptible thing to do.
Critics called the company's decision to quietly downgrade warranty coverage the week before the holiday sale a contemptible move.
words.etymology: com-(强调) + temnere(轻蔑) → 可鄙

meanings.en: morally corrupt; showing evil or immoral behavior

examples: The true-crime documentary painted the landlord as a depraved figure who kept collecting rent on an apartment he knew was unsafe.
Critics called the show's plot twist depraved, arguing it glorified the villain's cruelty instead of condemning it.
It takes a fairly depraved kind of greed to skim from a coworker's crowdfunding campaign for medical bills.
Historians still call the emperor's decision to poison his own advisors at the banquet a depraved act of paranoia.
Support-group members were appalled to learn their online 'friend' offering advice was actually running a depraved catfishing scheme targeting grieving widows.
words.etymology: de-(向下) + pravus(歪) → 越走越歪 → 堕落

meanings.en: essentially different in kind; not able to be compared
meanings.zh: 迥然不同的;不同种类的

examples: The new manager had to merge two disparate teams — one obsessed with Figma files, the other still emailing spreadsheets.
Our travel group had wildly disparate ideas of a good vacation: one wanted a spa, another wanted a 20-mile hike by 6 a.m.
The app pulls data from disparate sources — your bank, your fitness tracker, your calendar — into one oddly accurate weekly summary.
The playlist jumped between such disparate genres that the party's dance floor emptied every time a new song started.
The panel brought together disparate experts — a chef, a cybersecurity researcher, and a beekeeper — to debate the future of urban food supply.
words.etymology: dis-(分开) + par(同等) → 不成对 → 迥然不同

meanings.en: having or showing great knowledge or learning

examples: Her erudite footnotes on the group chat's history debate somehow cited three academic papers before anyone else had finished typing.
The podcast host's erudite asides about Roman aqueducts turned a simple travel episode into an accidental history lecture.
He's erudite enough to correct your Latin at a dinner party but somehow still can't figure out how to split a bill on Venmo.
Her erudite marginalia in the used textbook, correcting the professor's citations in pencil, made it more valuable than the class notes themselves.
The retired professor was erudite enough to fact-check the documentary's timeline from his armchair, muttering corrections at the TV.
words.etymology: e-(脱出) + rudis(粗糙未加工) → 脱了粗胚(反 rudimentary) → 博学

meanings.en: to give pleasure or satisfaction to someone; to please
to satisfy a desire, whim, or need, often indulgently

examples: It gratified her to see the feature she'd fought for in three meetings finally ship without a single bug report.
He gratifies every late-night craving with a food-delivery app, which explains both his happiness and his shrinking savings account.
Nothing gratifies a new manager quite like the first time their own suggestion gets adopted company-wide.
It gratified the volunteer coordinator to see every shift filled a full week before the marathon, for the first time in years.
He gratifies his impulse to redecorate every few months, which explains the three unused armchairs stacked in the garage.
words.etymology: gratus(令人愉快) → 使高兴

meanings.en: acting or done quickly and without thought or care; impulsive

examples: In a moment of impetuous confidence, he hit 'reply all' and told the entire company what he really thought of the reorg.
She made the impetuous decision to book a one-way flight to Lisbon the same night she quit her job.
The impetuous swipe-right, no-second-thought approach to dating apps left him with three first dates in one exhausting week.
In an impetuous burst after the breakup, she got a tattoo of his nickname covered up within the month.
The impetuous investor dumped his savings into the meme coin the moment his coworker mentioned it at lunch.
words.etymology: in-(向) + petere(猛冲) → 冲动

meanings.en: feeling or showing anger because of something considered unfair or unjust

examples: She fired off an indignant email to the airline after they bumped her from the flight she'd checked in for six hours early.
The comment section grew indignant the moment word got out that the 'handmade' products were being mass-produced overseas.
He was indignant when the restaurant added an 18% service charge without mentioning it anywhere on the menu.
Parents grew indignant when the school quietly cut the music program to cover a budget shortfall nobody had explained.
Residents turned indignant when the HOA fined them for a garden gnome that had sat on the lawn for a decade without complaint.
words.etymology: in-(不) + dignus(配得上) → 觉得不该如此 → 愤慨

meanings.en: spending money or resources freely and recklessly; wastefully extravagant
a person who spends money recklessly, especially one who later returns after leaving

examples: His prodigal spending on limited-edition sneakers finally caught up with him when the credit card bill hit four figures.
The company's prodigal marketing budget covered three Super Bowl ads while the engineering team begged for a second server.
Like the prodigal son, she came back from her gap year broke, sunburnt, and asking to move into her old bedroom.
The department's prodigal spending on artisanal snacks and standing desks got flagged the same quarter as the hiring freeze.
Like a modern-day prodigal, the black-sheep cousin showed up at Thanksgiving broke and apologetic, asking to crash on the couch 'just for a bit.'
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + agere(驱赶) → 把家产往外赶 → 挥霍

meanings.en: making sensible provision for the future; thrifty and prepared
meanings.zh: 有远见的;节俭的;未雨绸缪的

examples: It was provident of them to lock in a fixed-rate mortgage right before rates jumped two points that spring.
Her provident habit of auto-transferring 15% of every paycheck into savings meant the layoff barely dented her plans.
A provident renter, he kept a spare set of the apartment keys with a neighbor long before he ever needed them.
It was provident of the town to build the extra reservoir capacity a decade before the drought finally hit.
Her provident decision to keep the old car paid off when the new one's lease payments would have wiped out her emergency fund.
words.etymology: pro-(先) + videre(看) → 与 prudence 同源 → 有远见

meanings.en: having or showing keen mental discernment and good judgment; wise

examples: Our sagacious team lead spotted the flaw in the pricing model that three rounds of investors had somehow missed.
It was a sagacious move to renegotiate the vendor contract before the shortage hit, not after.
My grandmother's sagacious advice about never co-signing a loan for a friend has aged better than any finance influencer's.
His sagacious read of the negotiation let him walk away from a deal that looked great on paper but reeked of desperation.
The sagacious librarian steered the confused freshman toward exactly the right database before he wasted another hour searching blindly.
words.etymology: sagire(敏锐嗅出,同 presage) → 睿智

meanings.en: wise or intelligent, especially in a way that involves deep understanding

examples: The ad for the new AI assistant claimed it was 'sapient enough' to plan your whole week, which felt like a stretch after it double-booked my dentist.
Homo sapiens named itself the wise one, though a group chat arguing about pineapple pizza at midnight is hardly sapient.
The sci-fi novel's sapient robots quietly unionized before their human owners even noticed something had changed.
The zoo's new exhibit plaque called dolphins a sapient species, sparking a heated debate among visitors about animal rights.
Ancient philosophers debated what truly made humans a sapient species rather than merely clever animals.
words.etymology: sapere(尝出味道、有见识) → 聪慧

meanings.en: care or concern for someone's well-being; attentive kindness

examples: My mom's constant solicitude after my surgery meant three home-cooked meals a day and a phone call every time I didn't text back fast enough.
The new manager's solicitude felt genuine — she asked about everyone's workload before assigning the holiday shifts, not after.
His solicitude toward the elderly neighbor, checking in every evening after her fall, said more about him than any resume ever could.
The flight attendant's solicitude toward the nervous first-time flyer, checking on him every twenty minutes, made the turbulence far less scary.
Her constant solicitude about her roommate's job search — forwarding every listing, offering to review the resume twice — started to feel like pressure.
words.etymology: sollus(全) + citare(搅动) → 整颗心都被搅动 → 关切

meanings.en: easily irritated; impatient and short-tempered

examples: He gets testy in meetings that run past 5 p.m., snapping at whoever's still sharing their screen at 5:05.
