The customer service rep stayed calm through my testy tone even after I'd been on hold for forty-five minutes.
She's usually easygoing, but skip her morning coffee and she turns testy over the smallest scheduling change.
The referee grew testy after the third replay challenge in a row, snapping at both coaches to just let the call stand.
Traffic made him testy enough that he honked at a cyclist who technically had the right of way.
words.etymology: 古法语 teste(头) → 上头 → 易怒

meanings.en: to greatly dismay or horrify someone

examples: It appalled her to learn the 'organic' skincare line she'd been reselling for months was mixed in someone's garage.
The landlord's response — 'that's a you problem' — appalled tenants who'd been without hot water for a week.
I was appalled to see the group project I'd built alone get submitted under my teammate's name while I was on vacation.
It appalled the inspector to find the daycare's fire exits blocked by stacked furniture during a routine visit.
Neighbors were appalled when the developer bulldozed the community garden overnight without any public notice.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + pallere(发白) → 吓得脸白 → 使惊骇

meanings.en: showing great care, effort, and perseverance

examples: She was assiduous about logging every workout in her fitness app, even on nights she really didn't feel like it.
He assiduously proofread the pitch deck three times before sending it to the investors at 2 a.m.
My grandmother is assiduous about watering her balcony tomatoes every single morning before work.
The junior analyst was assiduous about cross-checking every figure in the report, even the ones nobody else bothered to verify.
He assiduously backed up his laptop every Friday evening, a habit that saved him when the hard drive failed the following Monday.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + sedere(坐) → 坐得住 → 勤勉

meanings.en: wishing to do what is right, especially thorough and dutiful in one's work

examples: The new intern is so conscientious that she double-checks every spreadsheet formula before the weekly report goes out.
Being a conscientious pet owner, he set three phone alarms so he'd never forget his dog's medication.
Landlords love conscientious tenants who report a leaky faucet the day it starts dripping, not three months later.
As a conscientious babysitter, she texted the parents a photo update every hour without being asked.
The conscientious auditor flagged the discrepancy even though reporting it meant delaying her own vacation by two days.
words.etymology: com-(共同) + scire(知) → 良知在场 → 尽责

meanings.en: showing a skillful use of underhand or dishonest tactics to achieve a goal

examples: He came up with a devious scheme to expense his weekend trip as a 'client dinner.'
She's devious enough to schedule the meeting right when she knows her manager will be stuck in traffic.
The scammer used a devious phishing email disguised as a delivery notification to steal his bank login.
The intern found a devious workaround to bypass the approval queue by submitting requests just under the review threshold.
Her devious plan to swap seats before the flight involved convincing a stranger she had a fear of window seats.
words.etymology: de-(离开) + via(路) → 偏离正道 → 狡猾

meanings.en: not clearly good, true, or reliable; of questionable quality
feeling doubt or uncertainty about something
meanings.zh: 半信半疑的;犹豫不决的

examples: I was dubious about the five-star reviews until I noticed the landlord had posted three of them himself.
She gave the influencer's 'miracle' supplement a dubious look before closing the app without buying it.
The startup's revenue numbers looked dubious, so the VC firm asked for a third-party audit before investing.
The contractor's dubious repair job started leaking again within a month, proving the low bid wasn't actually a bargain.
He remained dubious about his cousin's multi-level-marketing pitch, even after she promised he'd be 'practically guaranteed' a promotion.
words.etymology: duo(二) → 在两者之间打转 → 可疑

meanings.en: the capacity to produce a desired or intended result

examples: The clinic couldn't confirm the efficacy of the new allergy medication until the six-month trial results came in.
Her manager questioned the efficacy of another all-hands meeting when a two-line Slack message would do.
Reviewers kept debating the efficacy of the standing desk — did it really cut back pain, or was it just a placebo?
The school board debated the efficacy of the new anti-bullying curriculum after only a handful of teachers had actually finished the training.
Investors questioned the efficacy of the marketing overhaul when signups barely moved despite tripling the ad budget.
words.etymology: ex-(出) + facere(做) → 做得出结果 → 功效

meanings.en: having an unhealthy interest in death or disturbing subjects
meanings.zh: 病态的;对死亡等有不健康兴趣的

examples: He has this morbid habit of reading true-crime case files right before bed and then can't sleep.
It sounds morbid, but she keeps a doc titled 'if I die' with all her passwords for her sister.
The group chat took a morbid turn after someone shared a video of a car crash from the highway cam.
Her morbid habit of narrating exactly how each rollercoaster could kill her made her sister refuse to ride with her anymore.
His morbid sense of humor about his own diagnosis made the waiting room oddly bearable for everyone else in it.
words.etymology: morbus(疾病) → 病态

meanings.en: nearsightedness; difficulty seeing distant objects clearly
lack of foresight or imagination in thinking or planning

examples: Staring at his phone during every commute gave him early-onset myopia, according to his optometrist.
The company's quarterly-earnings myopia meant it kept cutting R&D just to hit this quarter's numbers.
Critics blamed the app's redesign flop on management myopia — nobody had asked actual users what they wanted.
Years of reading in dim light gave the whole family a shared myopia, so eye exams became a yearly ritual by age ten.
Critics blamed the airline's overbooking myopia for the summer of canceled flights, since nobody had planned for a hiring shortage.
words.etymology: myein(闭合) + ōps(眼) → 眯着眼看 → 近视

meanings.en: done with or requiring great care and thoroughness
meanings.zh: 煞费苦心的;细致费力的

examples: It took a painstaking three weeks to reconcile the spreadsheet after the migration corrupted half the invoice data.
She spent a painstaking afternoon color-coding her entire closet by season before the move.
Restoring the vintage motorcycle was a painstaking process — every rusted bolt had to be soaked and hand-cleaned.
The tattoo artist's painstaking linework took six hours for a piece barely bigger than a coin.
He gave the wedding seating chart a painstaking redo after learning two families hadn't spoken in a decade.
words.etymology: pains(辛苦) + taking → 肯下苦功 → 煞费苦心

meanings.en: to give formal consent to an agreement, making it officially valid

examples: The board still has to ratify the merger before Friday's press release can go out.
Once both roommates ratify the new chore chart in the group chat, it goes on the fridge.
The union members voted to ratify the contract after management agreed to the remote-work clause.
Shareholders will ratify the stock split at next month's virtual annual meeting, assuming no last-minute objections surface.
The city council refused to ratify the new bike-lane budget until the transportation committee resubmitted revised numbers.
words.etymology: ratus(已确定的) + facere(做) → 使确定 → 批准

meanings.en: to pay someone for services rendered or work done

examples: Freelancers on the platform are remunerated within 48 hours of the client approving the invoice.
The company remunerates beta testers with gift cards instead of cash, which annoyed half the Discord server.
She wanted to know exactly how she'd be remunerated for overtime before agreeing to the crunch weekend.
The museum remunerates guest lecturers with a flat honorarium rather than an hourly rate, regardless of prep time.
Volunteers on the trail-building crew aren't remunerated at all, though the park service throws them a pizza party each fall.
words.etymology: re-(回) + munus(酬劳、职务) → 回赠 → 支付报酬

meanings.en: showing dedication, persistence, and diligence

examples: His sedulous approach to language learning meant twenty flashcards every single morning on the subway, no exceptions.
The reviewer was sedulous about catching typos, flagging even a stray comma in the pull request.
Years of sedulous saving finally let her put a down payment on the studio apartment.
The intern was sedulous about labeling every cable in the server room before the big office move.
Her sedulous habit of backing up photos every Sunday night saved the entire wedding album when her laptop died.
words.etymology: 拉丁 sedulo(专心地) → 一门心思 → 孜孜不倦

meanings.en: to prevent someone from accomplishing a plan or action

examples: The launch was thwarted at the last minute when the payment gateway API went down during the live demo.
Her plan to surprise him with a birthday trip was thwarted the moment he checked their shared calendar.
Airport security thwarted an attempt to board with a knife hidden inside a laptop case.
The toddler's nap-time escape plan was thwarted by a squeaky floorboard right outside his bedroom door.
Their attempt to sneak a surprise puppy past the no-pets clause was thwarted when the landlord did a random inspection.
words.etymology: 古诺斯语 þvert(横着) → 横插一杠 → 阻挠

meanings.en: existing beyond what is openly stated or admitted; deliberately hidden, especially of motives

examples: He offered to help her move, but everyone suspected an ulterior motive — he wanted to borrow her truck next weekend.
The 'free' financial seminar had an ulterior purpose: upselling attendees on an overpriced trading course.
She wondered if his sudden interest in her promotion had an ulterior motive tied to the open manager slot.
The colleague who kept complimenting her code review had an ulterior aim: he wanted her seat on the steering committee.
Their neighbor's sudden offer to walk the dog each morning had an ulterior reason: he wanted an excuse to see her roommate.
words.etymology: ulter(更远的) → 藏在更远处的 → 别有用心

meanings.en: not vigilant or cautious about danger; easily fooled

examples: Scammers target unwary shoppers during Black Friday with fake 'order confirmation' texts that link to phishing sites.
An unwary tourist left his phone on the café table for ten seconds and it was gone.
The app preys on unwary users who skim past the subscription terms and get charged $60 a month.
Pickpockets on the crowded train target unwary commuters staring at their phones instead of their bags.
The fake charity caller preys on unwary donors who feel too guilty to hang up the phone.
words.etymology: un- + ware(留意) → 不留神 → 不谨慎

meanings.en: practicing strict self-discipline and abstaining from indulgence
a person who practices extreme self-discipline and abstention

examples: After burning out on takeout and Netflix, he went almost ascetic — no sugar, no streaming, just gym and books.
The monk lived an ascetic life in a one-room cell, owning nothing but a bowl and two robes.
Her minimalist apartment, with its bare walls and single mattress, made her look like an ascetic who'd sworn off comfort.
After the diagnosis, he adopted an almost ascetic diet, cutting out sugar, alcohol, and anything processed.
The tech founder, once famous for private jets, reinvented himself as an ascetic who eats the same three meals daily.
words.etymology: 希腊 askein(操练) → askētēs(修炼者) → 苦行

meanings.en: (economics) to organize an industry or group of producers into a cartel to control prices or output
meanings.zh: (经济学)使卡特尔化;组成价格联盟

examples: Regulators accused the three airlines of quietly cartelizing transatlantic routes, coordinating fares within a few dollars of each other.
Once OPEC members agreed to cartelize oil output, global crude prices jumped nearly twenty percent within a month.
Fertilizer manufacturers were accused of quietly agreeing to cartelize supply, keeping prices high through a drought that should have lowered demand.
Container shipping lines effectively cartelized transpacific routes during the pandemic, and freight rates tripled within a single quarter.
Coffee exporters in three countries tried to cartelize bean prices, but a bumper harvest in a fourth country broke the agreement.

relatedForms.zh: 卡特尔;企业联合;价格联盟

words.etymology: 意大利 cartello(告示、纸牌) ← carta(纸) → 一纸盟约 → 结成价格联盟

meanings.en: to be logically consistent; to stick together and form a unified whole
meanings.zh: (逻辑上)连贯一致;凝聚在一起

examples: The project plan didn't cohere at all — the budget section contradicted the timeline slide right next to it.
His alibi failed to cohere once the detective compared it against the parking-garage timestamps.
The design team worked hard to make the app's onboarding flow cohere with the rest of the brand's tone.
The band's new album never quite coheres — half the tracks sound like leftovers from three different sessions.
Her thesis chapters wouldn't cohere until her advisor pointed out she'd been arguing two contradictory claims the whole time.
words.etymology: com-(一起) + haerere(黏附) → 黏成一片 → 连贯

meanings.en: to conspire secretly, especially to do something illegal or dishonest

examples: Regulators fined the two airlines for colluding to fix baggage fees across every route they shared.
Employees suspected the two managers were colluding to funnel overtime hours to their own friends.
The landlord and the inspector were colluding to pass buildings that clearly failed fire code.
Investigators believe the two bidders colluded at the estate auction, taking turns dropping out so the other could win cheap.
Students accused the study group of colluding on the take-home exam after three papers used identical wrong answers.
words.etymology: com-(一起) + ludere(演戏) → 合演一出 → 勾结

meanings.en: an idea or feeling a word invokes beyond its literal meaning

examples: 'Cheap' has a negative connotation, so the marketing team swapped it for 'affordable' in the ad copy.
In her culture, the word for 'ambitious' carries a slightly negative connotation, unlike in most Western workplaces.
He picked 'downsizing' instead of 'layoffs' because it has a softer connotation, even though it means the same thing.
The hiring manager crossed out 'aggressive' on the job posting because of its negative connotation and wrote 'driven' instead.
Calling the neighborhood 'up-and-coming' carries a connotation of gentrification that longtime residents find pretty insulting.
words.etymology: com-(附带) + notare(标记) → 附带标出的意思 → 内涵

meanings.en: to worship or regard as a god; to treat as infallible

examples: Tech Twitter tends to deify founders right up until the fraud lawsuit drops.
Sports documentaries have a habit of deifying athletes instead of showing the messy years before the title.
She half-jokingly deifies her cardiologist, crediting him with saving her dad's life after the heart attack.
Gym influencers tend to deify certain coaches online, treating their training programs as beyond question or critique.
The biography stopped short of deifying the general, showing the messy retreats along with the famous victories.
words.etymology: deus(神) + facere(做) → 神化

meanings.en: the act or policy of discouraging behavior through fear of consequences

examples: The city installed bright floodlights in the parking garage purely as a deterrence against car break-ins.
HR argued that publicly announcing the firing served as deterrence for anyone tempted to fudge expense reports.
Some economists doubt that a $50 late fee is enough deterrence to stop people from missing rent deadlines.
The school added see-through backpacks as a deterrence measure after a string of locker thefts last spring.
Some managers think a strict two-strikes policy works as deterrence, though it mostly just scares away good employees before they slip up.
words.etymology: de-(离开) + terrere(使恐惧) → 吓退 → 威慑

meanings.en: disagreement with an official or majority opinion
to hold or express opinions that differ from the official or majority view

examples: One engineer voiced dissent in the design review, insisting the login flow was two steps too many.
She dissented from the team's decision to skip QA testing before the holiday release.
The company's Slack channel became a hub of quiet dissent after the return-to-office mandate went out.
Only one board member dissented from the acquisition vote, but her memo circulated widely afterward.
Muted dissent spread through the newsroom after editors cut the investigative piece without explanation.
words.etymology: dis-(分开) + sentire(感觉、认为) → 想法分岔 → 异议

meanings.en: to make something, typically undesirable, continue indefinitely

examples: Posting only the highlight-reel vacation photos just perpetuates the myth that everyone else's life is perfect.
Critics say the show's casting choices perpetuate outdated stereotypes about tech founders.
Paying interns nothing perpetuates a system where only wealthy kids can afford to break into the industry.
Recommending only chart-topping songs perpetuates a loop where the same handful of artists get all the streams.
Keeping salary ranges secret perpetuates the pay gap that the company claims it wants to close.
words.etymology: per-(始终) + petere(前行) → 一路不停 → 使永续

meanings.en: devoutly religious
making a show of virtue, often hypocritically

examples: Her grandmother is deeply pious, lighting a candle and praying every morning before checking her phone.
He gave a pious little speech about sustainability right before boarding his fourth flight that month.
The company's pious statements about 'putting employees first' rang hollow after the layoff email went out on a Friday.
Every Sunday, her pious uncle skips brunch to volunteer at the shelter, no matter how tired he is.
The landlord's pious talk about 'community' evaporated the second a tenant asked for a repair.
words.etymology: 拉丁 pius(敬神尽责) → 虔诚

meanings.en: thought out or planned in advance, especially a crime

examples: The prosecutor argued the fraud was premeditated, pointing to emails drafted weeks before the fake invoices went out.
Her resignation looked spontaneous, but the polished portfolio and lined-up job offer suggested it was premeditated.
It wasn't a premeditated prank — someone just left the whiteboard marker uncapped and the cat did the rest.
Detectives concluded the break-in was premeditated once they found the spare key duplicated a month earlier.
Her toast sounded off-the-cuff, but the timed jokes and rehearsed pauses gave away how premeditated it really was.
words.etymology: prae-(预先) + meditari(反复思量) → 预谋

meanings.en: to respond to a gesture or feeling by making a similar or corresponding one

examples: He texted 'good morning' every day for a month before she finally reciprocated.
The company reciprocates referral bonuses — if your friend hires someone you referred, you both get $500.
She brought soup when I was sick, so I reciprocated by watering her plants during her trip to Bali.
He always reciprocates dinner invitations within a week, refusing to let anyone else pick up two tabs in a row.
She complimented his presentation, hoping he'd reciprocate during her review next month, but he never mentioned it.
words.etymology: re-(回) + pro-(去) → 一来一往 → 回报

meanings.en: to give or do something in return for a feeling or action, especially love or a favor

examples: His crush on his coworker went unrequited for two years until the office holiday party finally forced the conversation.
She requited his years of quiet support by naming him best man at her wedding.
The neighborhood requited the volunteer firefighters' effort with a block party and a hand-painted thank-you banner.
The old professor's patience with struggling students was requited years later when one of them funded a new scholarship in his name.
She finally requited her sister's decade of babysitting by planning the entire baby shower herself.
words.etymology: re-(回) + quit(清偿) → 还清这份情 → 报答

meanings.en: to feel or show deep respect or admiration for someone

examples: Junior developers revere her not for her title but for the three-hour debugging session she once did for a stranger's PR.
He still revered his old basketball coach, texting him every time he closed a big deal.
The startup's employees revered the founder until the leaked emails changed everything overnight.
Line cooks revere the head chef less for her Michelin star than for the way she remembers everyone's birthday.
Students still revere the retired professor, packing his guest lectures decades after he stopped grading papers.
words.etymology: re-(强调) + vereri(敬畏) → 尊敬

meanings.en: to cheat someone out of money or property through deception
a fraudulent scheme

examples: He swindled three elderly neighbors out of their savings with a fake 'roof repair' scam.
The crypto influencer ran a swindle disguised as an exclusive investment club, and the group chat only found out after withdrawals froze.
She realized too late that the 'too good to be true' apartment listing was a swindle designed to grab the deposit.
The contractor swindled the young couple by billing for permits he never actually filed.
A fake ticket seller swindled dozens of concertgoers outside the venue minutes before doors opened.
words.etymology: 德语 schwindeln(发晕、行骗) → 把人转晕 → 诈骗

meanings.en: (of something bad) to become less intense, severe, or widespread

examples: The rideshare surge pricing finally abated once the concert crowd cleared out around midnight.
Her knee pain abated after a few weeks of physical therapy, and she went back to running.
Public backlash over the price hike hasn't abated at all — the app still has one-star reviews pouring in daily.
The wildfire smoke finally abated after three days, and the city lifted its outdoor-exercise warning.
Customer complaints about the app's redesign abated once the team quietly restored the old search bar.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + battuere(击打) → 打压下去 → 减弱

meanings.en: having a strong, unpleasant, bitter smell or taste
(of speech or manner) bitter and harsh

examples: An acrid smell of burnt popcorn filled the entire office kitchen after someone microwaved it for six minutes.
The candle promised 'fresh linen' but actually smelled acrid, like melted plastic.
His acrid comment about her 'participation trophy' promotion ended the team lunch in awkward silence.
An acrid haze from the nearby wildfires hung over the city for most of the week.
The mechanic recognized the acrid smell of burning brake pads the second she opened the garage door.
words.etymology: acer(尖锐、辛辣) → 刺鼻

meanings.en: characterized by anger and bitterness, especially in speech or argument
meanings.zh: (言辞、争论等)激烈的;充满怨恨的

examples: The roommates' group chat turned acrimonious the moment someone brought up the unpaid electric bill.
Their divorce grew acrimonious over custody of the dog, not the apartment or the savings account.
The merger talks fell apart after an acrimonious dispute over who would keep the company name.
The HOA meeting turned acrimonious the moment someone brought up the unauthorized backyard shed again.
Contract talks between the union and the airline grew acrimonious after management leaked a lowball offer to the press.
words.etymology: acer(尖锐) → 言辞带刺 → 激烈充满怨恨

meanings.en: to supply or infuse a substance, such as soil, water, or liquid, with air

examples: The greenskeeper aerated the fairway every fall, punching thousands of tiny holes so the roots could finally breathe.
The barista aerated the milk for exactly twelve seconds before it hit that silky microfoam texture.
Wastewater engineers aerate the tanks continuously so the bacteria have enough oxygen to break down the sludge.
She aerates the compost bin every few days so it doesn't turn into a smelly, soggy mess.
The sommelier aerated the young red wine in a decanter for an hour before serving it.
words.etymology: 希腊 aēr(空气) → 使通气

meanings.en: a person who believes it is impossible to know whether God exists
(especially in technology) not specific to or dependent on one particular platform or system; neutral
meanings.zh: (技术上)中立的;不依赖特定平台的

examples: He grew up Catholic but calls himself agnostic now, unsure whether he believes in anything beyond what he can test.
Our new dashboard was built to be cloud-agnostic, so it runs the same whether the client uses AWS or Azure.
She's agnostic about which framework the team uses, as long as the API stays consistent.
Raised by two atheists, she calls herself agnostic instead, open to the idea but unconvinced either way.
The payments team built the checkout flow currency-agnostic from day one, so launching in new markets meant no rewrite.
words.etymology: a-(无) + gnōsis(知识) → 不可知论者

meanings.en: very eager or curious to hear or see something

examples: The whole group chat was agog after she posted a blurry photo captioned 'big news coming Monday.'
Fans were agog for the finale, refreshing the streaming app every ten minutes on release night.
The interns were agog when they heard the CEO would sit in on their standup for the first time.
The whole dorm floor was agog after someone spotted moving trucks outside the new neighbor's unit.
Kids at the assembly were agog the moment the principal wheeled out the mystery donated arcade machine.

meanings.en: the state of having simultaneously conflicting feelings or attitudes toward something

examples: She felt real ambivalence about the promotion — more money, but also more nights away from her kids.
His ambivalence toward the wedding invite showed in how long he left it on 'maybe' before RSVPing.
There's a lot of ambivalence in the office about the new open floor plan — some love it, some are already wearing headphones full-time.
He felt a strange ambivalence about the job offer abroad, torn between the salary bump and leaving his aging parents.
Her ambivalence about adopting a second dog showed every time she added and removed the shelter tab from her browser.
words.etymology: ambi-(两边) + valere(有力) → 两边势均力敌 → 矛盾心理

meanings.en: a desirable or useful feature of a building or place, especially a pleasant or comfortable one (often plural)
pleasantness or agreeableness, especially in a person's manner or a situation

examples: The listing promised 'luxury amenities,' but the rooftop pool turned out to be a plastic kiddie pool with two folding chairs.
After the layoffs, the office amenities disappeared one by one — first the free snacks, then the espresso machine.
Even amid the chaos of moving, she noticed the small amenities of the new neighborhood: a bakery, a park bench, quiet mornings.
The co-working space advertises a nap pod as an amenity, though it's really just a beanbag behind a curtain.
Half the building's amenities, like the rooftop grill and the package room, are still locked behind a broken key fob system.
words.etymology: amoenus(宜人的) → 让人舒服的东西 → 便利设施

meanings.en: having no clearly defined shape or form; lacking organization or structure
meanings.zh: 无定形的,不成形的;无明确结构的

examples: The startup's org chart was amorphous for the first year — job titles meant nothing and everyone just did whatever was urgent.
The dough stayed amorphous no matter how long she kneaded it, refusing to hold the shape of a proper loaf.
His retirement plan was still amorphous: 'travel somewhere, maybe write a book' was about as specific as it got.
The committee's mission statement stayed amorphous for two years, too vague to actually guide a single decision.
Smoke from the factory drifted into an amorphous gray cloud that hung over the valley all afternoon.
words.etymology: a-(无) + morphē(形状) → 无定形

meanings.en: strong hostility or ill will

examples: Years after the merger, animosity between the two former CEOs still surfaces in passive-aggressive LinkedIn posts.
The animosity between the neighbors started over a fence line and escalated into dueling security-camera lawsuits.
She tried to hide her animosity toward her sister in the family group chat, but the emojis gave her away.
Old animosity between the two co-founders resurfaced the moment their names appeared on the same funding panel.
There's real animosity between the two coding bootcamp cohorts, all because of a prank during orientation week.
words.etymology: animus(心气、怒气) → 敌意

meanings.en: to cause someone to become hostile; to provoke or annoy

examples: Replying-all with sarcasm is a great way to antagonize the entire department before your first coffee.
The new manager antagonized the whole team in week one by scrapping remote Fridays without asking anyone.
Don't antagonize the algorithm — one flagged comment and your account gets shadow-banned for a month.
Cutting overtime pay right before the holidays antagonized a workforce that was already stretched thin.
He antagonized his little brother all through dinner just to see how long it took their mom to notice.
words.etymology: anti-(对抗) + agōn(竞技) → 摆到对面 → 使敌对

meanings.en: a deep-seated feeling of dislike or aversion

examples: He has a quiet antipathy toward open-plan offices, dating back to a year of listening to a coworker's phone calls.
Her antipathy toward crash diets comes through in every comment she leaves under those 'lose 10 pounds fast' ads.
There's a long-standing antipathy between the marketing and engineering teams that even free pizza can't fix.
Longtime fans developed a real antipathy toward the reboot the moment the trailer changed the villain's backstory.
There's mutual antipathy between the two delivery apps' drivers, who compete for the same curbside parking spots.
words.etymology: anti-(反) + pathos(感受) → 反着感受 → 反感

meanings.en: showing or feeling little interest, enthusiasm, or concern
meanings.zh: 冷漠的,不关心的,缺乏热情的

examples: By the third round of layoffs, even the most loyal employees had gone apathetic, updating their résumés during standups.
He seemed apathetic about the promotion, shrugging when HR called with the offer letter.
Voter turnout dropped again this year — pollsters blame an apathetic electorate exhausted by nonstop campaign ads.
The jury looked apathetic by the trial's third week, doodling through testimony that once had them riveted.
Most of the class went apathetic about the group project once it became clear only two people were doing the work.
words.etymology: a-(无) + pathos(感受) → 无感 → 冷漠

meanings.en: (rhetoric) a figure of speech in which a speaker raises a subject by claiming to pass over or not mention it
meanings.zh: (修辞学)假省略法;欲言又止修辞

examples: The senator used apophasis beautifully: 'I won't even mention my opponent's bankruptcy,' he said, mentioning it at length.
Her toast was pure apophasis — 'I won't bring up the wedding-day meltdown' — and the whole room burst out laughing.
The product review was a masterclass in apophasis: 'I won't even bring up the battery life,' the reviewer wrote, then spent two paragraphs on it.
In his eulogy, the comedian used apophasis to devastating effect: 'I won't tell the story about the boat,' he said, and told it anyway.
The coach's press conference leaned on apophasis — 'I'm not going to talk about the referees' — followed by five minutes about the referees.

relatedForms.zh: 间接暗示的;(神学)否定式的

words.etymology: apo-(离开) + phasis(说) → 说「我不说」 → 假省略法

meanings.en: skillful and clever, especially in a subtle or creative way
meanings.zh: 巧妙的,精巧的,有技巧的

meanings.en: cunning or deceitful; skilled at achieving one's aims through indirect means

examples: Her artful edit of the resignation email turned a complaint into something that read almost like a compliment.
The negotiator's artful pause before naming a price made the buyer blink first every time.
He gave an artful non-answer to the reporter's question, saying a lot while committing to nothing.
The chef's artful plating turned a simple roast chicken into something that looked plucked from a magazine cover.
His artful dodge of the salary question kept the interview moving without him ever naming a number.
words.etymology: ars/art-(技艺) + -ful → 有技巧的

meanings.en: clever trickery, especially used to deceive
ingenious skill or clever craftsmanship

examples: The 'limited time only' banner is pure artifice — the discount code has worked every day for the past six months.
Beneath the influencer's artifice of a spontaneous morning routine were three retakes and a ring light.
The magician's artifice was so smooth that even the front row couldn't spot where the card went.
The 'sold out' countdown timer on the site is total artifice — refreshing the page just resets the clock.
The jeweler's artifice was in hiding the clasp so seamlessly that the necklace looked like a single unbroken loop of gold.
words.etymology: ars(技艺) + facere(做) → 做出来的手段 → 诡计

meanings.en: free from deceit or cunning; natural and unaffected
meanings.zh: 天真率直的,不做作的,朴实的

meanings.en: lacking skill or sophistication; crude

examples: My four-year-old's artless honesty — 'your soup tastes like the sink' — is more brutal than any performance review.
The startup's pitch deck was refreshingly artless: no jargon, just a screenshot of their revenue graph.
His artless attempt at flirting, a straight-up 'I like you, want to get dinner,' somehow worked better than any line.
The birthday card's artless scrawl — 'you are old but I still like you' — got taped straight to the fridge.
Her artless retelling of the accident, stumbling over details out of order, somehow made the jury trust her more.
words.etymology: ars(技艺) + -less → 不施技巧 → 天真率直

meanings.en: a system of government by one person with absolute power

examples: Employees joked that the 'flat hierarchy' was really an autocracy with one guy approving every Slack emoji.
Historians still debate whether the reforms slowed the empire's slide from monarchy into full autocracy.
The founder ran the board like an autocracy, calling votes only after he'd already decided the outcome.
The condo board runs like a tiny autocracy, with the president deciding paint colors without ever calling a vote.
What started as a scrappy group project slid into autocracy once one teammate claimed the only copy of the slides.
words.etymology: autos(自己) + kratos(权力) → 权力归己 → 独裁

meanings.en: hostile and aggressive
a nation or person engaged in war or conflict

examples: The customer got belligerent over a $3 delivery fee, screaming at the driver in the parking lot.
He turns belligerent after two drinks, picking fights with strangers about football.
The treaty required both belligerents to withdraw troops from the contested border within thirty days.
The coach got belligerent with the referee over a call that replay later proved correct.
He turned belligerent in the comments section the moment someone questioned his favorite team's draft picks.
words.etymology: bellum(战争) + gerere(进行) → 一身战意 → 好斗

meanings.en: well-meaning, kind, and generous
meanings.zh: 仁慈的,善意的,乐善好施的

examples: The landlord played benevolent, waiving a month's rent, then quietly raised it 15% at renewal.
Her boss has a benevolent streak — he covers the intern's lunch every Friday without making it a thing.
The app markets itself as a benevolent AI assistant, though the fine print sells your data to advertisers.
The scholarship fund looks benevolent on paper, but recipients still have to promote the sponsor's logo for four years.
Her benevolent uncle paid for the whole family reunion, then spent the weekend reminding everyone exactly how much it cost.
words.etymology: bene(好) + velle(愿望) → 存好心 → 仁慈

meanings.en: to reduce the quality or value of something; to lower in dignity
meanings.zh: 使贬值,降低质量;贬低,使掉价

examples: Flooding the market with knockoff sneakers debased the brand's whole 'limited edition' pitch overnight.
Critics argued the reboot debased the original film, swapping character depth for CGI explosions.
Constantly asking for favors debases a friendship into something that feels transactional.
Printing extra tokens whenever the treasury ran low quietly debased the game's entire in-app currency.
Handing out participation certificates for everything debases the ones kids actually worked hard to earn.
words.etymology: de-(向下) + base(低) → 拉低 → 贬值

meanings.en: to make a problem, situation, or negative feeling worse

examples: Skipping the standup didn't fix the bug backlog — it just exacerbated everyone's confusion about who owned what.
Doomscrolling before bed only exacerbates the anxiety he's trying to sleep off.
The delayed shipment exacerbated an already tense relationship with their biggest wholesale client.
The humid apartment exacerbated his allergies all summer until they finally fixed the leaking window seal.
Cutting the support team in half exacerbated response times right as the holiday order volume spiked.
words.etymology: ex-(彻底) + acerbus(苦涩尖刻) → 变本加苦 → 加剧

meanings.en: making great demands on someone's skill, attention, or effort; rigorous
meanings.zh: 严格要求的,要求严苛的(工作、任务等)

meanings.en: (of a person) very demanding and hard to satisfy

examples: The client's exacting revision notes turned a two-day mockup into a three-week ordeal.
She's an exacting editor — every comma gets questioned, every claim needs a source.
Getting the Michelin star meant meeting the inspector's exacting standards on plating, timing, and even napkin folds.
The visa application process is exacting about paperwork, rejecting applicants over a single missing signature.
Their grandmother is exacting about the holiday table setting, right down to which way the forks face.
words.etymology: ex-(出) + agere(驱使) → 硬要榨出来 → 要求严苛

meanings.en: generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful
meanings.zh: 宽宏大量的,大度的,慷慨的

examples: She was magnanimous in defeat, congratulating her opponent's campaign before the final results were even certified.
The senior engineer was magnanimous about the intern's bug, framing it as 'a great learning moment for the whole team.'
Rather than gloat, he made a magnanimous gesture and gave his rival's startup a glowing reference.
The retiring CEO was magnanimous at the handover, crediting the whole team instead of taking a solo victory lap.
Rather than dispute the split, he was magnanimous about the inheritance and let his siblings take the house.
words.etymology: magnus(大) + animus(心胸) → 宽宏大量

meanings.en: to shorten a text or work while keeping its main content
to reduce or restrict (rights, freedoms, or powers)

examples: The audiobook is an abridged version — the entire middle act got cut down to a twenty-minute chapter.
Lawyers argued the new policy would abridge employees' right to discuss pay with coworkers.
We abridged the 40-slide deck to six slides after the CEO said she only had ten minutes.
The publisher abridged the 900-page biography down to 300 pages for the paperback edition.
Civil liberties groups warned the curfew would abridge residents' right to move freely after dark.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + brevis(短) → 缩短 → 删节

meanings.en: a division into two branches or parts
meanings.zh: 分叉,分支;(意见、道路等的)分歧

examples: The trail hits a bifurcation at mile three — left goes to the summit, right loops back to the parking lot.
There's a growing bifurcation in the job market between remote-friendly companies and strict return-to-office holdouts.
The court ordered a bifurcation of the trial, separating the liability phase from the damages phase.
The river hits a bifurcation just past the old mill, splitting into two channels around a small island.
A bifurcation in the family business emerged once the siblings split it into a retail arm and an online arm.
words.etymology: bi-(二) + furca(叉) → 分叉

meanings.en: the quality of using few words; conciseness; shortness of duration

examples: His performance review was praised for its brevity — three bullet points instead of the usual two pages.
The brevity of the honeymoon (four days, thanks to blackout deadlines) didn't stop them from calling it perfect.
Text her the brevity version: 'running 10 late.' She doesn't need the whole traffic saga.
The eulogy was praised for its brevity — five minutes that said more than an hour of stories could have.
Twitter's character limit forces a kind of brevity that his rambling emails never had.
words.etymology: brevis(短) → 简短

meanings.en: the quality of being open, honest, and frank in speech

examples: With refreshing candor, the CEO admitted in the all-hands that the Q2 numbers were 'just bad, not challenging.'
I appreciated her candor when she said the pitch deck was boring — better to hear it before the investor meeting.
He answered the doctor's questions about his drinking with a candor that surprised even his wife.
Her manager's candor during the review — 'you're ready, but you're not asking for it' — actually landed the raise.
The witness answered the defense attorney's questions with a candor that visibly unsettled her own lawyer.
words.etymology: candere(发白发亮) → 亮堂堂不藏私 → 坦率

meanings.en: involving a sudden, violent upheaval or disaster; catastrophic
meanings.zh: 灾难性的,剧变的,毁灭性的

examples: The 2008 crash was cataclysmic for anyone who'd just bought a house with an adjustable-rate mortgage.
One cataclysmic server outage during the product launch wiped out a year of marketing buildup in an hour.
Their breakup felt cataclysmic at the time, though six months later she barely remembered his last name.
The flash flood was cataclysmic for the valley's small farms, wiping out an entire season's crop overnight.
Losing the patent lawsuit was cataclysmic for the startup, draining the cash they needed for the next funding round.
words.etymology: kata-(向下) + klyzein(冲刷) → 大水冲下 → 灾难性剧变

meanings.en: (of a route or process) long and winding; not direct
meanings.zh: 迂回的,绕圈子的,曲折的

examples: The GPS took us on a circuitous detour through three neighborhoods just to avoid a five-minute construction delay.
It took a circuitous chain of introductions — a friend of a coworker's cousin — to finally land the interview.
Customer support gave a circuitous explanation for the refund delay that somehow never answered the actual question.
The visa renewal took a circuitous path through four different government offices before anyone would stamp the form.
His explanation for the missing budget line was so circuitous that the auditor asked him to just start over.
words.etymology: circum-(环绕) + ire(走) → 绕圈子走 → 迂回

meanings.en: the use of many words to say something that could be expressed more directly; evasive speech
meanings.zh: 迂回累赘的说法,拐弯抹角的话

examples: The layoff email buried the actual news in so much circumlocution that people had to read it three times to realize they'd been let go.
Cut the circumlocution and just tell me if the flight's delayed or not.
Politicians are masters of circumlocution, spending five minutes not quite answering a yes-or-no question.
The insurance denial letter buried its actual reason in so much circumlocution that she had to call twice to understand it.
Cut through the circumlocution in the contract and just tell me who's liable if the shipment is late.
words.etymology: circum-(环绕) + loqui(说) → 绕着说 → 拐弯抹角

meanings.en: cautious and wary; carefully considering the consequences before acting
meanings.zh: 谨慎的,小心翼翼的,慎重的

examples: After getting burned by the last landlord, she's far more circumspect about signing anything without a lawyer's read.
He stayed circumspect in the interview, giving honest but carefully hedged answers about why he left his last job.
Doctors are circumspect about prescribing the new drug until more long-term data comes in.
After the last startup's stock options turned worthless, she's far more circumspect about accepting equity instead of salary.
He stayed circumspect around the new coworker, unsure yet whether office gossip would make it back to management.
words.etymology: circum-(环绕) + specere(看) → 四下张望 → 谨慎

meanings.en: to act in violation of a law, rule, or agreement
meanings.zh: 违反,违背(法律、规则、协议等)

examples: Subletting the apartment on Airbnb clearly contravenes the lease she signed last spring.
The influencer's undisclosed sponsorship contravened the platform's advertising guidelines.
Forcing everyone back five days a week seemed to contravene the flexible-work policy HR had promised at hiring.
Parking the food truck outside the school gate contravened a zoning rule nobody had enforced in years.
The factory's midnight dumping contravened the water district's runoff regulations, and a resident's video proved it.
words.etymology: contra-(反对) + venire(来) → 迎面对着来 → 违反

meanings.en: to cancel or revoke a previous order by giving a contrary one

examples: The regional manager countermanded the CEO's hiring freeze the same afternoon, and nobody knew which memo to follow.
She countermanded her earlier order for the flowers when the venue changed the color scheme.
The general's countermanded retreat order left half the unit confused about which way to move.
The assistant coach countermanded the starting lineup call the second the head coach turned toward the locker room.
Grandma quietly countermanded the no-dessert-before-dinner rule the moment the parents left for date night.
words.etymology: contra-(反) + mandare(下令) → 反向下令 → 撤销命令

meanings.en: a speech delivered with rhetorical force and passion, often for dramatic effect
meanings.zh: 慷慨激昂的演讲;朗诵,雄辩

examples: His TED talk was less a data presentation and more a declamation about why remote work will save civilization.
The debate coach made every student practice declamation until they could hold a room without notes.
Her wedding toast turned into a five-minute declamation on the meaning of true love, complete with hand gestures.
The valedictorian's speech turned into a ten-minute declamation about chasing your dreams, complete with a slow clap from the back row.
His closing argument was less a legal summary than a declamation on justice, delivered with both hands on the jury box rail.
words.etymology: de-(强调) + clamare(呼喊) → 高声陈词 → 慷慨演讲

meanings.en: to deprive of strength, ability, or fitness; to disable
meanings.zh: 使丧失能力,使不能正常行动;使残废

examples: A pulled hamstring incapacitated him two weeks before the marathon he'd trained a year for.
The ransomware attack incapacitated the hospital's entire scheduling system for three days.
Migraines incapacitate her so completely that she has to cancel every meeting and lie in a dark room.
Food poisoning from the office potluck incapacitated half the sales team right before the quarterly pitch.
A single power surge incapacitated the entire assembly line for six hours during the busiest week of the year.
words.etymology: in-(不) + capax(装得下) → 使装不下事 → 使丧失能力

meanings.en: showing clear thought and sharp understanding; direct and effective
meanings.zh: 敏锐的,一针见血的,深刻的

meanings.en: sharp or cutting, in a literal sense (of blades, blows, or features)
meanings.zh: 锋利的,尖锐的(字面义,较少用)

examples: Her incisive question during the earnings call — 'why is churn up if retention spend is also up?' — visibly rattled the CFO.
The editor's incisive notes cut the article from 2,000 rambling words down to a tight, punchy 800.
He's known for incisive one-line code reviews that expose the exact bug everyone else missed.
The professor's incisive comment on the thesis draft — 'this conclusion isn't earned yet' — sent her back to the data for a week.
The critic's incisive review skipped the plot summary entirely and went straight for the film's shaky pacing.
words.etymology: in-(进入) + caedere(切) → 一刀切进去 → 一针见血

meanings.en: to encourage or stir up violent, unlawful, or strong behavior

examples: The viral post was flagged for inciting a boycott before the company even had a chance to respond publicly.
His speech at the rally was later criticized for inciting the crowd to march on the courthouse.
Nothing incites panic buying at the grocery store faster than a single tweet about a storm warning.
The subreddit moderator was banned for inciting followers to mass-report a rival creator's channel overnight.
During the layoff announcement, one manager's sarcastic aside nearly incited a walkout right there in the cafeteria.
words.etymology: in-(向) + citare(催动) → 煽动

meanings.en: to stop up, close, or block (a passage or opening)
(of teeth) to meet or come together properly when the jaws close

examples: Years of fast food finally caught up with him — the scan showed an artery occluded almost completely.
Fallen leaves occluded the gutter, and the first real rainstorm sent water pouring straight into the basement.
The orthodontist explained that his back teeth weren't occluding properly, which was why he kept biting his cheek.
A build-up of scar tissue occluded the stent just eighteen months after it was implanted, sending him back to the ER with chest pain.
The delivery drone's camera kept sending blurry footage because a smear of bird droppings occluded half the lens.
words.etymology: ob-(挡住) + claudere(关闭) → 堵塞

meanings.en: stubbornly resistant to authority, control, or guidance
meanings.zh: 顽固不化的,难驾驭的,不服管教的

examples: The printer turned recalcitrant right before the deadline, jamming on page one of a forty-page report.
HR called him 'a recalcitrant employee' for the third time after he ignored yet another mandatory training reminder.
Getting the recalcitrant toddler into her car seat took longer than the actual drive to daycare.
The board's most recalcitrant member blocked the merger vote for the third meeting running, demanding yet another round of due diligence.
Nothing about the recalcitrant office router responded to a reset, so IT ended up replacing the whole unit before the client demo.
words.etymology: re-(向后) + calx(脚跟) → 尥蹶子往后踢 → 不服管教

meanings.en: avoiding the company of other people; living in seclusion
meanings.zh: 隐居的,遁世的,离群索居的

examples: The novelist went fully reclusive after her second book, cancelling every interview and moving off-grid.
He's grown reclusive since switching to remote work, going days without leaving the apartment or texting anyone back.
The reclusive founder hadn't given an interview in a decade, so the leaked email felt like a rare sighting.
Their downstairs neighbor grew reclusive after the divorce, only ever seen wheeling the trash bins out after midnight.
The chess prodigy turned reclusive after the scandal, deleting his social accounts and skipping every tournament that season.
words.etymology: re-(退) + claudere(关上) → 关起门来 → 隐居

meanings.en: to revive someone from unconsciousness or apparent death, especially through CPR
meanings.zh: 使苏醒,使复苏(尤指心肺复苏)

meanings.en: to revive or restore vigor to something that is failing or inactive
meanings.zh: 使复兴,使恢复活力(计划、品牌、经济等)

examples: Paramedics managed to resuscitate the runner who collapsed at mile twenty of the marathon.
The new CEO spent her first year trying to resuscitate a brand that hadn't launched a hit product in a decade.
They resuscitated the failing group chat with one meme, and suddenly everyone was texting again.
Off-duty nurse Elena managed to resuscitate the choking toddler before the ambulance even turned onto their street.
Lifeguards resuscitated the swimmer they pulled from the riptide, working chest compressions on the sand for nearly four minutes.
words.etymology: re-(再) + citare(唤起) → 重新唤醒 → 使苏醒

meanings.en: very enthusiastic, passionate, or fervent about something
meanings.zh: 热心的,热烈的,热情洋溢的

examples: She's an ardent supporter of the local candidate, knocking on doors every weekend before the election.
He remains an ardent fan of the show, rewatching the finale every year despite how it ends.
Their courtship was full of ardent, slightly embarrassing texts that she now denies ever sending.
He's an ardent cyclist who commutes twelve miles each way in the rain rather than ever take the bus.
The ardent vinyl collector drove four hours to a record fair just for a single pressing he'd been hunting for a decade.
words.etymology: ardere(燃烧) → 热烈

meanings.en: showing signs that something is likely to be successful; favorable
meanings.zh: 吉利的,吉祥的,预示成功的

examples: Landing the biggest client on day one felt like an auspicious start to the new fiscal year.
They picked an auspicious date for the store opening — the same day the subway station finally reopened outside.
It wasn't the most auspicious beginning to the road trip: a flat tire before they'd even left the driveway.
Getting a standing ovation at the dress rehearsal felt auspicious, though the director warned them not to get cocky before opening night.
The app cracked the top ten in the App Store within its first auspicious week, right before the funding round closed.
words.etymology: avis(鸟) + specere(看) → 观鸟占卜得吉 → 吉利

meanings.en: (of punishment) fitting and well-deserved, especially because severe
meanings.zh: (惩罚)罪有应得的;恰如其分而严厉的

examples: The judge called the CEO's five-year sentence for the pension fraud condign punishment, exactly proportionate to the damage he'd caused thousands of retirees.
HR argued that firing him on the spot for leaking client data was condign, not excessive, given how much the breach cost the company.
After the landlord illegally locked out three tenants, the $50,000 fine felt like condign retribution to everyone in the building's group chat.
The medical board called the ten-year license revocation condign, appropriate for a surgeon who had operated drunk on three separate occasions.
The university expelled the students who'd sold exam answers on Discord, a condign response the dean said protected everyone else's degree.
words.etymology: com-(完全) + dignus(相称) → 完全相称 → 罪有应得

meanings.en: belief or acceptance that something is true; credibility

examples: Once the leaked screenshots matched the whistleblower's timeline, reporters finally gave credence to her claims about the startup's fake revenue numbers.
Don't lend credence to every wellness influencer on TikTok who claims cold plunges cure anxiety — check whether there's actual research behind it.
The landlord's story about a 'burst pipe' gained no credence once we found the water bill hadn't changed in six months.
Seeing three empty desks on Monday morning gave sudden credence to the layoff rumors nobody in HR would confirm.
The professor finally gave credence to his excuse once the hospital text messages matched the exact night of the missed exam.
words.etymology: credere(相信) → 采信

meanings.en: a tendency to believe things too readily, without enough evidence; gullibility
meanings.zh: 轻信;易受骗;缺乏辨别力

examples: The scammer preyed on her credulity, convincing her over three phone calls that her bank account had been hacked by 'federal agents.'
That the app promises to double your investment in a week strains credulity, yet thousands of people still wire money to it every month.
Advertisers count on a certain amount of credulity — nobody actually believes the cream erases wrinkles overnight, but enough people buy it anyway.
It strains credulity that the AI-generated video of the mayor went unquestioned for two full days before anyone flagged it as fake.
The new intern's credulity made him an easy target for the office prank about a mandatory Saturday shift starting next week.
words.etymology: credere(相信) → 信得太容易 → 轻信

meanings.en: deserving blame for a wrong or failure

examples: The internal audit found the manager culpable for approving three months of falsified expense reports without ever checking a single receipt.
If the self-driving car's software ignored a known bug, is the engineer who shipped the update legally culpable for the accident?
She felt culpable for missing the red flags in her college roommate's spending, even though the credit card fraud wasn't remotely her fault.
The building inspector ruled the landlord culpable for ignoring three separate mold complaints before the ceiling finally caved in.
Investigators found the contractor culpable for skipping two required inspections on the parking garage before a section of it collapsed.
words.etymology: culpa(过错) → 有过失

meanings.en: hasty and superficial; done quickly without attention to detail
meanings.zh: 粗略的;草率的;走马观花的

examples: He gave the 40-page contract only a cursory glance before signing, and later discovered a clause auto-renewing his gym membership for two years.
The recruiter's cursory review of my resume — eleven seconds, according to LinkedIn's own analytics — decided whether I got an interview.
A cursory scroll through the apartment photos hid the mold in the bathroom, which only showed up during the in-person walkthrough.
He gave the pull request only a cursory review before approving it, and the bug he missed took down checkout for an hour.
A cursory background check missed the candidate's second employer entirely, and it only surfaced when a client recognized his name.
words.etymology: currere(跑) → 一路小跑掠过 → 粗略

meanings.en: behavior in keeping with good taste and propriety; polite formality

examples: Even after the Zoom call turned into a shouting match about the missed deadline, the CFO maintained perfect decorum and never once raised his voice.
Wearing pajama bottoms to a client dinner, even a virtual one, breaks every rule of workplace decorum HR ever wrote down.
Grandma still insists on decorum at the dinner table — phones face down, elbows off the tablecloth, no scrolling during dessert.
Even as her ex gave a passive-aggressive toast, the bride kept perfect decorum and just raised her glass with a tight smile.
The judge reminded both lawyers to maintain courtroom decorum after their sidebar arguments turned into an open shouting match.
words.etymology: decere(合宜) → 得体

meanings.en: moving from topic to topic without a clear plan; rambling
meanings.zh: 东拉西扯的;散漫的;不着边际的

examples: The standup meeting that's supposed to take ten minutes turned into a 45-minute discursive ramble about someone's weekend hiking trip.
Her podcast is delightfully discursive — she'll start reviewing a ramen shop and somehow end up telling you her grandmother's immigration story.
The therapist gently steered him back on track every time his answers drifted into discursive tangents about his coworkers.
The board minutes ballooned to nine pages because the chairman's discursive updates wandered from quarterly revenue to his recent kitchen renovation.
His best-man speech went so discursive that it covered summer camp, a breakup, and a fantasy football league before finally mentioning the groom.
words.etymology: dis-(四散) + currere(跑) → 到处乱跑 → 东拉西扯

meanings.en: tending to control others in an unpleasant, overbearing way

examples: Her domineering manager rewrote every Slack message before it went out, then took full credit for the campaign in the quarterly review.
He quit the startup after eight months under a domineering co-founder who scheduled 7 a.m. calls just to prove who was in charge.
Their domineering mother still calls to approve the paint colors in their new apartment, three states away.
Their domineering older sister planned every hour of the family reunion, down to assigned seating, without asking a single sibling's opinion.
The domineering landlord let himself into the apartment twice this month for 'inspections' that were never on the lease.
words.etymology: dominus(主人) → 端着主人架子 → 专横

meanings.en: (of a disease or species) regularly found in a particular area or group, often hard to eradicate
meanings.zh: (疾病、物种等)某地区特有的;地方性的,难以根除的

meanings.en: (of a problem) persistently and widely present within a particular group or system
meanings.zh: (问题)普遍存在的;根深蒂固的

examples: Burnout is practically endemic in the startup world, where 'we're a family' usually means unpaid overtime and no sick days.
Dengue fever is endemic to parts of Southeast Asia, so the travel clinic recommended repellent and long sleeves before our Bali trip.
Ghost jobs — listings companies never intend to fill — have become endemic on LinkedIn, wasting thousands of applicants' hours every week.
The axolotl is endemic to a single lake system outside Mexico City and has nearly vanished from the wild there.
Scope creep has become endemic to the agency's client projects, with nearly every contract ballooning past its original deadline.
words.etymology: en-(在内) + dēmos(某地民众) → 只在这一带 → 地方性

meanings.en: a person who takes particular pleasure in fine food and drink; a gourmet

examples: My roommate the epicure spent forty minutes comparing three olive oils before deciding which one deserved to go on our six-dollar pasta.
The app's algorithm now sorts restaurants by an 'epicure score,' which apparently just means how many truffle shavings they add to everything.
He's turned into a real epicure since moving to Portland, texting me photos of foraged mushrooms he's about to braise for dinner.
My uncle the epicure keeps a color-coded spreadsheet ranking every tasting menu he's tried across three continents.
As a true epicure, she plans entire vacations around a single tasting menu, booking the reservation months before the flights.
words.etymology: 享乐派哲学家 Epicurus(伊壁鸠鲁) → 美食家

meanings.en: well-suited to the occasion, especially in expression; apt or fortunately timed
meanings.zh: (言辞、举动)恰如其分的;贴切巧妙的;时机凑巧的

examples: Her toast at the wedding was so felicitous that even the bride's notoriously cynical uncle got misty-eyed.
Naming the budgeting app 'Copilot' turned out to be a felicitous choice — it launched right as everyone started comparing every product to an AI assistant.
It was almost felicitous timing: he got the job offer the same morning his lease renewal was due, so he didn't have to decide twice.
Scheduling the product demo for the same morning a competitor's app crashed turned out to be remarkably felicitous timing for the sales team.
Seating the two strangers next to each other at the conference dinner was a felicitous accident that led to a joint venture six months later.
words.etymology: felix(幸运、恰好) → 恰到好处 → 贴切

meanings.en: having or showing passionate intensity of feeling

examples: She's a fervent believer in the four-day workweek and will corner you at any party to explain the productivity data.
His fervent apology in the group chat — three paragraphs, two crying emojis — didn't stop everyone from muting the thread anyway.
Fans lined up outside the stadium at dawn, fervent in their hope that this was finally the season the team wouldn't choke.
She's a fervent composter who lectures every neighbor about food scraps within the first five minutes of meeting them.
His fervent objection to changing the team's logo turned a routine rebrand meeting into a forty-minute standoff.
words.etymology: fervere(沸腾) → 热烈

meanings.en: intense and passionate feeling, especially in support of a cause or belief

examples: The new hire pitched the rebrand with such fervor that the whole meeting forgot to ask whether anyone actually wanted a rebrand.
Fans queued outside the pop-up store with the fervor usually reserved for concert tickets, just to buy a limited-edition phone case.
Her fervor for the volunteer project faded fast once she realized 'flexible hours' meant every Saturday morning for a year.
Bidders raised their paddles with real fervor at the charity auction, chasing a vacation package well past what anyone would call a reasonable price.
The fan campaign to save the canceled show ran on pure fervor, flooding the network's inbox with fifty thousand emails in a week.
words.etymology: fervere(沸腾) → 热忱

meanings.en: to make someone appear guilty of a crime or wrongdoing; to provide evidence against

examples: He deleted the group chat the moment the investigation started, which only made the messages look more incriminating in hindsight.
Employees are told never to write anything in email that could incriminate the company later — 'put it on a call' is basically corporate law.
The dashcam footage ended up incriminating the other driver, who had told the insurance company a completely different story.
The office badge logs ended up incriminating him — he'd claimed to be sick, but the swipe data showed he'd come in for two hours.
During the deposition, he accidentally incriminated his own accountant, admitting the numbers had been adjusted before every audit for years.
words.etymology: in-(向) + crimen(罪) → 把罪往身上引 → 使负罪

meanings.en: to accuse of or show involvement in a fault or crime

examples: The intern's forwarded Slack messages ended up inculpating the whole marketing team in the leaked-campaign scandal, not just the one person who sent it.
His lawyer advised him to stay silent in the interview, since anything he said could inculpate him further in the fraud case.
The audit was careful not to inculpate the entire finance department when only one rogue approver had signed off on the fake invoices.
The forensic accountant's report ended up inculpating two vendors who'd been quietly splitting kickbacks on every contract for three years.
A single recovered text message inculpated the store manager in the inventory theft that had been blamed on overnight staff for months.
words.etymology: in-(向) + culpa(过错,同 culpable) → 归咎于

meanings.en: (law) behavior or material that is offensive to accepted standards of morality, especially of a sexual nature
meanings.zh: (法律)猥亵;不雅行为;有伤风化

examples: The prosecutor charged him with public indecency after witnesses reported the incident near the elementary school.
The broadcasting regulator fined the station for indecency after the uncensored clip aired during the afternoon time slot.
The city council debated a new indecency ordinance after complaints about the beachfront bar's late-night performances.
HR opened an indecency investigation after two interns reported comments the visiting speaker made during the training session.
Festival organizers scrambled to pull the headliner's set offline after complaints of indecency flooded in from parents in the family-friendly section.
words.etymology: in-(不) + decere(合宜,同 decorum) → 不成体统 → 猥亵

meanings.en: to formally charge with or accuse of a serious crime

examples: The federal grand jury voted to indict the former executive on eleven counts of wire fraud after the whistleblower's emails surfaced.
The documentary doesn't just tell his story — it quietly indicts an entire profession that looked the other way for a decade.
Prosecutors said they had enough evidence to indict him for insider trading the moment the SEC subpoenaed his text messages.
Prosecutors moved to indict the city councilman on bribery charges after auditors traced the cash to a shell company he controlled.
The pharmaceutical executive was indicted for pushing sales reps to downplay the opioid's addiction risk in every physician training session.
words.etymology: in-(向) + dicere(宣告) → 当众宣告其罪 → 起诉

meanings.en: a scheming or crafty plot, often secret, intended to accomplish some usually harmful end

examples: It took a whistleblower and eighteen months of leaked memos to expose the board's machinations to oust the founder without triggering a stock crash.
Behind the friendly all-hands presentation lay months of quiet machinations — reorgs planned, layoffs budgeted — that nobody on the floor knew about yet.
The reality show thrives on petty machinations: alliances built over cocktails, then broken the second someone gets a rose.
It took two resignations before anyone pieced together the machinations behind her sudden promotion over three more senior candidates.
The will's late amendment revealed months of quiet machinations by the eldest cousin to cut his siblings out of the inheritance entirely.
words.etymology: machina(机械、机关) → 设下机关 → 阴谋

meanings.en: occurring at a time that is suitable or advantageous

examples: She quit her job the week before the company's stock crashed — either incredibly opportune timing or she knew something the rest of us didn't.
Landing at exactly the moment his flight was delayed felt opportune; we grabbed coffee together instead of missing each other by an hour.
The venture fund waited for the most opportune moment in the news cycle to announce the acquisition, right after a rival's product recall.
He picked what felt like the opportune moment to propose, right after she got the promotion she'd been chasing for two years.
The rain stopped at the most opportune moment, ten minutes before the outdoor ceremony, and started again just as the last guest left.
words.etymology: ob-(朝向) + portus(港口) → 顺风正好进港 → 适时

meanings.en: more important than anything else; supreme

examples: In the pre-op briefing, the surgeon reminded the whole team that patient safety was paramount, above any pressure to finish the schedule on time.
For a first-time homebuyer, reading the inspection report is paramount — skip it and you might inherit a thirty-thousand-dollar foundation problem.
During the acquisition talks, keeping the deal secret from the press was treated as paramount, even more urgent than finalizing the price.
When negotiating the custody agreement, both lawyers agreed the children's routine was paramount, even if it meant neither parent got everything they wanted.
The startup's investors made clear that user data privacy was paramount after a competitor's breach wiped out half its user base overnight.
words.etymology: 盎格鲁法语 par amont(在其之上) → 高居其上 → 至高无上

meanings.en: carried out with minimum effort or reflection, as a mere routine duty
meanings.zh: 敷衍了事的;例行公事的;草率的

examples: The manager's perfunctory 'great job, team' at the end of every meeting stopped meaning anything after the third round of layoffs.
His performance review was so perfunctory — two lines, clearly copy-pasted from last year — that he wondered if his boss remembered his name.
She gave the smoke detector a perfunctory tap instead of actually testing the battery, and of course it died during the actual fire.
He gave the mandatory compliance training a perfunctory click-through, skipping every slide without watching a second of the actual video.
His apology text was so perfunctory — just 'my bad, won't happen again' — that she didn't bother replying for two days.
words.etymology: per-(草草走完) + fungi(履行) → 走个过场 → 敷衍

meanings.en: the process of obtaining goods, services, or supplies, especially for an organization

examples: The procurement department took six weeks to approve a forty-dollar standing desk, but somehow signed off on a two-hundred-thousand-dollar software contract in two days.
After the chip shortage, the company overhauled its procurement strategy, diversifying suppliers instead of relying on a single factory overseas.
Public procurement rules meant the city had to accept three competing bids before it could even repaint the crosswalks.
During the shortage, the hospital's procurement team scrambled to source N95 masks from six different overseas suppliers within a single week.
The school district's procurement process for new laptops dragged on for eight months, so half the classrooms started the year without them.
words.etymology: pro-(为了) + curare(照料) → 张罗置办 → 采购

meanings.en: having or showing a strong desire for revenge; spiteful

examples: After she reported him to HR, he got vindictive and started quietly excluding her from every meeting invite he controlled.
The ex left a string of one-star reviews on her new boyfriend's small business, which felt less like feedback and more like a vindictive campaign.
The coach benched the player for the whole season over one late arrival — the team called it discipline, but it looked vindictive to everyone watching.
Her former boss got vindictive after she quit for a competitor, giving a deliberately vague reference that tanked two job offers.
He kept the security deposit for a scuff on the wall out of pure vindictive spite after the tenant reported him to the city.
words.etymology: vindicare(索还、主张,同 vindicate) → 讨回来 → 报复性

meanings.en: behavior, speech, or manner that is artificial and adopted to impress others

examples: His British accent turned out to be pure affectation — he grew up in Ohio and picked it up after one semester abroad.
Ordering the omakase and photographing every single course felt less like appreciation and more like affectation for the Instagram grid.
She dropped the fake enthusiasm and corporate jargon the moment the camera stopped rolling, as if the whole meeting had been an affectation.
Sprinkling French phrases into every email struck the whole team as affectation, especially since he'd only ever been to Paris on a layover.
Carrying the same unread hardcover to every coffee shop felt like affectation, a prop for the aesthetic rather than something she actually read.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + facere(做) → 硬做出来的样子 → 矫揉造作

meanings.en: (medicine) the use of drugs to induce a loss of sensation or consciousness during a medical procedure

examples: The anesthesiologist adjusted the general anesthesia dosage the moment the patient's heart rate spiked on the monitor.
She opted for local anesthesia so she could stay awake and chat through the entire wisdom-tooth extraction.
Post-op nausea is common after general anesthesia, so the nurse kept a basin within reach for the first hour.
The vet explained the risks of general anesthesia before the elderly dog's dental surgery, given his history of heart trouble.
She chose epidural anesthesia during labor and still swears it was the best decision of the entire delivery.
words.etymology: an-(无) + aisthēsis(感觉) → 麻醉

meanings.en: shameless and undisguised, especially in wrongdoing
meanings.zh: 厚颜无耻的;明目张胆的

examples: Claiming he'd 'never received' the invoice, right after replying to it twice, was a barefaced lie and everyone on the call knew it.
Copying her coworker's entire slide deck and presenting it as her own idea the next morning was a barefaced act of theft.
The barefaced audacity of charging a 'resort fee' at a motel next to the highway made the whole checkout process feel like a scam.
Turning in an essay copied word-for-word from a classmate's 2019 submission was such a barefaced act of plagiarism that the professor reported it the same afternoon.
Cutting straight to the front of the three-hour concert line and claiming a 'friend was holding a spot' was barefaced enough that the whole queue booed.
words.etymology: bare(裸露) + faced → 脸都不遮 → 厚颜无耻

meanings.en: making a certain situation or outcome likely or possible; favorable to

examples: An open-plan office with constant Slack pings is not exactly conducive to the deep focus the job actually requires.
Doctors say a consistent bedtime and no phone in the room are far more conducive to good sleep than any melatonin gummy.
The landlord's decision to allow pets and add a rooftop garden made the building far more conducive to actually meeting your neighbors.
The company converted a storage closet into a nap pod, betting it would be more conducive to afternoon focus than another pot of coffee.
Cooking together every Sunday turned out to be far more conducive to actually talking than any of the scheduled 'family meetings' ever were.
words.etymology: com-(一起) + ducere(引导) → 把事引过去 → 有助于

meanings.en: to cause someone to lose loyalty or affection, making them discontented or rebellious

examples: Three rounds of unpaid overtime and a canceled bonus were enough to disaffect even the most loyal engineers on the team.
The sudden return-to-office mandate disaffected employees who had relocated across the country during two years of remote work.
Constant last-minute schedule changes gradually disaffected the part-time staff, and half of them quit within the same month.
Canceling the promised bonus pool the same week executives got raises thoroughly disaffected the warehouse crew, and half of them applied elsewhere within days.
The network's decision to cancel the fan-favorite show mid-cliffhanger disaffected a fanbase that had defended it loyally for six seasons.
words.etymology: dis-(脱开) + affect(情感依附) → 心脱开了 → 使离心

meanings.en: to give someone or something a higher moral or dignified quality; to elevate

examples: Volunteering at the shelter every Sunday didn't make him rich, but he said it ennobled the rest of his week in a way his job never did.
The documentary tries to ennoble the gig-economy delivery driver as a modern folk hero, though most of them would just rather get paid more.
Surviving chemo together seemed to ennoble their marriage, stripping away years of petty arguments about whose turn it was to do dishes.
He talks about pouring coffee like it's a craft, as if the ritual of it somehow ennobles an otherwise ordinary minimum-wage shift.
Fostering three kids through the worst of the pandemic seemed to ennoble the whole family, even as it drained their savings and their sleep.
words.etymology: en-(使) + noble(高贵) → 使高尚

meanings.en: to praise highly in speech or writing, especially someone who has died
meanings.zh: (尤指在葬礼上)颂扬;称颂;赞美

examples: At the retirement party, three coworkers took turns eulogizing a manager none of them had actually enjoyed working for.
Tech journalists rushed to eulogize the founder's 'visionary genius' within hours of the IPO, conveniently forgetting the two startups that failed before it.
Her brother eulogized their grandfather with stories nobody in the family had heard before, and the whole room was in tears by the end.
At the shutdown all-hands, the founder eulogized the failed startup for twenty minutes, thanking a product almost nobody had actually used.
Coworkers gathered at the dive bar to eulogize her decade at the agency, exaggerating every deadline she'd supposedly saved single-handedly.
words.etymology: eu-(好) + logos(话) → 净说好话 → 颂扬

meanings.en: the act of freeing someone or something from a difficulty, constraint, or entanglement

examples: His extrication from the failing startup took a lawyer, a messy non-compete negotiation, and four months of awkward silence in the group chat.
Firefighters spent nearly an hour on the extrication of the driver, who was pinned when the car folded around the guardrail.
Getting out of the timeshare contract required a full year of paperwork; the extrication cost almost as much as the vacations it was meant to fund.
Her extrication from the multi-level marketing downline took months of blocked calls and an uncomfortable Thanksgiving before her sister finally stopped pitching her on skincare.
Canceling the gym membership required three phone calls, a certified letter, and a full month's notice — an extrication almost harder than the workouts themselves.
words.etymology: ex-(出) + tricae(纠缠、麻烦) → 从缠绕里出来 → 脱身

meanings.en: treating serious issues with deliberately inappropriate humor; flippant
meanings.zh: 轻浮的;不合时宜地开玩笑的;油腔滑调的

examples: When his manager asked why the deploy broke production, he made a facetious joke about 'moving fast and breaking things,' which did not land well.
I wasn't being facetious when I said the rent was insane — I genuinely checked four apps and it's $2,800 for a studio.
Her facetious reply to the layoff announcement, something about 'finally getting that gap year,' didn't go over well in the all-hands chat.
His facetious 'at least the fire drill wasn't during a client call' comment landed badly with coworkers who'd actually lost their desks in the flood.
She replied to the formal complaint email with a facetious 'noted, will do better lol,' which the compliance team did not find funny.
words.etymology: 拉丁 facetus(诙谐、俏皮) → 不合时宜地逗趣

meanings.en: lacking efficiency, competence, or a sense of responsibility; ineffective
meanings.zh: 无能的;不负责任的;软弱无力的

examples: The feckless project manager missed every deadline and blamed 'communication issues' on a team that communicated constantly.
Critics called the mayor feckless for promising to fix the subway across three campaigns while nothing about the commute actually changed.
Her feckless roommate kept 'meaning to' pay his share of the rent, three months running, until she finally changed the locks.
The feckless building super promised to fix the boiler three winters in a row, and tenants are still layering blankets every January.
