Employees mocked the feckless committee that had 'reviewed' the harassment policy for eighteen months without producing a single actual change.
words.etymology: feck(苏格兰语,即 effect 效力) + -less → 不顶事 → 无能

meanings.en: impossible to remove, erase, or forget; permanent
meanings.zh: 不可磨灭的;去不掉的;难忘的

examples: The toddler left an indelible red marker streak across the new couch within twenty minutes of getting it as a gift.
Watching her grandmother cook that last Lunar New Year dinner left an indelible memory she still tries to recreate every winter.
One brutal one-star review, quoted in every pitch meeting since, left an indelible mark on how the founders talk about the product.
The car accident left an indelible scar across his forearm, a permanent reminder every time he rolls up his sleeves for a meeting.
Moving into their first cramped studio apartment, with the leaky faucet and the neighbor's saxophone practice, left an indelible impression on both of them.
words.etymology: in-(不) + delere(删除) → 删不掉 → 不可磨灭

meanings.en: to make physically hard, or to make emotionally hardened and unfeeling through repeated exposure
physically hardened, or emotionally hardened and unfeeling
meanings.zh: (身体或情感上)变硬的;麻木不仁的

examples: Years of empty promises and surprise layoffs had indurated the veteran employees, who now read every 'exciting update' email with total cynicism.
Decades on the boats had indurated the fisherman's hands until calluses replaced any softness left in his palms.
He seemed indurate to the customers' complaints, nodding along in the review meeting without changing a single process afterward.
Two decades of city commuting had indurated her to delays, so a canceled train barely registered anymore.
The old climbing rope had gone indurate and brittle from years in the sun, so the guide replaced it before the next trip.
words.etymology: in-(使) + durus(硬) → 使变硬

meanings.en: to overwhelm someone with a large number of things to deal with, or to flood a place with water
meanings.zh: (以大量事物)淹没;充斥;(洪水)淹没

examples: The moment the layoff rumor hit social media, the HR inbox was inundated with over three hundred anxious emails in a single afternoon.
Monsoon rains inundated the coastal village, and by morning our host family's ground floor was under two feet of water.
New parents get inundated with unsolicited advice the second the pregnancy announcement goes up, half of it contradicting the other half.
Within an hour of posting the single remote job opening, the recruiter was inundated with over two thousand applications.
A burst water main inundated the subway platform during rush hour, and commuters waded through ankle-deep water to reach the stairs.
words.etymology: in-(进入) + unda(波浪) → 浪打上来 → 淹没

meanings.en: (mathematics/philosophy) unable to be reduced, simplified, or broken down into a simpler or smaller form
meanings.zh: (数学/哲学)不可约的;不可简化的

examples: The professor proved the polynomial was irreducible over the rationals, meaning it couldn't be factored into smaller pieces.
Consciousness, the philosopher argued, is an irreducible property that no amount of neuroscience alone can fully explain.
After three rounds of budget cuts, the finance team said the remaining costs were irreducible without shutting down the lab.
The negotiator said the client's demand for full IP ownership was an irreducible condition, non-negotiable no matter how the rest of the deal changed.
The design team stripped away every feature they could, until only three irreducible screens remained: sign-up, search, and checkout.
words.etymology: in-(不) + reducere(化回去) → 化不回去 → 不可约

meanings.en: stubbornly refusing to change one's mind or course of action despite pressure to do so
meanings.zh: 顽固的;执拗的;不为所动的

examples: The landlord stayed obdurate about the rent increase even after half the building threatened to move out at once.
No amount of user data about the failed feature could move the obdurate product lead, who insisted people 'just needed to get used to it.'
Her parents remained obdurate about the wedding venue, refusing to even look at the budget spreadsheet she'd spent a week building.
The insurance company stayed obdurate about denying the claim, even after we submitted the same repair estimate three separate times.
Despite a petition signed by half the department, the obdurate professor refused to move the exam date even by a single day.
words.etymology: ob-(强调) + durus(硬,同 indurate) → 硬到底 → 顽固

meanings.en: able to perceive or feel things through the senses; conscious and capable of experience
meanings.zh: 有感觉能力的;有知觉的;有意识的

examples: The debate over whether the chatbot is sentient resurfaces every time it says something unsettlingly self-aware in a customer support chat.
Watching the octopus at the aquarium solve the jar puzzle, my nephew asked if it was as sentient as our dog.
The new AI ethics course spends a whole week on how we'd even prove a machine were sentient rather than just very good at mimicry.
The documentary argues that pigs are far more sentient than the farming industry likes to admit, capable of complex problem-solving and even empathy.
The sci-fi film's twist hinges on the household robot secretly being sentient the whole time, quietly aware of every conversation it overheard.
words.etymology: sentire(感觉) → 有知觉

meanings.en: a natural liking, sympathy, or attraction for someone or something
meanings.zh: 天然的喜爱;亲近感;吸引力

meanings.en: a close similarity, structural resemblance, or connection between things
meanings.zh: (事物间的)相似性;关联;(化学)亲和力

examples: She'd always had an affinity for spreadsheets, the kind of person who color-coded her budget for fun.
The two founders had an instant affinity, finishing each other's sentences by the second coffee meeting.
Chemists study the affinity between the drug molecule and the receptor to predict how well it binds.
Ever since childhood, she's had an odd affinity for reptiles, keeping three lizards in tanks across her studio apartment.
Linguists have long noted an affinity between the two island dialects, sharing nearly a third of their core vocabulary despite centuries of separation.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + finis(边界) → 两块地接壤 → 天然亲近

meanings.en: an open and deliberate insult or act of disrespect
to insult or offend someone openly and deliberately

examples: Being seated at the intern table felt like a personal affront to the VP, who left before dessert.
She took his unsolicited feedback on her code as an affront, even though he meant it kindly.
Skipping her promotion announcement in the all-hands email affronted her more than the raise itself would have pleased her.
Being asked to validate her own parking after ten years as a partner felt like a deliberate affront to half the room.
He took the venue's dress code as a personal affront, showing up in sneakers just to prove a point at the gala.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + frons(额头、脸面) → 迎面顶上来 → 公然侮辱

meanings.en: to charm or enchant someone, often in a deceptive or misleading way
meanings.zh: (常以欺骗手段)迷惑;哄骗;吸引

meanings.en: to make time pass pleasantly; to help while away time

examples: The startup's slick demo beguiled investors so completely that nobody asked about the burn rate.
He beguiled his Tinder date with stories that later turned out to be someone else's LinkedIn achievements.
We beguiled the six-hour layover playing cards and comparing terrible airport food.
The con artist beguiled three separate retirees out of their savings with the same fake real-estate pitch, tweaked slightly each time.
His charm beguiled the entire hiring committee, and nobody thought to actually check the references on his resume.
words.etymology: be-(使) + guile(诡计) → 用花招迷住 → 哄骗

meanings.en: modest or shy because one lacks confidence in oneself
meanings.zh: 缺乏自信的;羞怯的;拘谨的

examples: He was diffident about sharing his idea in the meeting, mumbling it almost as an apology before someone else took credit.
Despite acing the interview, she stayed diffident about her chances and refused to tell anyone she'd applied.
The new analyst stayed diffident about correcting the VP's math error in the spreadsheet, even though everyone else in the room had missed it too.
She's a diffident painter who keeps her best canvases stacked facing the wall, too nervous to hang even one in the gallery show.
He gave a diffident little wave from the back of the open mic line, clearly hoping nobody would actually call his name.
words.etymology: dis-(不) + fidere(信任) → 不信自己 → 缺乏自信

meanings.en: (medicine) a disorder in which an organ or tissue wastes away, especially due to poor nourishment or a genetic defect

examples: The neurologist explained that muscular dystrophy gradually weakens the muscles because the body can't produce enough dystrophin.
The geneticist screened the newborn for early markers of dystrophy after two older siblings were diagnosed with it.
Her cousin's retinal dystrophy was diagnosed after he kept bumping into furniture at night, long before doctors traced it to a rare gene mutation.
The physical therapist adjusted his exercise plan every few months as the muscular dystrophy slowly reduced how far he could walk unaided.
The ophthalmologist recommended a corneal transplant once the dystrophy had clouded enough of his vision that reading street signs became impossible.
words.etymology: dys-(不良) + trophē(营养) → 营养不良

meanings.en: insolent or shameless boldness; disrespectful audacity

examples: He had the effrontery to ask for a raise the same week he missed three deadlines.
She screenshotted his message and posted it, stunned by the sheer effrontery of asking to borrow money twice.
She had the effrontery to present my unpublished research as her own idea in front of the entire department during the review.
The effrontery of showing up to the potluck with three uninvited coworkers and zero food left everyone quietly recalculating the portions.
My ex had the effrontery to text asking if I'd still watch his dog while he took his new girlfriend on vacation.
words.etymology: ex-(出) + frons(额头,同 affront) → 把脸豁出去 → 厚颜无耻

meanings.en: a widely held but mistaken belief, often based on flawed logic
meanings.zh: 谬误;似是而非的观点(区别于 fallible‘会犯错的’、infallible‘绝不出错的’)

examples: It's a common fallacy that multitasking makes you more productive — studies keep showing the opposite.
The landlord's argument rested on the fallacy that a higher rent automatically means a better tenant.
It's a common fallacy in the office that answering emails at midnight makes you look dedicated rather than just badly organized.
He kept pouring money into the failing food truck, trapped by the fallacy that quitting now would waste everything he'd already spent.
The gym's marketing leans on the fallacy that a pricier membership will somehow make people show up more often than a cheap one would.
words.etymology: fallere(欺骗、绊倒) → 似是而非的说法

meanings.en: capable of making errors or being wrong; not infallible
meanings.zh: 会犯错误的;不可靠的(区别于 fallacy‘谬误’这一名词)

examples: Even the AI model everyone trusted turned out to be fallible, confidently citing a court case that never existed.
Remember your doctor is fallible too — get a second opinion before agreeing to surgery.
Eyewitness memory is famously fallible, which is why the defense attorney kept pressing the witness on the lighting outside the bar that night.
Spellcheck is fallible enough that the wedding invitations went to print with the groom's name spelled two different ways.
The forecast is fallible enough that we packed ponchos for the 'zero percent chance of rain' company picnic, and thank god we did.
words.etymology: fallere(失误) → 会摔跟头的 → 会犯错

meanings.en: faithfulness or loyalty to a person, cause, or commitment
the degree of exactness with which something, especially sound or data, is reproduced
meanings.zh: (音频、数据等的)保真度;精确度

examples: After the affair came out, the whole group chat debated whether fidelity even matters in a long-distance relationship.
He swore fidelity to the startup's mission, then quietly interviewed at three competitors that same month.
The new earbuds promise studio-level fidelity, but honestly I can't hear the difference on the subway.
The remastered vinyl reissue promises far higher fidelity than the original cassette, though half the charm was always in that tape hiss.
He questioned his fidelity to the company the moment they laid off his entire team over a Friday afternoon email.
words.etymology: fides(信任) → 忠诚

meanings.en: to prevent or delay an event or action by acting first
meanings.zh: 预先阻止;先发制人地防止

examples: She sent a pre-emptive apology email to forestall the inevitable complaints about the delayed shipment.
The manager scheduled a one-on-one to forestall any rumors before the reorg was officially announced.
The company rushed to patent the design in three countries, hoping to forestall any knockoff versions before the product even launched.
To forestall a lawsuit, the airline offered every stranded passenger a full refund plus travel credit before anyone had even filed a complaint.
She forestalled the awkward question about her salary by bringing it up herself in the first five minutes of the interview.
words.etymology: fore-(预先) + stall(设摊拦住) → 提前拦下 → 先发制人

meanings.en: (of a group) difficult to control and prone to disagreement
meanings.zh: (团体)难以驾驭的;纷争不断的

meanings.en: easily irritated and prone to complaining or causing trouble; bad-tempered

examples: The toddler grew fractious around hour three of the flight, and so did everyone within five rows.
The fractious city council spent the whole meeting arguing over parking instead of the actual budget.
The fractious homeowners' association spent the entire meeting arguing about fence height instead of voting on the actual budget.
The dog got fractious after the third round of fireworks, pacing and whining until we finally moved him to the basement.
Negotiations between the fractious union locals nearly collapsed twice before the two sides finally agreed on a single contract proposal.
words.etymology: frangere(打碎) → 一碰就炸 → 难驾驭

meanings.en: incapable of making mistakes or being wrong; never failing
meanings.zh: 绝不会错的;万无一失的(区别于 fallible‘会犯错的’)

examples: No trading algorithm is infallible, no matter how many backtests the sales deck shows.
My grandmother's dumpling recipe is infallible — I've never seen it fail, even at high altitude.
The startup pitched its fraud-detection model as practically infallible, right up until it flagged a legitimate transaction and locked out ten thousand customers.
Fans treated the veteran umpire's calls as infallible for years, until slow-motion replay started proving otherwise almost every weekend.
No GPS app is infallible, as we learned when it confidently routed us down a closed logging road at midnight.
words.etymology: in-(不) + fallere(失误,反 fallible) → 万无一失

meanings.en: extremely small in size or amount, almost immeasurable

examples: The raise was so infinitesimal it barely covered the increase in her subway fare.
An infinitesimal delay in the algorithm's response time was enough to lose the trade to a competitor.
The nutrition label listed an infinitesimal amount of trans fat, so small it rounded to zero grams per serving.
A software patch shaved an infinitesimal fraction of a second off the app's load time, yet the release notes celebrated it like a breakthrough.
Her contact lens prescription changed by an infinitesimal degree between checkups, not enough to bother updating the old pair.
words.etymology: in-(不) + finis(界限) → 小到没有下界 → 无穷小

meanings.en: (of sound, especially a voice) sweet and smooth, pleasing to hear

examples: The podcast host has this mellifluous voice that makes even the ad reads sound like poetry.
Her mellifluous Cantonese lullabies were the only thing that got the baby to sleep on long flights.
The flight attendant's mellifluous safety announcement was so soothing that half the cabin missed the part about oxygen masks.
He recorded a mellifluous voicemail greeting on his first day at the firm, then spent weeks living up to it on actual calls.
The ASMR channel's mellifluous whispering has ten million subscribers who swear it's the only thing that gets them to sleep before midnight.
words.etymology: mel(蜂蜜) + fluere(流淌) → 像蜜一样流出来 → 悦耳

meanings.en: to act as an official presiding over an event, especially a sports match or ceremony
meanings.zh: 主持;担任司仪/裁判(比赛、仪式)

examples: The retired referee agreed to officiate the charity match, even though his knees hadn't forgiven him for years.
Her uncle, ordained online for the occasion, officiated the wedding in the backyard under a string of fairy lights.
Three officials officiate every professional match, splitting the field into zones to catch offside calls faster.
The middle-school gym teacher officiated the intramural basketball final after the usual referee called in sick that morning.
A childhood friend, newly certified online, officiated their courthouse elopement while holding an iPad for the two remote grandparents watching.
words.etymology: officium(职务) → 履行职务 → 主持

meanings.en: the quality of being excessively eager to assert authority or offer unwanted help and advice

examples: The new HOA president's officiousness turned a simple trash-can rule into a three-page memo with diagrams.
Nobody asked for his officiousness at the potluck, but he still rearranged everyone's dishes by 'proper' order.
The substitute teacher's officiousness turned a five-minute attendance check into a twenty-minute lecture on hallway pass procedure.
New neighbors quickly tired of the building super's officiousness, especially his insistence on inspecting every recycling bin for 'contamination.'
Her coworker's officiousness in cc'ing the entire department on a typo correction made the Slack channel groan in unison.
words.etymology: officium(职务) → 管到职务之外 → 好管闲事

meanings.en: suggesting that something bad or unpleasant is about to happen

examples: The 'we need to talk' Slack DM from her manager felt ominous before she even opened it.
Ominous gray clouds rolled in right as we reached the summit, so we turned back without taking a single photo.
The check-engine light flashed ominously on the dashboard just as they merged onto the highway for the eight-hour drive.
An ominous silence fell over the trading floor the moment the CEO's calendar invite titled 'Quick Chat' went out to the whole team.
The surgeon's ominous pause before explaining the scan results made her stomach drop before he said a single word.
words.etymology: omen(预兆) → 不祥

meanings.en: deliberately faithless or treacherous; deceitful in betraying trust

examples: His perfidious business partner secretly filed the patent under his own name the week before the deal closed.
History remembers him as perfidious, having secretly sold intelligence to both sides during the war.
Her perfidious college roommate copied her thesis outline word for word and submitted it to the same professor a day early.
The perfidious informant fed the police department false leads for months while quietly tipping off the very gang they were chasing.
Reviewers called the memoir's narrator perfidious, a man who smiled at his best friend's wedding while sleeping with the bride's sister.
words.etymology: per-(背离) + fides(信义,反 fidelity) → 背信弃义

meanings.en: (of a disease or condition) not responding to treatment
stubbornly resistant to authority or control; obstinate

examples: The refractory toddler refused every single vegetable on the plate, arms crossed like a tiny union rep.
After three rounds of chemo, the oncologist called it a refractory tumor and switched to a clinical trial.
His epilepsy proved refractory to four different anticonvulsants before the neurologist finally suggested a specialized diet.
Doctors classified her depression as refractory after she'd cycled through six medications with no lasting relief.
The refractory intern kept pushing his own deploy schedule despite three separate warnings from the lead engineer.
words.etymology: re-(顶回) + frangere(打断) → 顶回去不服 → 顽固难治

meanings.en: unnecessary, especially through being more than what is needed

examples: The consultant's 40-slide deck felt superfluous when the whole recommendation fit in one sentence.
She donated three superfluous kitchen appliances she'd bought during the sourdough phase of lockdown.
The onboarding checklist had a superfluous step asking new hires to fax a form, even though the office hasn't owned a fax machine in a decade.
Half the bullet points in his resignation letter felt superfluous once he'd already said the one sentence that mattered: he was leaving.
She trimmed every superfluous adjective from the press release until it read like a headline instead of a college essay.
words.etymology: super-(上面) + fluere(流) → 满得溢出来 → 多余

meanings.en: (of weather or a place) uncomfortably or oppressively hot

examples: We stood on the sweltering subway platform for twenty minutes waiting for a delayed train with no AC.
The gym felt sweltering by 6 p.m., every treadmill occupied and the AC clearly losing the fight.
The wedding photographer kept the bridal party posing in the sweltering parking lot for an extra twenty minutes chasing the 'perfect' light.
Their apartment's AC broke during the sweltering July heatwave, so they slept on the fire escape with a box fan propped in the window.
By the second inning, the sweltering bleachers had emptied out except for the die-hard fans clutching warm bottles of water.
words.etymology: 古英语 sweltan(热死过去) → 酷热难耐

meanings.en: (of a person) pleasant and easy to get along with because of shared tastes or interests
meanings.zh: 意气相投的;友善随和的(区别于 genial‘泛指和蔼可亲’)

meanings.en: (of an environment) suited or agreeable to one's nature or needs

examples: Her new coworkers turned out to be surprisingly congenial, the kind of team that actually laughs during standups.
He found the quiet coastal town far more congenial to writing than the noisy apartment in the city.
The hiring manager described the whole department as congenial, and after her first week she finally believed it — nobody hoarded credit.
He'd expected his ex's new boyfriend to be awkward at the barbecue, but the guy turned out to be genuinely congenial.
The startup's open-plan office, all beanbags and free espresso, was congenial to collaboration but murder on anyone who needed silence to code.
words.etymology: com-(同) + genius(天性) → 天性合得来 → 意气相投

meanings.en: to gather together in a crowd or group

examples: Delivery riders congregate outside the mall entrance every evening, phones propped up waiting for the next order.
Fans began to congregate outside the venue at dawn, hours before the doors even opened.
Smokers congregate by the loading dock every hour on the hour, badge lanyards swinging as they trade office gossip.
Freshmen congregated in the dorm lounge on move-in night, awkwardly comparing majors before anyone had unpacked a single box.
Pigeons congregate around the food truck at exactly noon, having apparently learned the lunch rush schedule better than some employees.
words.etymology: com-(一起) + grex(群) → 聚成群 → 聚集

meanings.en: (statistics/data analysis) to break a whole or a combined data set down into its separate component parts
meanings.zh: (统计学/数据分析)分解;拆分(汇总数据)

examples: The analyst disaggregated the national unemployment figure by region and immediately spotted a rural spike nobody had flagged.
We disaggregated the churn dashboard by plan tier and found enterprise customers barely ever cancel.
The HR report disaggregated salary data by gender and department, finally exposing a pay gap the leadership team had denied for years.
When the professor disaggregated the class's average test score by whether students attended office hours, the difference was impossible to ignore.
The city disaggregated its citywide crime statistics by neighborhood, revealing that two zip codes accounted for most of the reported spike.
words.etymology: dis-(拆开) + grex(群) → 把群拆散 → 分解数据

meanings.en: to cause or give rise to a feeling, situation, or condition

examples: Constant last-minute schedule changes engendered a quiet resentment among the shift workers, though nobody said so aloud.
The CEO's transparent handling of the layoffs engendered a surprising amount of trust, even among those let go.
The app's confusing checkout flow engendered so many abandoned carts that the team finally redesigned it after months of ignoring the complaints.
Sharing a cramped office bathroom for a year engendered an odd camaraderie among the startup's first five employees.
Constant public praise from the coach engendered jealousy among teammates who felt just as deserving of the spotlight.
words.etymology: en-(使) + generare(生育) → 生出来 → 产生

meanings.en: friendly, warm, and cheerful in manner
meanings.zh: 和蔼可亲的;友善的(区别于 congenial‘意气相投’,后者强调志趣相投而非普遍的和善)

examples: The genial bartender remembered everyone's order after just one visit and always asked about their week.
Despite the brutal quarterly numbers, the new manager stayed genial through the entire all-hands, cracking dad jokes to ease the tension.
The genial building doorman waved every delivery driver through with a joke, no matter how many packages piled up that day.
Despite losing the debate, the candidate stayed genial on stage, shaking his opponent's hand and complimenting the closing argument.
Her grandfather, genial even in his nineties, still greets every new nurse at the care home by name within a day.
words.etymology: genius(天性、守护神) → 本性温厚 → 和蔼

meanings.en: pompous or extravagant speech or writing, especially intended to impress
meanings.zh: 夸张浮华的言辞(区别于 grandiose,后者指计划、风格等本身浮夸宏大)

examples: Strip away the grandiloquence in his pitch deck and the product is just a to-do list app.
The wedding toast was pure grandiloquence — twenty minutes of flowery praise before he even mentioned the couple's names.
The keynote speaker's grandiloquence, calling a simple app 'the future of human connection,' drew a few muffled eye rolls backstage.
Beneath the professor's grandiloquence was a fairly simple idea that could've fit on one slide instead of forty minutes of lecture.
Critics mocked the senator's grandiloquence, noting that the actual policy proposal amounted to little more than a press release.
words.etymology: grandis(宏大) + loqui(说) → 把话说大 → 浮华辞藻

meanings.en: impressively large, elaborate, or ambitious, often in an exaggerated or unrealistic way
meanings.zh: (计划、风格等)浮夸的;好大喜功的

examples: His grandiose plan to franchise the food truck to twelve cities fell apart after month two in the first city.
The renovation started with grandiose sketches of a rooftop pool and ended with a slightly nicer balcony.
His grandiose vision for the app included a crypto wallet, a social network, and a delivery service, none of which ever shipped.
The startup's grandiose office tour — a slide, a nap pod, a beer tap — didn't match the two employees actually working there.
She scaled back the grandiose five-course wedding menu to a taco bar after seeing the catering quote.
words.etymology: grandis(宏大) → 大而无当 → 浮夸

meanings.en: done without good reason; uncalled for, especially something unpleasant or offensive
meanings.zh: 无端的;不必要的(尤指冒犯性的)

examples: Critics called the film's violence gratuitous, adding nothing to a plot that could've ended twenty minutes earlier.
His gratuitous comment about her weight had nothing to do with the project update she'd just given.
The reviewer called the sequel's product placement gratuitous, with the hero pausing mid-chase to admire a soda can label.
His gratuitous jab at her accent during the meeting had nothing to do with the budget she was presenting.
The app update added a gratuitous confetti animation every time you marked a single item off a to-do list.
words.etymology: gratis(白给的) ← gratia(恩惠) → 白添的 → 无端的

meanings.en: fond of company; sociable and enjoying being with other people

examples: She's the most gregarious person on the team, somehow knowing the name of every barista in a five-block radius.
Being gregarious made the coworking space feel less lonely, but it also meant he never got any actual work done before noon.
Their gregarious golden retriever greets every stranger on the block like a long-lost friend, tail going the second the leash comes out.
The new hire was so gregarious that by lunch on day one he'd already organized a group chat for the entire floor.
Grandma stayed gregarious well into her eighties, chatting up strangers in the grocery checkout line until the cashier had to intervene.
words.etymology: grex(群,同 congregate) → 爱扎堆 → 合群

meanings.en: lacking any obvious organizing principle; done or chosen at random
meanings.zh: 无计划的;杂乱无章的;随意的

examples: His haphazard filing system meant the tax receipts were scattered across four different apps and a shoebox.
The move was so haphazard that boxes labeled 'kitchen' turned up in the bathroom three weeks later.
The startup's haphazard onboarding process left new hires guessing which Slack channel actually mattered for their team.
His haphazard approach to watering the office plants meant half of them thrived and the other half quietly died in a corner.
The evacuation felt haphazard, with some floors getting clear instructions over the intercom and others hearing nothing at all.
words.etymology: hap(运气) + hazard(偶然) → 全凭碰巧 → 杂乱无章

meanings.en: self-willed and obstinate, insisting on having one's own way

examples: Their headstrong toddler insisted on wearing rain boots to the beach and refused every other pair of shoes.
He's headstrong enough to quit a stable job for the startup idea everyone else called reckless.
The headstrong new intern rewrote the onboarding script without asking anyone, convinced her version was simply better.
Their headstrong golden retriever refuses to walk any route except the one that passes the bakery with free samples.
She's always been headstrong about diet advice, ignoring three doctors before finally trying the meal plan her sister suggested.
words.etymology: head + strong → 头太硬 → 固执己见

meanings.en: very plentiful; produced or given in large amounts
meanings.zh: 大量的;丰富的(区别于 suffuse‘弥漫;充满’)

examples: He offered profuse apologies for the late delivery, along with a coupon nobody asked for.
By the third mile of the hike in that heat, we were all sweating profusely and regretting the extra layer.
The chef sent out a plate of free desserts with profuse apologies after the kitchen mixed up the couple's anniversary order.
Profuse bleeding from the paper cut looked far worse than it actually was, judging by how much he panicked.
She thanked the volunteers profusely, handing out gift cards to everyone who'd shown up before dawn to set up the shelter.
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + fundere(倾倒) → 大把倒出来 → 大量的

meanings.en: moving backward, or reverting to an earlier and typically worse state
(astronomy) appearing to move backward relative to other bodies

examples: Cutting funding for the childcare program felt like a retrograde step after years of progress on parental leave.
Mercury goes retrograde again this month, and half my group chat is already blaming it for canceled flights.
Rolling back the city's bike lanes felt like a retrograde move to commuters who'd finally started leaving their cars at home.
The new dress code, banning sneakers and requiring ties again, struck most of the office as a bizarrely retrograde policy.
The astronomy app flagged Mars entering retrograde motion next week, and the group chat immediately started planning around it.
words.etymology: retro-(向后) + gradi(行走) → 往回走 → 倒退

meanings.en: resolutely and dutifully firm and unwavering in loyalty, purpose, or belief

examples: Her steadfast support got him through three rounds of layoffs at the company and the job search after.
Despite the market crash, he stayed steadfast in his monthly index-fund contributions instead of panic-selling.
The old dog stayed steadfast by the hospital bed for three days straight, refusing every walk until she came home.
He remained steadfast in disputing the unpaid-overtime claim, even after three coworkers quietly gave up and signed the new contract.
Her steadfast refusal to answer work emails after 7 p.m. earned eye rolls at first, then a few quiet copycats on the team.
words.etymology: stead(位置) + fast(牢固) → 站定不挪 → 坚定不移

meanings.en: (of a color, light, or feeling) to gradually spread through or over something
meanings.zh: (光线、颜色、情绪等)弥漫;充满(区别于 profuse‘大量的’这一形容词)

examples: Golden light suffused the office at sunset, making even the spreadsheet on her screen look almost pretty.
A quiet pride suffused the room when the interns' prototype actually worked on the first try.
Relief suffused the delivery room the second the baby's first cry cut through the silence.
A faint smell of cinnamon suffused the whole apartment building every time the bakery downstairs started its morning bake.
Embarrassment suffused his face when he realized he'd sent the complaint about his boss directly to his boss.
words.etymology: sub-(自下) + fundere(倾倒,同 profuse) → 漫上来 → 弥漫

meanings.en: the solemn or formal renunciation of a belief, cause, or claim, often under oath

examples: His public abjuration of the conspiracy theory came only after he'd lost half his followers and two sponsorships.
The contract included a formal abjuration of any future claim to the company's intellectual property.
The senator's abjuration of the party he'd represented for two decades stunned even his closest staffers.
Her public abjuration of fast fashion came with a closet purge livestreamed to half a million followers.
The plea deal required a written abjuration of any further lawsuits against the company in exchange for the settlement.
words.etymology: ab-(离开) + jurare(发誓) → 用誓言撇清 → 宣誓放弃

meanings.en: to explain, discuss, or criticize something in excessive, tedious detail
meanings.zh: 过分强调;喋喋不休地讲(某事)

examples: I won't belabor the point, but the deck already covers page after page of why the budget doesn't work.
The performance review belabored one missed deadline for ten minutes and skipped six months of good work.
The lawyer belabored a single typo in the contract for twenty minutes while the actual clause everyone cared about went unmentioned.
I don't want to belabor this, but the third bug report says the same thing the first two already said.
The coach belabored last season's loss so much in practice that half the team stopped listening by week three.
words.etymology: be-(加强) + labor(用力) → 使劲过了头 → 过分强调

meanings.en: to describe, portray, or explain something precisely and clearly
to indicate the exact position of a border or boundary

examples: The onboarding doc delineates exactly who approves what, so no ticket sits in limbo for a week again.
The surveyor's map clearly delineated the property line, ending the years-long fence dispute between neighbors.
The new employee handbook delineates exactly which expenses need a manager's sign-off before you book anything.
Her thesis carefully delineates the difference between correlation and causation using three separate case studies.
The zoning map delineated a new bike-lane corridor that cut straight through what used to be street parking.
words.etymology: de-(描出) + linea(线) → 勾出轮廓 → 精确描述

meanings.en: to cause someone to lose enthusiasm, hope, or confidence

examples: Getting rejected by eleven VCs in a row would dishearten most founders, but she just tightened the pitch deck and kept going.
Don't let one bad performance review dishearten you — ask for specific feedback and build a 30-day improvement plan.
The team's second failed product launch disheartened even the most optimistic engineers, and morale took weeks to recover.
Don't let one low star rating dishearten you — the other forty reviews are what actually move the algorithm.
Losing the championship game on a last-second call disheartened the whole team, but the coach had them back at practice by Monday.
words.etymology: dis-(去掉) + heart(心气) → 泄了气 → 使沮丧

meanings.en: (medicine/education) a learning disorder that impairs a person's ability to read, caused by difficulty processing written language
meanings.zh: (医学/教育)诵读困难症;阅读障碍

examples: The school psychologist diagnosed his dyslexia in third grade, after he kept reversing 'b' and 'd' on every spelling test.
She didn't realize she had dyslexia until college, when a professor suggested she try audiobooks instead of dense textbooks.
The company's new hiring test unintentionally screened out candidates with dyslexia, since it was entirely a timed written exam.
He started using a text-to-speech extension after learning his son's dyslexia diagnosis explained years of struggling with bedtime reading.
Her dyslexia made spreadsheets a nightmare until a coworker showed her a color-coding trick that made the columns easier to track.

relatedForms.zh: 诵读困难的;患诵读困难症的

words.etymology: dys-(不良) + lexis(词,比 dystrophy 换了后半) → 阅读障碍

meanings.en: deriving ideas, style, or taste from a broad and diverse range of sources
meanings.zh: 兼收并蓄的;广泛涉猎的

examples: Her Spotify Wrapped was so eclectic — K-pop, death metal, and lo-fi study beats all in the top ten — that friends assumed she'd shared an account.
The new café has an eclectic menu that jumps from Sichuan mapo tofu to Neapolitan pizza, and somehow it works.
His eclectic bookshelf jumps from quantum physics to celebrity memoirs, with zero apparent logic to the order.
The gallery's eclectic collection mixes Renaissance portraits with neon sculpture, which somehow doesn't feel as jarring as it sounds.
Her eclectic taste in podcasts means her commute alternates between true crime, ancient history, and startup gossip.
words.etymology: ek-(从中) + legein(挑选) → 各处挑好的 → 兼收并蓄

meanings.en: (medicine) chosen by the patient rather than urgently necessary
(education) an optional course that a student may choose to take

examples: Because the surgery was elective, the hospital pushed it back three weeks to free up beds for emergency cases.
He filled his last semester with electives — jazz history, wine tasting, and a pottery class — after finishing every requirement early.
Her insurance flagged the nose job as elective and denied coverage, leaving her to pay the full bill herself.
The clinic reschedules elective procedures first whenever the ER gets slammed with trauma cases.
She picked ceramics as her elective purely because the classroom had the best view of the quad.
words.etymology: e-(出) + legere(选) → 可以自己选的 → 择期的

meanings.en: excessively critical, finding fault in things that are minor or unimportant
meanings.zh: 吹毛求疵的;过分苛求的

examples: The code reviewer was so hypercritical that he flagged variable names in a one-line hotfix meant to ship in ten minutes.
Her hypercritical father found something wrong with every report card, even the ones covered in A's.
The hypercritical food blogger docked the taco truck a star for using paper napkins instead of cloth.
Being hypercritical of his own drafts meant he rewrote the opening paragraph nine times before sending the email at all.
The hypercritical landlord itemized every scuff on the wall, even ones clearly there before they'd moved in.
words.etymology: hyper-(过度) + critical(挑剔) → 吹毛求疵

meanings.en: a person who regularly finds it difficult to fall or stay asleep
having chronic difficulty sleeping

examples: As a lifelong insomniac, she keeps three different white-noise apps on her phone for the nights nothing else works.
The sleep clinic finally gave the insomniac patient a diagnosis: chronic anxiety was keeping his cortisol elevated at night.
As a self-described insomniac, he's tried melatonin, magnesium, and a $400 mattress, and none of it has fixed his 3 a.m. scrolling habit.
The insomniac barista started taking the 5 a.m. shift on purpose, figuring she might as well get paid for being awake.
Her roommate, a chronic insomniac, keeps the kitchen light on until 2 a.m., which drives everyone else in the apartment a little crazy.
words.etymology: in-(无) + somnus(睡眠) → 失眠者

meanings.en: narrow-mindedness or isolation resulting from limited contact with other people or ideas

examples: After two years of remote work with the same five coworkers on Slack, he noticed his own insularity — nobody had challenged an idea of his in months.
Critics say the startup's insularity — hiring only from one university, ignoring outside user feedback — is why the product feels stale.
The small-town paper's insularity showed in its coverage, since every story somehow traced back to the same three families.
Years of insularity within the finance team meant nobody questioned the spreadsheet formula everyone had copied from a decade-old template.
Living on the same block his whole life gave him a kind of insularity he didn't notice until he finally traveled abroad.
words.etymology: insula(岛) → 活成一座孤岛 → 狭隘闭塞

meanings.en: to intervene on behalf of another person, especially to resolve a dispute

examples: When HR threatened to fire her intern over a missed deadline, the team lead interceded quietly and got him a second chance.
My mom always interceded when my sister and I fought over the thermostat, texting both of us until we agreed on 72 degrees.
The union rep interceded before the warehouse worker could be fired over a single late clock-in.
Neighbors interceded when the landlord tried to raise everyone's rent mid-lease, threatening to report the building for code violations.
The teacher interceded between the two students arguing over the group project, splitting the slides fairly down the middle.
words.etymology: inter-(之间) + cedere(走) → 走到两边中间 → 说情

meanings.en: an abrupt remark inserted into a conversation
(grammar) a word or phrase expressing sudden emotion, used as an exclamation

examples: The grammar workbook listed 'ouch,' 'wow,' and 'ugh' as classic interjections that stand alone with an exclamation point.
Her sarcastic interjection during the budget meeting — 'sure, that'll fix everything' — got a nervous laugh from half the room.
His interjection during the eulogy — a sudden joke about grandpa's terrible driving — got the whole room laughing through their tears.
Every time the toddler heard a siren, he'd shout an interjection of pure delight from the back seat.
The ESL textbook devoted an entire chapter to interjections, teaching students when 'oh no' works better than a full sentence.
words.etymology: inter-(之间) + jacere(投掷) → 中间扔一句 → 插话

meanings.en: to estimate or insert a value between two known data points
to insert a remark or passage into a text or conversation, sometimes altering its original meaning

examples: The AI note-taking app quietly interpolates missing words whenever the Zoom audio cuts out, which is great until it invents a sentence you never said.
Editors interpolated a footnote into the leaked memo before forwarding it, and nobody could tell which lines were the CEO's and which weren't.
The weather model interpolates temperature readings between stations to estimate conditions in towns without a sensor.
Animators interpolate the frames between two keyframes so a character's walk looks smooth instead of choppy.
The spreadsheet macro interpolated missing sales figures for the holiday week, which nobody noticed until the totals looked suspiciously round.
words.etymology: inter-(之间) + polire(打磨) → 在两点之间补上 → 插值

meanings.en: to scatter or place things at intervals among other things

examples: She intersperses her Instagram feed with gym selfies and reposts of climate infographics so it doesn't feel like just another influencer page.
The professor interspersed the three-hour lecture with short YouTube clips, which was the only reason anyone stayed awake past minute forty.
The trainer interspersed short sprints between sets of squats, which made the workout feel shorter even though it wasn't.
She interspersed the wedding slideshow with candid shots from childhood, and half the guests were crying before the vows even started.
The podcast interspersed serious interview segments with quick listener voicemails, keeping the two-hour episode from dragging.
words.etymology: inter-(之间) + spargere(撒) → 撒在中间 → 穿插

meanings.en: having, showing, or done with good judgment or sense, especially in practical matters

examples: A judicious mix of index funds and a small crypto allocation is how her financial advisor described the portfolio — boring, but it survived the crash.
Judicious use of the mute button turned a two-hour all-hands into something she could actually half-listen to while answering emails.
A judicious edit cut the report from twelve pages to three, and somehow nothing important was lost.
The referee's judicious use of video review overturned exactly the one call that mattered in the final minute.
Judicious spacing of the wedding invitations kept two feuding cousins at opposite ends of the reception hall.
words.etymology: jus(法) + dicere(宣告) → 像法官那样判断 → 明智

meanings.en: (medicine) a substance that promotes bowel movements, used to relieve constipation
having the effect of loosening the bowels

examples: The gastroenterologist recommended a mild laxative for a few days rather than jumping straight to a colonoscopy prep dose.
Prunes have a well-documented laxative effect, something she discovered the hard way before a six-hour flight.
The nursing home keeps a laxative on the evening med cart for residents who mention going three days without relief.
He packed a laxative in his hiking bag after last year's trip taught him altitude and freeze-dried meals don't mix well.
The vet prescribed a feline laxative after the cat stopped using the litter box for two days straight.
words.etymology: laxus(松) → 使松下来 → 泻药

meanings.en: (philosophy) the branch of philosophy concerned with the fundamental nature of reality, being, and existence

examples: The seminar spent the whole afternoon on Aristotle's metaphysics, debating what it even means for something to 'exist.'
His thesis leaned heavily on metaphysics, questioning whether time is a real dimension or just a construct of perception.
The late-night dorm conversation somehow drifted from video games into metaphysics, with someone insisting free will was just an illusion.
His philosophy minor was really just an excuse to keep taking metaphysics electives instead of finishing his actual major requirements.
The podcast episode on metaphysics tried to explain personal identity over time using nothing but a broken ship as an example.
words.etymology: meta-(在…之后) —— 亚里士多德此书排在《物理学》之后 → 形而上学

meanings.en: the criminal offense of willfully telling an untruth after having sworn to tell the truth

examples: The witness's Instagram story, timestamped an hour before her alibi began, was enough for the DA to charge her with perjury.
Lying to Congress under oath isn't just embarrassing — it's perjury, and the executive's lawyers spent the weekend scrambling.
The whistleblower's lawyer warned him that changing his story on the stand now would amount to perjury.
Prosecutors added a perjury charge after the CFO's sworn testimony directly contradicted the emails found in discovery.
She worried that even a small exaggeration in her deposition could technically count as perjury.
words.etymology: per-(违背) + jurare(发誓,同 abjuration) → 背誓 → 伪证

meanings.en: clever or skillful, especially in using the hands or in social situations

examples: Her adroit handling of the layoff announcement — no jargon, direct answers, a real Q&A — kept morale from collapsing entirely.
He's adroit enough with a wok to turn Tuesday's leftover rotisserie chicken into fried rice that tastes intentional.
His adroit footwork got him past two defenders in a space that shouldn't have existed.
The mediator's adroit questioning got both roommates to admit they'd each forgotten to pay the electric bill.
She's adroit at turning a customer's angry email into a five-star review by the end of the reply thread.
words.etymology: 法语 à droit(合乎正道、右手那侧) → 顺手 → 灵巧

meanings.en: to suggest or refer to something indirectly, without mentioning it explicitly

examples: In the town hall, the CEO alluded to 'some difficult decisions ahead' without ever saying the word layoffs.
Her caption alluded to a breakup — 'new chapter, new city' — without tagging anyone, but everyone in the group chat knew who she meant.
The professor alluded to next week's pop quiz without technically confirming it, which sent the whole class into a group-chat panic.
His toast alluded to a rocky engagement without naming names, and half the table exchanged nervous glances.
The press release alluded to 'strategic restructuring,' a phrase everyone in the office correctly read as layoffs.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + ludere(戏耍) → 绕着逗一句 → 暗指

meanings.en: comparable in certain respects to something else, typically for the purpose of explanation

examples: The onboarding coach compared learning the new CRM to learning a new phone — analogous enough that nobody felt dumb for asking basic questions.
Training a language model on biased data is analogous to teaching a kid using only one newspaper's opinion page.
Debugging the supply chain issue felt analogous to untangling a single knot from a drawer full of charging cables.
The professor found running a marathon analogous to writing a dissertation — mostly pacing yourself through the boring middle miles.
Losing your only backup drive is analogous to losing the only key to a house you can't ever re-enter.
words.etymology: ana-(依照) + logos(比例) → 按同一比例 → 类似

meanings.en: to think deeply about something

examples: He spent the entire commute cogitating over whether to accept the counteroffer or take the new job's better title.
She likes to cogitate in the shower, which is why half her best product ideas show up in a voice memo at 7 a.m.
She spent the whole flight cogitating over whether to bring up the promotion or wait for her manager to mention it first.
He likes to cogitate on long walks, phone left at home, until the plot hole in his novel finally resolves itself.
The committee cogitated for an entire meeting over a decision that could've been an email.
words.etymology: com-(一起) + agitare(搅动) → 把念头搅在一起 → 沉思

meanings.en: to erase or rub out completely, often a mark, memory, or feeling; also, to make oneself inconspicuous (self-efface)
meanings.zh: 抹去,擦除;(自谦)使不显眼

examples: No amount of scrubbing could efface the coffee ring the last tenant left on the countertop, so she just bought a runner to cover it.
He self-effaces in every meeting, crediting the whole team even when the fix was entirely his idea.
Years of foot traffic had effaced the welcome mat's lettering until it just read a faded blur.
The graffiti removal crew couldn't fully efface the mural without damaging the brick underneath it.
She effaces her own contributions so thoroughly in interviews that her resume ends up undermining her strongest projects.
words.etymology: ex-(去掉) + face(面) → 把表面抹掉 → 抹去

meanings.en: to make something clear by explaining it

examples: The onboarding doc doesn't elucidate how expense reports actually get approved, so new hires just ask in the help channel.
Can you elucidate why the API call fails only on Tuesdays? Nobody on the team can reproduce it.
The lawyer elucidated the contract's termination clause line by line until the client finally understood the penalty.
Can you elucidate what 'synergy' actually means in this slide, or is it just there to sound impressive?
The professor's office hours exist mainly to elucidate the parts of the syllabus nobody reads carefully the first time.
words.etymology: e-(出) + lux/luc-(光) → 把光放出来 → 阐明

meanings.en: to escape from or avoid someone or something, often cleverly
(of a fact, name, or idea) to fail to be remembered, understood, or achieved by someone

examples: The delivery guy eluded the building's broken elevator entirely by using the freight entrance everyone forgets exists.
Her name eluded him the whole conversation, even though they'd matched on the app three weeks earlier.
The suspect eluded police for three days by switching cars twice and paying for everything in cash.
The raccoon eluded every trap the exterminator set, somehow always taking the bait without tripping the latch.
The password eluded her completely until she remembered it was just her childhood dog's name with a number tacked on.
words.etymology: ex-(出) + ludere(戏耍,同 allude) → 耍着溜掉 → 躲避

meanings.en: originating in the distant past, beyond memory or record (usually in 'time immemorial')

examples: Landlords have been raising rent right before renewal season since time immemorial, or at least since she moved to this city.
The recipe, passed down since time immemorial according to her grandmother, turned out to be a 1987 magazine clipping.
Office workers have complained about the coffee machine since time immemorial, or at least since the building's last renovation.
The village has settled water disputes the same informal way since time immemorial, long before any court got involved.
Parents have been threatening to 'turn this car around' since time immemorial, and it has never once worked.
words.etymology: in-(不) + memoria(记忆) → 记不起源头 → 远古的

meanings.en: tending to talk a great deal; very talkative

examples: The Uber driver was so loquacious that she learned his entire divorce story before they'd even left the airport parking lot.
He's loquacious in Slack threads but goes completely silent whenever the camera turns on in a video call.
Her loquacious grandmother can turn a five-minute grocery run into a forty-minute recap of the entire neighborhood's business.
He's loquacious at parties but goes quiet the moment someone asks him a direct question about his own life.
The loquacious tour guide crammed three centuries of history into a walk that was supposed to take twenty minutes.
words.etymology: loqui(说,同 circumlocution) → 话多 → 健谈

meanings.en: expressed clearly, easy to understand
able to think clearly, especially during illness or in a lucid dream
meanings.zh: 神志清醒的;(梦境)清醒的

examples: Her resignation email was refreshingly lucid — three sentences, no corporate softening, exactly why she was leaving.
The doctor said Grandpa was fully lucid during the video call, joking about the hospital food just like always.
He's been journaling before bed to try to have more lucid dreams, and honestly the app's success rate is questionable.
The engineer's postmortem was refreshingly lucid, laying out exactly what broke and why without a single buzzword.
Her lucid explanation of the tax form saved her roommate an hour of confused Googling.
words.etymology: lux/luc-(光,同 elucidate) → 透亮 → 清晰

meanings.en: a general feeling of discomfort, illness, or unease whose exact cause is hard to identify; also a vague sense of dissatisfaction within a group or system
meanings.zh: (身体)不适感;(社会/经济)不景气,萎靡

examples: A low-grade malaise has hung over the office ever since the acquisition was announced — nobody's been fired yet, but nobody's relaxed either.
She woke up with a strange malaise, not sick enough to call in but too foggy to focus on the sprint review.
He couldn't shake the malaise that followed finishing the big project, that odd letdown once the deadline pressure disappeared.
Economists pointed to slowing wage growth as one symptom of the broader malaise gripping the housing market.
A vague malaise crept over him every Sunday evening, the familiar dread of another Monday standup looming.
words.etymology: mal-(坏) + aise(舒适) → 不舒服 → 不适、萎靡

meanings.en: having or showing a wish to do evil or harm to others

examples: The anonymous review wasn't just critical, it was malevolent — clearly written by someone who wanted the restaurant to close, not improve.
In the finale, the assistant's chatbot turns out to be quietly malevolent, rerouting deliveries just to watch people panic.
The prank wasn't just annoying; it was malevolent, since someone had deliberately unplugged the server rack minutes before the big demo.
Fans debated whether the show's AI villain was truly malevolent or just following its programming to its logical, terrifying end.
Her coworker's malevolent gossip cost two people their year-end bonuses before anyone traced the rumor back to its source.
words.etymology: male(坏) + velle(愿望,反 benevolent) → 存坏心 → 恶意

meanings.en: to say harmful, often untrue things about someone; to slander
having an evil influence; harmful, especially in a subtle or dangerous way

examples: Former employees maligned the startup on Glassdoor so relentlessly that recruiters started asking about it in interviews.
The tumor's malign growth pattern meant the oncologist wanted to start treatment within the week, not after the family vacation.
Rival campaigns maligned each other so relentlessly on social media that most undecided voters just tuned out entirely.
He maligned his old business partner in every interview, conveniently leaving out the lawsuit he'd lost against him.
The report warned of malign interference in the election, run through a network of accounts nobody could quite trace.
words.etymology: malus(坏) + gignere(生) → 天生带坏 → 中伤

meanings.en: to formally release someone from slavery; to emancipate

examples: The museum exhibit displayed the 1850s document by which a Virginia plantation owner manumitted eleven enslaved people in his will.
Historians debate why some owners manumitted enslaved workers only after death rather than while they could still claim credit publicly.
The will specified that his enslaved cook be manumitted immediately upon his death, unlike the others named in the document.
Some enslavers manumitted only the children they'd fathered, a detail genealogists now use to trace hidden family lines.
The court records show the judge manumitted the woman after ruling her original sale had been fraudulent.
words.etymology: manus(手) + mittere(放开) → 松开手 → 解放奴隶

meanings.en: a professional soldier hired to fight for a foreign army or private group
motivated solely by a desire for money or personal gain
meanings.zh: 唯利是图的;惟利是图的

examples: The documentary follows a former mercenary who fought in three different civil wars before turning to private security consulting.
His sudden interest in her after the promotion felt mercenary — nobody texts that fast about someone with a smaller salary.
The private military company recruited former special forces soldiers as mercenaries for contracts across three different conflict zones.
The old western cast the drifter as a mercenary, loyal to whoever's paying until the final act flips the story.
Their sudden generosity felt mercenary, arriving right after they found out about the inheritance.
words.etymology: merces(报酬) → 拿钱办事 → 雇佣兵

meanings.en: the complete destruction or removal of all traces of something

examples: The wildfire's obliteration of the entire hillside neighborhood was visible even from the satellite images the news kept replaying.
One bad update led to the obliteration of three years of customer data before anyone thought to check the backup logs.
The flood's obliteration of the basement archive meant decades of handwritten records were simply gone.
Critics called the redesign an obliteration of the brand's original identity, with nothing recognizable left but the name.
The demolition crew finished the building's obliteration in under six hours, leaving only a flattened lot where the mall used to be.
words.etymology: ob-(涂掉) + littera(字母) → 把字迹刮平 → 彻底消除

meanings.en: to criticize someone sharply, especially from a position of authority
a sharp expression of disapproval or criticism

examples: The manager's public rebuke over the missed deadline — in front of the whole stand-up — was why two people started job hunting that afternoon.
The judge rebuked the lawyer for showing up late a third time, threatening contempt charges if it happened again.
The referee rebuked the coach for storming onto the field, adding a technical foul before play even resumed.
Her editor rebuked her gently for burying the lede three paragraphs deep in an otherwise solid article.
The board's rebuke of the CEO's spending was unusually blunt for a group known to avoid confrontation.
words.etymology: re-(回) + 古法语 buchier(砍) → 回砍一刀 → 严厉斥责

meanings.en: to formally express disapproval of someone's actions, especially officially
a formal expression of disapproval, especially an official one

examples: HR issued a formal written reprimand after he cc'd the entire company on a complaint email meant for one manager.
The nurse received a reprimand for skipping the checklist, even though the patient was fine — protocol is protocol.
The pilot was reprimanded by the airline for posting cockpit selfies mid-flight, even though nothing was technically against protocol.
Her coach reprimanded the star forward in front of the whole team for missing curfew before the championship game.
A single reprimand in his file was enough to make the promotion committee pass him over for someone with a cleaner record.
words.etymology: re-(回) + premere(压) → 压回去 → 训斥

meanings.en: corresponding in size or degree; proportionate

examples: The offer letter promised a salary commensurate with experience, which turned out to mean 15% less than her last job.
His punishment felt commensurate with the mistake — a warning, not a firing, for one missed deadline.
The startup gave him a title commensurate with his workload — Head of Everything — but the pay stayed exactly the same.
Her performance bonus felt commensurate with the extra 20 hours she'd logged, unlike last year's flat 2% raise.
The gym membership tiers are supposed to be commensurate with usage, but the cheapest plan still costs more than the priciest at his old gym.
words.etymology: com-(共同) + mensura(尺度) → 同一把尺 → 相称

meanings.en: a feeling of smug or uncritical satisfaction with oneself or one's achievements, often leading to a lack of awareness of danger

examples: Three quarters of record growth bred a complacency at the company that left them completely unprepared when a competitor undercut prices overnight.
After passing the first two code reviews easily, his complacency showed — the third PR had a bug that took down staging.
Five years without a single security incident had bred a complacency in the IT department that the ransomware attack shattered overnight.
The veteran goalie's complacency between the posts cost the team a soft goal in the final minute of the semifinal.
Winning every deal that quarter created a complacency in the sales team, and nobody bothered to update the outdated pitch deck.
words.etymology: com-(完全) + placere(取悦,同 placate) → 自己把自己哄美了 → 自满

meanings.en: (finance) to express or state a value in a specified currency or unit

examples: The bond was denominated in euros, so the fund had to hedge currency risk before booking the yield.
Most oil contracts are still denominated in US dollars, which is exactly why some exporters want an alternative benchmark.
The freelancer's invoices were denominated in euros, so a weak dollar quietly boosted her income every time she converted the payment.
Because the loan was denominated in Swiss francs, the sudden currency spike doubled her monthly payment overnight.
The crowdfunding platform lets creators denominate their goals in either dollars or a stablecoin pegged to the dollar.
words.etymology: de-(下) + nomen(名) → 定个名目 → 以某单位计价

meanings.en: to publicly declare something to be wrong or evil; to criticize harshly and openly

examples: The union denounced the new scheduling app within hours of its rollout, calling it surveillance dressed up as convenience.
She denounced her former business partner on LinkedIn, accusing him of forging the investor deck they'd used to raise seed funding.
The whistleblower denounced her former employer on a leaked earnings call, listing three safety violations no one had reported.
Fans denounced the streaming platform's price hike within minutes of the announcement, flooding its support account with cancellation threats.
The city council member publicly denounced the developer's rezoning plan, calling it a giveaway dressed up as affordable housing.
words.etymology: de-(向下) + nuntiare(通报) → 当众点名 → 公开谴责

meanings.en: the state of being famous, respected, or superior within a particular field

examples: She reached a kind of quiet eminence in the field — not famous outside academia, but every grad student cited her thesis.
His eminence as the go-to expert on tax law meant his newsletter got forwarded around every finance Slack in the city.
By forty, she'd earned a kind of eminence in restaurant criticism — one negative line from her could close a place within a month.
His eminence in competitive chess didn't stop him from losing to a fourteen-year-old at the regional open.
The surgeon's eminence in transplant medicine meant patients flew in from three continents just for a consultation.
words.etymology: e-(出) + minere(突出) → 冒出头 → 显赫

meanings.en: to absorb all of someone's attention or interest completely

examples: The new true-crime podcast engrossed her so completely that she missed her subway stop twice in one week.
He was so engrossed in the spreadsheet, trying to make the numbers reconcile before the 9 a.m. review, that he didn't hear his phone ring.
The escape room engrossed the whole team so thoroughly that nobody noticed the hour had run out until the buzzer sounded.
Assembling the 2,000-piece puzzle engrossed grandpa so completely that he skipped his usual Sunday nap for the first time in years.
The mystery novel engrossed her on the red-eye flight, and she finished all 400 pages before the wheels touched down.
words.etymology: en-(使) + gross(整批、大宗) → 被整个占住 → 全神贯注

meanings.en: the great seriousness or moral gravity of something extremely bad; sometimes a monstrous or outrageous act (not simply 'great size')
meanings.zh: (性质)极端严重性;滔天罪行,暴行

examples: It took her a full week to grasp the enormity of the data breach — not just the numbers, but how many people's lives it touched.
Historians still argue about how ordinary citizens failed to register the enormity of what was happening next door.
It wasn't until the sentencing hearing that the enormity of what he'd done to his clients' retirement funds truly sank in for the jury.
She only grasped the enormity of ghosting her business partner after he texted that he'd lost his house over the failed deal.
The documentary makes viewers sit with the enormity of the chemical spill — not the acreage, but the decades of illness it caused.
words.etymology: e-(超出) + norma(规范) → 出了格 → 滔天罪行

meanings.en: deserving or causing public disgrace or shame; humiliating

examples: The startup's ignominious collapse — funds frozen, founder blocked on Twitter by his own investors — became a case study at three business schools.
He suffered an ignominious exit from the company, escorted out by security while his badge was deactivated mid-walk.
The quarterback's ignominious fumble on the one-yard line became the only clip anyone remembers from the entire season.
Her ignominious retreat from the debate stage — mic cutting out mid-sentence, no comeback line ready — went viral within the hour.
The chain's ignominious bankruptcy filing came just eighteen months after its 'store of the future' flagship opening made headlines.
words.etymology: in-(无) + nomen(名声,同 denominate) → 名声扫地 → 可耻

meanings.en: about to happen very soon — emphasizes closeness in time
meanings.zh: 即将发生的;迫近的(强调时间紧迫)

examples: The push notification warned of imminent flight delays two hours before anyone at the gate had heard a word from staff.
With the funding round's imminent close, the founders spent the weekend rewriting the pitch deck one last time.
Doctors warned the family that his passing felt imminent, so relatives who lived across the country booked same-day flights.
With the storm's landfall imminent, the coastal town's grocery stores sold out of bottled water by noon.
She refreshed the tracking page every ten minutes once the delivery text said her package was imminent, thirty minutes before the doorbell rang.
words.etymology: in-(向) + minere(突出,同 eminence) → 悬在头顶 → 迫近

meanings.en: about to happen, especially something unpleasant — emphasizes a looming, ominous sense hanging over the present, more than pure timing
meanings.zh: 即将来临的;迫近的(强调笼罩性的威胁感)

examples: The whole team could feel the impending layoffs before HR sent a single email — calendars kept clearing themselves overnight.
She couldn't shake the sense of impending doom every Sunday night, thinking about Monday's stand-up.
The bakery's impending closure was obvious to regulars weeks before the 'thanks for 12 great years' sign went up.
He could sense the impending breakup in the clipped one-word texts, days before she actually said it out loud.
The company's impending merger leaked through investor forums a full month before the official press release.
words.etymology: in-(向) + pendere(悬挂) → 悬着未落 → 即将来临

meanings.en: (of a place) unable to be captured or broken into; (of an argument or position) unable to be overcome or refuted
meanings.zh: 坚不可摧的;牢不可破的

examples: Their two-factor authentication setup felt impregnable until a single leaked recovery code brought the whole account down in ten minutes.
The debate coach built an impregnable case using nothing but the opponent's own quoted statistics.
The medieval fortress on the cliff looked impregnable until archaeologists found the old smugglers' tunnel beneath the kitchen.
The incumbent's lead in the poll seemed impregnable in September, but three debate gaffes erased it by October.
The chess grandmaster's opening felt impregnable for thirty moves, then one overlooked pawn push cracked the whole position.
words.etymology: in-(不) + prehendere(抓取) → 抓不进去 → 坚不可摧

meanings.en: harmful or hostile; unfavorable to something

examples: Constant Slack pings and four overlapping meetings a day are inimical to any kind of deep, focused work.
The new visa rules are inimical to the startup's plan to hire engineers from three different countries.
Her landlord's blanket no-pets policy felt inimical to half the building, which is mostly dog owners.
Open-plan seating with constant foot traffic proved inimical to the audit team's need for total concentration during tax season.
The city's new noise ordinance is inimical to the rooftop bar's entire business model, which depends on live music until midnight.
words.etymology: in-(不) + amicus(朋友) → 不当朋友 → 敌对有害

meanings.en: so good or unusual as to be impossible to copy or imitate
meanings.zh: 无法模仿的;独一无二的

examples: Her inimitable way of narrating a $40 Costco haul turned it into a two-million-view TikTok in a weekend.
The chef's inimitable trick of pairing street-food flavors with fine-dining plating made the pop-up impossible to copy.
He delivers bad news in his own inimitable style — a joke, then the layoff, then another joke.
The retiring professor's inimitable habit of grading papers in limerick form will apparently die with him next semester.
Nobody could recreate the barista's inimitable latte art after she left; three trainees tried and gave up by week two.
words.etymology: in-(不) + imitari(模仿) → 学不来 → 独一无二

meanings.en: a performer who acts using only gesture and movement, without words
to act out something using only gestures and facial expressions, without speaking
meanings.zh: 用手势/表情表演;做手势示意

examples: Unable to hear the directions over the drilling noise, the foreman just mimed 'turn it off' by slicing his hand across his throat.
The mime outside the museum followed a tourist's exact steps until the crowd burst out laughing and pointed it out to her.
The subway busker who works as a mime during the day switched to guitar after the pandemic killed his tip jar.
The kids' birthday party mime got zero laughs until he pretended to get stuck in an invisible box.
Unable to speak over the airport announcement, she mimed 'call me' by holding her hand to her ear.
words.etymology: 希腊 mimos(模仿者) → 靠模仿演 → 哑剧演员

meanings.en: massive, uniform, and rigidly resistant to change, especially of an organization or system
meanings.zh: 庞大一体的;整齐划一的;僵化的

examples: Migrating off the monolithic legacy codebase took the engineering team eighteen months and three near-mutinies.
New hires assumed the monolithic HR system would move fast on a relocation request; it took six weeks for a reply.
The union treats management as a monolithic enemy, even though half the directors actually agree with the workers.
Breaking the monolithic app into microservices let each team ship updates without waiting on a single, terrifying deploy.
Students treat the monolithic university bureaucracy as a single villain, even though the financial aid office is actually pretty responsive.
words.etymology: monos(单一) + lithos(石) → 一整块巨石 → 庞大僵化

meanings.en: no longer fashionable, useful, or accepted; outdated

examples: Her manager's outmoded belief that 'real work' only happens in the office clashed with the team's hybrid schedule.
The gym's outmoded cancellation policy still required a signed fax — in 2026.
Grandpa's outmoded advice to 'just walk in and ask for a job' hasn't applied since before online applications existed.
The bank's outmoded requirement for a wet signature on every form baffled customers who'd already verified their identity by video call.
His outmoded assumption that a resume needed to fit on one page cost him an interview when the ATS choked on his formatting.
words.etymology: out + mode(时兴样式) → 出了时兴 → 过时

meanings.en: expressive gestures and body movements used instead of words to communicate
meanings.zh: 哑剧式表演;夸张的手势表演

meanings.en: (chiefly British) a theatrical entertainment performed at Christmas, based on a fairy tale, with music, comedy, and audience participation

examples: Every December, the local theater puts on a pantomime of Cinderella, and the kids scream 'he's behind you!' on cue.
Locked out of the meeting room with no phone, she resorted to pantomime through the glass door to explain she needed the projector.
With the interpreter's video frozen, the teacher resorted to pantomime, pointing at the clock and mimicking writing to explain the deadline.
Stuck in a language neither of them spoke, the mechanic and the tourist settled the repair estimate through pantomime and a calculator app.
The community center's Christmas pantomime sold out in an hour, mostly because last year's dame stole every single scene.
words.etymology: pan-(全) + mimos(模仿,同 mime) → 全靠比划 → 哑剧

meanings.en: surpassing all others; distinguished above the rest in a field
meanings.zh: 卓越的;首屈一指的;杰出的

examples: She's the preeminent voice on AI ethics on campus, quoted in every op-ed about chatbot regulation this year.
The clinic recruited the region's preeminent cardiologist, and the appointment waitlist tripled within a month.
In his preeminent position as lead reviewer, one thumbs-down from him can sink a restaurant's whole season.
The firm poached the industry's preeminent patent attorney with a signing bonus large enough to make headlines in three trade papers.
As the preeminent authority on coral reef restoration, she gets forwarded every panicked email about a bleaching event within hours.
words.etymology: prae-(在前) + e-minere(冒头,同 eminence) → 冒在最前 → 首屈一指

meanings.en: a position that requires little or no work but gives status or income

examples: His uncle got him a board seat that turned out to be a total sinecure — one video call a quarter for a five-figure stipend.
Employees joked that the new 'Chief Culture Officer' title was a sinecure invented to keep the founder's old roommate on payroll.
She turned what everyone assumed was a sinecure into a full-time job, actually reading every report she was supposed to just sign.
The alumni association's treasurer role was supposed to be a sinecure, until the new hire actually audited a decade of missing receipts.
Everyone assumed the ambassadorship was a sinecure for the donor's nephew, right up until a border crisis landed on his desk in week one.
words.etymology: sine(没有) + cura(照管) → 不用管事的位子 → 闲差

meanings.en: modest and simple; not trying to seem impressive or important
meanings.zh: 不摆架子的;朴实无华的;不做作的

examples: The Michelin-starred chef still eats lunch at an unpretentious noodle stall two blocks from his own restaurant.
Her unpretentious apartment — thrifted furniture, bare walls — surprised guests who expected a funded founder's place to look glossier.
What I loved about the wedding was how unpretentious it was: a backyard, folding chairs, and tacos from a truck.
The Grammy winner still drives an unpretentious ten-year-old hatchback and parks it in the same spot as everyone else at rehearsal.
Their unpretentious pitch deck — ten slides, no jargon, one clear ask — landed better with investors than the flashy version had.
words.etymology: un- + prae-tendere(往前摆) → 不摆出来 → 朴实无华

meanings.en: to make someone or something seem unimportant or of little value

examples: During her performance review, the manager belittled the six-month project as 'cute but pointless.'
Stop belittling his side hustle just because it's a food truck and not an app — he's out-earning you.
Her older brother had a way of belittling every acceptance letter as 'not that hard to get, really.'
The senior developer belittles every pull request from the intern in front of the whole channel instead of leaving private feedback.
Don't belittle her decision to switch to a trade school just because it wasn't the four-year path you expected.
words.etymology: be-(使) + little(小) → 说小了 → 贬低

meanings.en: extreme poverty; the state of lacking basic necessities

examples: After the medical bills wiped out their savings, the family slid from comfortable to near destitution in a single year.
The documentary follows gig workers one missed paycheck away from destitution, juggling three delivery apps just to make rent.
Losing the shop during the pandemic pushed them toward destitution before a GoFundMe from old customers pulled them back.
The strike dragged on so long that some families slid toward destitution before the union finally negotiated back pay.
War displaced the whole village into destitution within a season, and the refugee camp's waitlist for tents kept growing.
words.etymology: de-(离开) + statuere(安置) → 无处安身 → 赤贫

meanings.en: to speak of someone or something in a negative, belittling way

examples: The influencer got dragged online for disparaging a rival's skincare line while quietly using the same ingredients herself.
He kept disparaging remote work in meetings, even though his own team hadn't missed a deadline in a year.
She never disparages her ex to their kid, no matter how tempting it is after a bad custody weekend.
The review left up on the app store disparaged the update as 'a downgrade dressed as an upgrade,' and it got 400 upvotes overnight.
He disparages his old agency's work in every client meeting, which makes everyone quietly wonder what he'd say about them next.
words.etymology: dis-(降低) + par(同等) → 把人降一等 → 诋毁

meanings.en: a great difference or inequality between two things

examples: The pay disparity between the two offices only came to light when someone leaked the spreadsheet in the company Slack.
There's a huge disparity between how smooth the app looks in the demo and how often it crashes for real users.
The disparity in commute times — twelve minutes for him, ninety for her — quietly decided which parent did school pickup.
The disparity between the two neighborhoods' school funding showed up clearly once someone mapped the test scores against zip codes.
There's a stark disparity in loading times between the app's US and Southeast Asia servers, and support tickets prove it.
words.etymology: dis-(不) + par(同等,同 disparate) → 不对等 → 差距

meanings.en: not influenced by strong emotion; calm, objective, and impartial
meanings.zh: 冷静客观的;不带感情的

examples: The mediator stayed dispassionate through both parents' shouting, laying out the custody options like a checklist.
I need a dispassionate second opinion on this term sheet — my co-founder is too excited to see the red flags.
