Her dispassionate tone while reading the layoff list made it feel worse, not better, than if she'd cried.
The judge's dispassionate reading of the verdict gave nothing away, even though the courtroom was holding its breath.
Her dispassionate review of his manuscript flagged every plot hole without once mentioning how much she liked the characters.
words.etymology: dis-(无) + pati(承受激情) → 不动感情 → 冷静客观

meanings.en: a deadlock; a situation with no apparent way forward

examples: Salary negotiations hit an impasse when the recruiter refused to budge above the original offer by even a dollar.
The roommates reached an impasse over the thermostat — one wants 65, the other 74 — and now there's a shared spreadsheet.
Talks over the custody schedule stalled at an impasse until the lawyers suggested splitting summer break down the middle.
The city council hit an impasse over the bike-lane proposal, with both sides refusing to change a single vote.
Contract talks between the studio and the writers stalled at an impasse over streaming residuals for the third week running.
words.etymology: in-(不) + passer(通过) → 走不通 → 僵局

meanings.en: showing or feeling no emotion; expressionless
meanings.zh: 面无表情的;无动于衷的

examples: The investor stayed impassive through the entire pitch, and the founder left with no idea whether it had landed.
Her face was impassive when the doctor read the test results, but her hands were shaking under the table.
He's impassive during every performance review, which somehow makes the good ones feel just as tense as the bad ones.
The poker dealer stayed impassive as the final card flipped, giving away nothing about the hand she'd just watched unfold.
Her impassive expression during the eviction notice unsettled the landlord more than tears would have.
words.etymology: in-(不) + pati(被触动) → 触不动 → 面无表情

meanings.en: to make someone or something poor, or to deplete its resources

examples: Three straight years of drought impoverished the farming co-op, forcing half the families to sell their land.
Stacking five monthly subscriptions — streaming, cloud storage, a meal kit — quietly impoverishes people who never total the bill.
The overfishing off the coast has impoverished a fishing village that once exported to three countries.
Years of underinvestment impoverished the school district's science labs until most classes shared a single working microscope.
The currency collapse impoverished pensioners overnight, wiping out savings that had taken decades to build.
words.etymology: in-(使) + pauper(贫穷) → 使贫困

meanings.en: bizarre or unfamiliar; extremely unconventional
meanings.zh: 稀奇古怪的;离谱的;怪异的

examples: His outlandish plan to pay rent in a token he'd minted himself somehow got two roommates to agree to a trial month.
The wedding planner pitched an outlandish theme — an underwater ceremony with rented mermaids — and the couple loved it.
Her outlandish claim that she'd cured her back pain with cold plunges and no doctor got 40,000 shares before a physician debunked it.
His outlandish proposal to replace the office elevator with a slide got more upvotes on the suggestion board than any real fix.
The influencer's outlandish grocery haul — $600 of ingredients for one recipe video — got mocked across three platforms by morning.
words.etymology: out-land(外邦的) → 一看就不是本地的 → 稀奇古怪

meanings.en: domineering; unpleasantly controlling of others

examples: Her overbearing mother-in-law rearranged the entire nursery while they were still at the hospital, 'just to help.'
The overbearing project lead rewrote everyone's client emails into his own tone before letting them send anything.
Being overbearing about the group project's font choice was, in retrospect, not the hill to die on.
His overbearing older brother showed up uninvited to 'help' negotiate the car price and ended up insulting the dealer instead.
The overbearing HOA president fined three neighbors over lawn-gnome placement before anyone had even unpacked from moving day.
words.etymology: over(压过) + bear(承压) → 压人一头 → 专横

meanings.en: a smallness of number or amount; a scarcity

examples: The paucity of affordable one-bedrooms near the office pushed half the new hires into a two-hour commute.
Reviewers slammed the app update for its paucity of features compared to the beta everyone had loved.
Given the paucity of evidence in the pitch deck, the VC asked for actual user numbers before the next meeting.
Given the paucity of qualified candidates who'd relocate for the salary offered, the recruiter reopened the search after a single week.
The paucity of parking near the new stadium turned every game night into a forty-minute hunt for a spot.
words.etymology: paucus(少,同 pauper 一族) → 稀少 → 缺乏

meanings.en: childish, immature, or silly, especially in a way unbecoming of an adult

examples: The CEO's puerile Twitter feud with a competitor knocked two points off the stock before lunch.
Their group chat descended into puerile nicknames and fart-joke GIFs about ninety seconds after it was created.
Calling your coworker's idea 'dumb' in front of the whole team was a puerile way to handle the disagreement.
The senator's puerile nickname for his opponent overshadowed every actual policy point in the debate recap.
His puerile prank note taped to the shared fridge did nothing to help his campaign for office manager.
words.etymology: puer(男孩) → 小孩子气 → 幼稚

meanings.en: quick, witty conversation or exchange of clever remarks
meanings.zh: 机智的应答;妙语连珠的对话

examples: The two podcast co-hosts' rapid-fire repartee is honestly the only reason anyone still listens.
Their first-date repartee over text was so sharp she screenshotted it to show the group chat.
He has no real repartee left for family dinners; every joke has already been made three Thanksgivings in a row.
The two lawyers' courtroom repartee was sharp enough that the judge had to hide a smile behind the gavel.
Their sibling repartee at the reunion dinner had the whole table laughing before the appetizers even arrived.
words.etymology: re-(回) + partir(出击) → 一剑回敬 → 机智应答

meanings.en: violently split or divided, often by conflict (usually 'riven by/with')

examples: The startup was riven by infighting after the co-founders' public breakup, and half the team quit within a month.
Their family group chat stayed riven over politics long after the actual election had been decided.
The department, riven between the old guard and the new hires, couldn't agree on a single onboarding process.
The band was riven by creative differences for a decade before they finally agreed to record one last album together.
The neighborhood association, riven over the new bike lane, hasn't managed a single unanimous vote in over a year.
words.etymology: 古诺斯语 rífa(撕开) → 被撕裂

meanings.en: a person who spends money in an extravagant, wasteful way
extravagant or wasteful with money

examples: His roommates call him a spendthrift over the $9 oat-milk lattes, but he's the one who always pays rent on time.
Her spendthrift habits — same-day online hauls, impulse concert tickets — finally caught up when the card got declined at checkout.
The grandfather set up a spendthrift trust so his notoriously extravagant grandson could only draw a fixed monthly amount.
Her college roommate was a total spendthrift, blowing an entire paycheck on concert merch within an hour of it landing.
His spendthrift approach to the renovation budget meant the kitchen alone ate what was supposed to cover the whole house.
words.etymology: spend(花) + thrift(积蓄) → 把积蓄花光 → 败家子

meanings.en: to remove someone from a position of power, especially a ruler
to testify formally, especially under oath in a legal proceeding

examples: The board voted to depose the CEO after a leaked memo showed he'd known about the data breach for months.
Her assistant was deposed for six hours by opposing counsel before the harassment case even reached trial.
The generals who deposed the president promised elections within a year, which nobody in the group chat believed.
Shareholders moved to depose the founder after the leaked chat logs showed he'd hidden the burn rate for two quarters.
The barista was deposed for four hours about the night of the robbery, repeating the same three details every time.
words.etymology: de-(下) + ponere(放,同 deposition) → 从位子上放下来 → 罢黜

meanings.en: light, delicate, and translucent, especially of fabric

examples: She layered a diaphanous scarf over the swimsuit for the beach shoot, more suggestion than actual coverage.
The bridal shop's diaphanous curtains let in just enough light to make every dress look ethereal in photos.
Morning fog hung diaphanous over the trailhead, thin enough to see the sun but too dense to see the summit.
The dancer's diaphanous costume caught the stage lights in a way that made every spin look like it was trailing smoke.
The lampshade's diaphanous silk let just enough light through to make the reading nook feel warm instead of glaring.
words.etymology: dia-(穿过) + phainein(显现) → 光能透出来 → 轻薄透明

meanings.en: unable to be appeased, pacified, or changed; relentless
meanings.zh: 难以安抚的;不可平息的;不可动摇的

examples: Her implacable opposition to the merger turned every board meeting into a two-hour standoff.
The landlord was implacable about the late fee — no excuse, not even a hospital stay, moved him an inch.
He became her implacable rival the moment she got the promotion he'd been counting on.
The reviewer was implacable about typos, rejecting the same manuscript three times over commas alone.
Once she'd decided the vendor was overcharging, she became implacable, refusing every counteroffer until they matched the original quote.
words.etymology: in-(不) + placare(平息,反 placate) → 哄不住 → 难以安抚

meanings.en: to press or urge someone persistently, often to an annoying degree

examples: Recruiters kept importuning her on LinkedIn even after she'd said three times she wasn't job-hunting.
He importuned his parents for a down payment through the entire Thanksgiving dinner until they finally caved.
The startup's sales team importuned the same procurement manager weekly for four months before landing the contract.
Ticket scalpers importuned everyone in line outside the arena, doubling their price the closer it got to showtime.
The nonprofit's intern importuned the same three donors every week for a bigger check until the director stepped in.
words.etymology: in-(不) + portunus(顺风入港,反 opportune) → 挑不对时候缠人 → 强求

meanings.en: impossible to restrain or hold back; irresistibly energetic
meanings.zh: 抑制不住的;难以压制的

examples: Her irrepressible enthusiasm for the project survived three rounds of budget cuts and a canceled launch date.
The toddler's irrepressible giggling during the solemn toast somehow made the whole room feel a little lighter.
He's irrepressible in meetings, cracking jokes even when the quarterly numbers are genuinely bad.
Her irrepressible optimism about the failing bakery kept the whole staff showing up even after the landlord posted the eviction notice.
The rookie's irrepressible energy on the sidelines was the only thing keeping morale up during a five-game losing streak.
words.etymology: in-(不) + re-premere(压回,同 reprimand) → 压不住

meanings.en: to place two things side by side, especially for comparison or contrast

examples: The exhibit juxtaposes AI-generated portraits with hand-painted ones, daring visitors to guess which is which.
Her Instagram grid juxtaposes glossy vacation shots with brutally honest captions about her anxiety.
The article juxtaposes the CEO's 'we're a family' memo with the layoff email sent two hours later.
The documentary juxtaposes footage of the factory's opening day with drone shots of the same building rusting a decade later.
Her thesis juxtaposes two translations of the same poem, line by line, to show how much a translator's choices actually matter.
words.etymology: juxta(紧挨) + poser(放) → 挨着放 → 并置

meanings.en: relating to charitable giving; generous in promoting the welfare of others

examples: The tech billionaire's philanthropic foundation funds vaccine research, though critics say it's mostly a tax strategy.
Her philanthropic streak started small — a $10 monthly donation — and grew into a full nonprofit by thirty.
The company matches employees' philanthropic donations dollar for dollar, up to $500 a year.
The retired athlete's philanthropic foundation quietly covers tuition for a dozen kids from his old neighborhood every year.
Their wedding registry redirected gifts to a philanthropic fund for the town's flooded library instead of a china set.
words.etymology: philein(爱) + anthrōpos(人) → 爱人 → 慈善

meanings.en: to make someone less angry or hostile; to appease

examples: The airline offered a $50 voucher to placate passengers stranded overnight, which placated almost no one.
He tried to placate his sister by agreeing to host Thanksgiving, but she was still mad about the wedding toast.
Management sent a company-wide apology to placate staff after the surprise return-to-office announcement.
The restaurant comped dessert to placate the table that had waited ninety minutes for a reservation, but the one-star review still went up.
He tried to placate his editor with an early draft, but two typos on the first page made things worse.
words.etymology: placare(平息) ← placere(取悦) → 安抚

meanings.en: calm and peaceful; not easily upset or excited

examples: The lake stayed placid all morning, perfect for the paddleboard yoga class that always sells out on weekends.
He runs standups with this placid, unbothered voice — no matter how bad the outage is, it never changes.
Her placid response to the parking ticket surprised everyone; last time it happened, she cried in the car.
The therapist's placid demeanor never cracked, even when the client screamed through the entire fifty-minute session.
Their placid golden retriever slept through the fire alarm test that had every human in the building covering their ears.
words.etymology: placere(平静取悦,同 placate) → 平静

meanings.en: self-important; arrogantly grand in manner, speech, or appearance
meanings.zh: 自负的;浮夸的;自命不凡的

examples: The keynote speaker's pompous name-dropping made the whole panel cringe before he'd even reached slide two.
Her uncle gets pompous after two glasses of wine, lecturing everyone about wine regions he's never actually visited.
The reply-all email, full of pompous corporate jargon, could have just said 'the deadline moved to Friday.'
The new hire's pompous email signature listed four certifications nobody in the department had ever heard of.
His pompous toast at the rehearsal dinner name-dropped every celebrity he'd ever met and somehow never mentioned the groom.
words.etymology: 拉丁 pompa(盛大游行) → 摆排场 → 自负浮夸

meanings.en: not securely held or positioned; dangerously likely to fall, fail, or collapse
meanings.zh: 不稳定的;危险的;岌岌可危的

examples: Freelance gig work leaves a lot of people in a precarious financial spot — a great month, then nothing for six weeks.
The ladder's precarious balance on the wet balcony tiles didn't stop him from climbing up for one more photo.
Her visa status is precarious enough that she avoids even minor traffic tickets.
The startup's precarious cash position meant payroll depended entirely on one client paying their invoice on time.
Balanced on a precarious stack of moving boxes, he reached for the last mug on the top shelf.
words.etymology: precari(祈求) → 得靠求来才保得住 → 岌岌可危

meanings.en: an inclination or tendency toward a particular condition or behavior, often prior or inherited

examples: The genetic test flagged a predisposition to high cholesterol, so now she actually reads nutrition labels.
Growing up with an anxious parent gave him a predisposition to catastrophize every unread work email.
The therapist explained that a predisposition to burnout isn't destiny — it just means he needs firmer boundaries at work.
Family history gave her a predisposition to migraines, so she keeps a strict sleep schedule no matter how late the deadline runs.
Coaches now screen young athletes for a predisposition to certain knee injuries before clearing them for contact drills.
words.etymology: prae-(预先) + disponere(安排) → 事先就摆好了 → 倾向

meanings.en: overstepping what is proper or polite; excessively forward or bold
meanings.zh: 冒昧的;放肆的;自以为是的

examples: It felt presumptuous to CC the CEO on a two-day-old support ticket, but the intern did it anyway.
Isn't it a little presumptuous to book a joint honeymoon before she's even said yes?
He forwarded his own performance review to HR with a presumptuous note asking for an early promotion.
It seemed presumptuous for the new associate to redecorate the shared office before anyone had agreed on a color scheme.
Signing the group up for the marathon before asking anyone else felt presumptuous, even if his heart was in the right place.
words.etymology: prae-(预先) + sumere(取用) → 没问就先拿 → 放肆

meanings.en: the quality of having strong moral principles; honesty and integrity

examples: The auditor's reputation for probity was the only reason the board trusted the numbers without a second review.
Years of financial probity earned the credit union manager the town's trust — right up until the embezzlement scandal broke.
She built her whole personal brand on probity, so the leaked emails did more damage to her than to almost anyone else.
The whole hiring committee vouched for his probity, which made the plagiarism accusation two months later even harder to believe.
Decades of probity on the parish council meant nobody thought to double-check the treasurer's spreadsheet.
words.etymology: probus(正直优良) → 正直

meanings.en: splendid and expensive-looking; lavish
meanings.zh: 奢华的;豪华的(尤指食物、装饰)

examples: The wedding planner unveiled a sumptuous ten-course tasting menu that blew through the couple's entire catering budget in one sitting.
Their new penthouse has a sumptuous marble bathroom with heated floors, the kind you only see in five-star hotel reels.
He booked a sumptuous suite for their anniversary, then spent the whole night stressing about the credit card statement.
The magazine's holiday spread featured a sumptuous roast dinner styled with so much gold flatware it looked almost fake.
Their sumptuous hotel breakfast buffet alone cost more than the flight that got them there.
words.etymology: sumptus(开销) ← sumere(取用) → 花得起 → 奢华

meanings.en: to place one thing over another so both remain partly visible

examples: The photo app lets you superimpose a beach sunset onto any background, which explains half the vacation posts on her feed.
The architect superimposed the flood-zone map onto the site plan and realized half the proposed building sat underwater.
AI face-swap tools now superimpose one person's expression onto another's video in real time, which is equal parts impressive and unsettling.
The weather app superimposes the storm's projected path directly onto your street, updating every fifteen minutes.
She superimposed last year's budget onto this year's spreadsheet just to see how badly the new hires had blown past it.
words.etymology: super-(在上) + imponere(放上去) → 叠加

meanings.en: likely to be influenced, affected, or harmed by a particular thing
meanings.zh: 易受影响的;易感的(疾病、情绪、劝说等)

examples: After three all-nighters finishing the deck, she was completely susceptible to whatever cold was going around the office.
Teenagers scrolling late at night are especially susceptible to targeted ads disguised as 'authentic' influencer recommendations.
He's always been susceptible to flattery, which is exactly why the sales rep opened with three compliments before the pitch.
Older routers left on factory settings are especially susceptible to the botnet exploit researchers disclosed last month.
Jet-lagged and underslept, he was susceptible to every impulse buy the airport duty-free shop had on display.
words.etymology: sub-(自下) + capere(接住) → 一来就接住 → 易受影响

meanings.en: a person who flatters someone powerful to gain favor

examples: Every all-hands meeting, the new hire turns into a sycophant, laughing at the CEO's jokes a beat too long and too loud.
The startup's board was full of sycophants who never once challenged the founder's wildly optimistic revenue projections.
She noticed the intern only agreed with whoever spoke last in the meeting — a textbook sycophant angling for a good review.
The talk show host surrounded himself with sycophants who laughed at every joke, even the ones that clearly hadn't landed.
She could always spot the office sycophant — the one who suddenly loved pickleball the same week the CEO took it up.
words.etymology: 希腊 sykon(无花果) + phainein(揭发) → 告密者 → 马屁精

meanings.en: (of a desire, thirst, or feeling) impossible to satisfy or extinguish
meanings.zh: 无法满足的;不可抑制的(欲望、渴望等)

examples: After the marathon, his thirst felt unquenchable — he went through four bottles of water before he even reached the car.
The startup founder had an unquenchable curiosity, reading patent filings for fun on the weekends.
Her unquenchable appetite for true-crime documentaries meant she'd finished every major streaming catalog by the second month of the pandemic.
The toddler's unquenchable need to press every elevator button turned a two-minute ride into a full building tour.
His unquenchable ambition pushed him to apply for a promotion he wasn't remotely qualified for, twice in one year.
words.etymology: un- + quench(浇熄、解渴) → 浇不灭 → 无法满足

meanings.en: to accept or comply with something reluctantly, without protest

examples: Exhausted from arguing about the lease, David finally acquiesced and let his roommate keep the entire deposit.
She acquiesced to the landlord's rent hike rather than deal with apartment-hunting in this market again.
Rather than fight the new return-to-office mandate, most of the team quietly acquiesced and started commuting three days a week.
After a month of pushback, the school board acquiesced and reinstated the after-school program parents had petitioned for.
She acquiesced to her sister's seating chart for the reception rather than relitigate the guest list one more time.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + quiescere(安静下来) → 静下来接受 → 默许

meanings.en: excessively eager to acquire money or possessions; greedy for gain
meanings.zh: 贪婪的;渴望占有财物的

examples: His acquisitive streak kicks in every flash sale — three new gadgets arrive before the last box is even unpacked.
The private equity firm's acquisitive strategy meant buying up struggling local chains one quarter after another.
Her acquisitive approach to her closet means a new haul every payday, whether she needs it or not.
The tech giant's acquisitive spree swallowed four small AI startups in a single quarter, each one folded quietly into an existing product.
His acquisitive habit of grabbing every free conference tote bag left his hallway closet completely unusable.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + quaerere(寻求) → 一味求取 → 贪婪

meanings.en: formal or official approval; praise

examples: The junior analyst practically glowed after the partner nodded in approbation over her risk model.
On social media, approbation now shows up as likes, shares, and the rare verified-account reply.
He kept chasing his father's approbation long after he'd already built a company worth more than his father's entire career.
The chef watched the food critic's table all night, desperate for even a flicker of approbation on her face.
His parents' approbation mattered less once his own kids started clapping every time he nailed the bedtime story voices.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + probare(评为优,同 probity) → 认可

meanings.en: a person who aspires to achieve something, especially a position of distinction
meanings.zh: 有抱负的人;渴望成功者;候选人

examples: As a mayoral aspirant with almost zero name recognition, he spent every weekend knocking on doors in the district.
The gym floor is full of aspirant bodybuilders filming their sets for an audience that mostly isn't watching.
She was one of a hundred aspirants for the same product-manager role, so she led her resume with the one metric that actually moved.
As an Olympic aspirant training before dawn every day, she'd already given up two years of a normal social life.
The talent show drew hundreds of aspirants, most of whom hadn't sung in front of anyone besides a shower head.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + spirare(呼吸) → 一口气往上冲 → 有抱负者

meanings.en: having a strong desire to possess something that belongs to someone else
meanings.zh: 觊觎的;垂涎的(尤指他人之物)

examples: She shot a covetous glance at her coworker's corner office the second the promotion was announced.
Watching his old roommate's startup get acquired for eight figures left him quietly covetous of a life he used to mock.
The younger cousins grew covetous of the family cabin the moment grandma mentioned the will.
He couldn't hide how covetous he felt watching his neighbor's contractor install a new deck in just two weekends.
At the estate sale, she grew covetous of a chipped mid-century lamp the moment three other people reached for it.
words.etymology: 拉丁 cupere(渴求) → 觊觎

meanings.en: to cause someone to lose enthusiasm, hope, or confidence

examples: Three straight quarters of missed targets began to dispirit even the most optimistic members of the sales team.
The coach refused to let one bad loss dispirit the rookies before the playoffs even started.
The endless string of rejected pull requests began to dispirit the new hire before her first month was even over.
Rain hammered the course for six miles straight, and by the final stretch it had dispirited half the runners.
Yet another canceled launch date left the marketing team visibly dispirited, scrolling job boards during lunch instead of talking strategy.
words.etymology: dis-(去掉) + spiritus(气息、精神) → 泄了那口气 → 使沮丧

meanings.en: inclined to argue or dispute; fond of arguing

examples: The family group chat turns disputatious every Thanksgiving the moment someone brings up politics.
He's the most disputatious person in stand-ups, questioning every estimate until the fifteen-minute meeting runs to forty-five.
Their book club got surprisingly disputatious over whether the ending was genius or just lazy writing.
The HOA meeting turned disputatious within minutes, neighbors shouting over each other about the new parking rules.
Their wedding-planning group chat got disputatious fast, with three different opinions on the seating chart escalating into all caps.
words.etymology: dis-(各自) + putare(盘算) → 各算各的账 → 好争论

meanings.en: not considered respectable in character, appearance, or conduct

examples: The apartment listing looked great until we found the disreputable landlord's reviews full of withheld deposits.
She bought the 'designer' bag from a disreputable reseller on Instagram, and it arrived smelling like glue.
He kept borrowing money from an increasingly disreputable list of payday-loan apps just to cover rent.
The used car turned out to have a rebuilt title, and reviews later revealed the dealership's disreputable habit of hiding accident history.
He bought concert tickets from a disreputable scalper outside the venue, and half the barcodes turned out to be duplicates.
words.etymology: dis-(不) + reputare(评价) → 评不上去 → 声名狼藉

meanings.en: spoken or done without preparation or rehearsal

examples: When the projector died mid-pitch, she delivered an entirely extemporaneous version of the deck from memory.
His extemporaneous toast at the rehearsal dinner got more laughs than the one he'd spent a week writing.
The interviewer skipped the prepared questions and asked for an extemporaneous answer instead, just to see how he'd think on his feet.
When the guest canceled ten minutes before airtime, the podcast host filled the whole hour with extemporaneous stories about her worst interviews.
The professor's pop quiz required a fully extemporaneous five-minute talk on whatever topic she pulled from a hat.
words.etymology: ex tempore(当场) ← tempus(时间) → 即兴

meanings.en: (chemistry/materials science) a substance present in a material that reduces its purity or quality

examples: The mass spectrometer flagged trace impurities in the batch — just 0.02% sulfur, but enough to fail the pharma-grade spec.
Doping silicon with tiny amounts of boron introduces impurities that give the wafer its semiconductor properties.
The water treatment plant traced the metallic taste to trace impurities leaching from an aging section of iron pipe.
The jeweler ran an assay on the gold chain and found enough impurities to knock its purity down from 18 karat to barely 14.
A skincare startup recalled an entire serum batch after lab tests turned up impurities in the raw hyaluronic acid supplier sent.
words.etymology: in-(不) + purus(纯) → 杂质

meanings.en: stated or appearing to be true, but not necessarily so

examples: The ostensible reason for the layoffs was 'restructuring,' though everyone suspected it was really the failed product launch.
His ostensible purpose for the coffee chat was networking, but he clearly just wanted a referral.
The ostensible goal of the offsite was team bonding; the real goal, everyone agreed, was avoiding the office for two days.
The ostensible purpose of the surprise inspection was safety compliance, though the landlord clearly just wanted to check for pets.
Her ostensible reason for canceling the trip was a work deadline, but her Instagram story from the beach said otherwise.
words.etymology: ob-(朝外) + tendere(伸展,同 ostentatious) → 摆出来的那一面 → 表面上的

meanings.en: to treat someone with hostility or cruelty, especially because of their race, religion, or beliefs
meanings.zh: 迫害;欺压(尤指因种族、宗教或信仰)

meanings.en: to harass or annoy someone persistently

examples: Employees who reported the harassment said they were quietly persecuted afterward, passed over for projects and excluded from meetings.
Throughout history, religious minorities have been persecuted and forced to practice their faith in secret.
Reporters persecuted the retired athlete with questions about the scandal every single time he left his house.
Dissident bloggers in the region have been persecuted for years simply for criticizing the ruling party online.
The refugees described being persecuted for their faith back home, their church burned down twice before they finally fled.
words.etymology: per-(不停) + sequi(追赶) → 穷追不舍 → 迫害

meanings.en: a trite, overused remark offered as if it were profound

examples: The manager's performance review was a string of platitudes — 'just believe in yourself,' 'growth takes time' — and zero actual feedback.
Her LinkedIn post about 'grinding through adversity' was pure platitude, liked four hundred times by people who skimmed the first line.
Instead of addressing the layoffs directly, the CEO's email leaned on platitudes about 'exciting new chapters.'
The condolence card was full of platitudes like 'time heals all wounds,' which felt hollow while packing up his desk.
Every motivational poster in the break room offered the same platitude about teamwork, right above the broken coffee machine nobody fixed.
words.etymology: 法语 plat(平、扁) → 平得没味道 → 陈词滥调

meanings.en: an attempt to make a false appearance seem true; a false show
a claim, especially a false or unjustified one, to some quality or accomplishment

examples: He kept up the pretense of being slammed at work just to dodge his in-laws' weekend visit.
Under the pretense of 'needing space,' she was already messaging someone new on a dating app.
The intern made no pretense of understanding the codebase and just asked for help right away.
She maintained the pretense of loving her in-laws' cooking for six years before finally admitting she couldn't stand it.
He made no pretense of being an expert skier and stuck to the bunny slope the entire weekend.
words.etymology: prae-(在前) + tendere(伸展) → 摆在前面挡着 → 伪装

meanings.en: conformity to accepted standards of behavior or morals; correctness

examples: HR sent a reminder about propriety at the holiday party after last year's karaoke incident.
Some coworkers questioned the propriety of the manager dating someone on his own team.
She kept a strict sense of propriety at work, never once venting about her boss in the group chat.
The etiquette coach spent the entire session on propriety, insisting the toast come after dessert, not during the entrée.
Some longtime members whispered about the propriety of the new board chair also owning shares in a competing firm.
words.etymology: proprius(自己的、本分的) → 守住本分 → 得体

meanings.en: (of an animal) bred from parents of the same breed, with no crossbreeding
an animal of purebred lineage

examples: The breeder charged triple for the purebred Labrador puppies, papers and pedigree included.
The shelter mostly takes in mixed breeds, but every so often a purebred turns up without any papers at all.
The kennel club judges inspected each purebred collie's coat and gait before ranking them for Best in Show.
She spent months on a waitlist for a purebred Bengal kitten, only to fall for a scruffy shelter mix instead.
The vet's intake form asked whether the puppy was purebred or a mix, and the owner just shrugged.

meanings.en: complaining in a petulant or whining manner

examples: The customer sent a querulous email every single day the refund hadn't cleared, each one longer than the last.
His querulous tone about splitting the dinner bill made everyone regret inviting him.
By the third delayed flight, even the calmest passengers had turned querulous with the gate agent.
Her elderly neighbor left a querulous voicemail almost every trash day, convinced the bins were somehow always in the wrong spot.
By the fourth reschedule, his querulous texts to the contractor had turned into a running joke among the whole family group chat.
words.etymology: queri(抱怨) → 爱抱怨

meanings.en: a state of calmness, stillness, or tranquility

examples: She finally found some quietude on the cabin trip, phone left in a drawer for three straight days.
The office empties out by seven, and a strange quietude settles over the open floor plan.
He credits early-morning runs, before the streets fill up, for the only quietude he gets all day.
The reading room's quietude lasted until a toddler two tables over discovered how loudly a picture book could be dropped.
After the kids finally fell asleep, she sat on the porch for twenty minutes just to soak in the quietude.
words.etymology: quies(安静,同 acquiesce) → 宁静

meanings.en: to rebuke or reprimand someone, typically in a mild way
meanings.zh: 责备;告诫(语气通常较温和)

examples: The teacher gently reproved him for scrolling his phone under the desk during the lecture.
Her manager reproved her, calmly but firmly, for missing the deadline without a heads-up.
He reproved his little brother for leaving dishes in the sink again, though it never seems to stick.
The head chef reproved the line cook, quietly but pointedly, for plating the dish without wiping the rim first.
Grandma reproved him for putting his elbows on the table, the same way she had every Sunday dinner since he was six.
words.etymology: re-(回) + probare(评定) → 把评价打回去 → 责备

meanings.en: to fail to resist pressure, temptation, or another negative force; to give in
meanings.zh: 屈服于;抵挡不住(压力、诱惑等)

meanings.en: to die as a result of an illness or injury

examples: After holding out through the entire meeting, he finally succumbed to the leftover birthday cake in the break room.
Running on four hours of sleep all week, she eventually succumbed to a nasty cold by Friday.
Her grandfather succumbed to the illness after a long fight, surrounded by family in hospice care.
He held off buying new sneakers for months, then finally succumbed to a flash sale at midnight.
The old oak tree succumbed to the beetle infestation after three dry summers in a row.
words.etymology: sub-(在下) + cumbere(躺倒,同 incumbent) → 躺平 → 屈服

meanings.en: to spoil, impair, or weaken the effectiveness or quality of something
to make a legal document or agreement invalid

examples: A single missing signature vitiated the entire contract, forcing both sides back to the negotiating table.
One overcooked ingredient vitiated what had otherwise been a flawless tasting menu.
The lawyer argued that the seller's undisclosed defect vitiated the sale agreement entirely.
One tone-deaf slide in the middle vitiated an otherwise flawless investor pitch, and the room's energy never recovered.
A cracked lens vitiated the telescope's otherwise razor-sharp images, blurring every photo of the eclipse.
words.etymology: vitium(缺陷、恶习) → 掺进毛病 → 损害

meanings.en: a difficult or unpleasant situation; hardship

examples: The founder talked openly about the adversity of nearly running out of runway twice before the Series A.
She trained through months of adversity — a torn ligament, a canceled sponsorship — before finally qualifying for the marathon.
Losing both parents within a year was the kind of adversity that reshaped how he thought about work-life balance.
Growing up translating for her parents at every doctor's appointment was its own quiet adversity that shaped how she leads meetings today.
The team's biggest adversity wasn't the budget cuts — it was rebuilding trust after the previous manager was walked out mid-quarter.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + vertere(转) → 迎面转过来 → 逆境

meanings.en: to make a wrongdoing seem less serious by providing partial excuses
meanings.zh: (为过错)找借口开脱;减轻(罪责)

examples: His lawyer argued extenuating circumstances: he'd been laid off that same week and missed the court date by accident.
HR weighed the extenuating factors — a family emergency, a broken-down car — before deciding not to fire him.
The professor wouldn't extenuate the late submission, even after hearing about the hospital visit.
The judge cited extenuating circumstances — a defaulted power bill and a sick child — before reducing the fine by half.
The property manager agreed to extenuate the late fee once she saw the hospital paperwork explaining the missed rent payment.
words.etymology: ex-(出) + tenuis(薄) → 把事说薄 → 开脱减轻

meanings.en: done or said without previous thought or preparation
without preparation; spontaneously

examples: The whole team ended up in an impromptu meeting the moment the server crashed at 2 a.m.
What started as a quick coffee turned into an impromptu five-hour road trip to the coast.
With no notes and no warning, she had to speak impromptu in front of the entire board.
The whole apartment turned into an impromptu dance floor the second the neighbor's playlist synced with ours over Bluetooth.
Their manager called an impromptu happy hour the moment the client finally signed after eight months of negotiations.
words.etymology: in promptu(现成地) ← promere(取出) → 张口就来 → 即兴

meanings.en: not harmful or offensive; harmless

examples: An innocuous comment about the budget spiraled into a forty-minute argument in the Monday meeting.
The email looked innocuous enough — just a shipping update — until the link turned out to be a phishing scam.
She meant it as an innocuous joke about his outfit, but he didn't speak to her for the rest of the shift.
The extension looked innocuous enough, just a PDF converter, until it started quietly mining crypto in the background.
What seemed like an innocuous scheduling mix-up turned into a three-way shouting match over whose calendar invite was 'final.'
words.etymology: in-(不) + nocere(伤害) → 无害

meanings.en: (engineering/manufacturing) the quality of components being able to be substituted for one another without adjustment

examples: Standardizing bolt sizes across the product line gave the factory full interchangeability, so any warehouse could fulfill any order.
The whole modular furniture system depends on the interchangeability of panels, so a shelf from 2015 still fits a 2024 frame.
The new USB-C standard was supposed to guarantee interchangeability, yet some cables still can't handle fast charging on certain phones.
The hospital standardized on one ventilator brand specifically for the interchangeability of replacement parts during supply shortages.
Switching database vendors was painless because the ORM was built around strict interchangeability between the two systems' query engines.

meanings.en: (of damage or loss) impossible to repair or put right
meanings.zh: 无法弥补的;不能修复的

examples: The leaked screenshots did irreparable damage to the influencer's reputation within a single afternoon.
Water pooled under the laptop overnight, and the technician said the motherboard damage was irreparable.
The argument opened an irreparable rift between the two co-founders, and the company split in two within a month.
The moving company dropped the antique piano down two flights of stairs, leaving irreparable damage no restorer could fix.
Years of overfishing left the reef with irreparable damage, and the marine biologists stopped calling it a recovery site altogether.
words.etymology: in-(不) + reparare(修复) → 修不回来 → 无法弥补

meanings.en: many and various; of many different kinds
a pipe or chamber with several openings that channels fluid or gas, especially in a vehicle's engine

examples: Her reasons for quitting were manifold: the pay, the commute, the manager, the 9 p.m. Slack pings.
The redesigned app brought manifold improvements, from faster load times to a cleaner checkout flow.
The mechanic said the exhaust manifold had cracked, which explained the rattling noise on the highway.
The intake manifold was caked in carbon buildup, which explained why the engine idled so rough after the road trip.
A hairline crack in the manifold let air leak into the fuel mixture, tanking the car's mileage for weeks before anyone noticed.
words.etymology: many + fold(折、重) → 多重 → 多种多样

meanings.en: to completely destroy a building or town, typically by knocking it down
meanings.zh: 夷为平地;彻底摧毁(注意与'raise'反义,非同一词)

examples: The old shopping mall was razed last spring to make way for a cluster of luxury condos.
The wildfire razed an entire block of the neighborhood before crews got it under control.
City council voted to raze the abandoned factory rather than spend millions renovating it.
Preservationists protested for months, but the city razed the century-old theater anyway to build a parking structure.
The developer razed six blocks of rent-controlled housing in a single summer to clear the site for a glass tower.
words.etymology: 拉丁 radere(刮削) → 刮平 → 夷为平地

meanings.en: relating to a system as a whole, rather than to particular parts; widespread
(medicine) affecting the entire body rather than a single organ or part

examples: The audit revealed systemic issues in the hiring process, not just one manager's bad judgment.
Analysts warned that a single bank's collapse could trigger systemic risk across the entire financial market.
Doctors said the untreated infection had gone systemic, spreading well beyond the original wound.
The report described the outages as systemic, rooted in a decade of underinvestment rather than one server catching fire.
Coaches called the losing streak systemic, pointing to burnout and turnover in the front office, not just bad luck on the field.
words.etymology: syn-(共同) + histanai(立) → 立成一个整体 → 系统性

meanings.en: a state of great disturbance, confusion, or uncertainty
meanings.zh: 混乱;动荡(强调纷乱不安的状态)

examples: Her inbox was in complete turmoil after the product launch went sideways overnight.
He was in emotional turmoil for weeks after the breakup, unable to focus on anything at work.
The newsroom fell into turmoil the second the story broke, with three editors fighting over the headline.
The trading floor fell into turmoil the instant the surprise rate hike hit the screens, phones ringing from every desk at once.
Her family's finances were in quiet turmoil for months before anyone admitted the business loan had gone unpaid.

meanings.en: a violent or sudden change or disruption to something
meanings.zh: 剧变;动荡(强调突发的巨大变化)

examples: The company went through a massive upheaval after the CEO resigned and half the leadership team followed.
Moving across the country for the new job caused more personal upheaval than she'd expected.
AI tools have triggered a real upheaval in the design industry, and half her freelance clients disappeared in a year.
The neighborhood went through years of upheaval once the city announced the new light-rail line would cut straight through Main Street.
Streaming triggered a slow-motion upheaval in the music industry, and record stores that survived the '90s finally started closing for good.
words.etymology: up + heave(用力掀) → 从底下掀起来 → 剧变

meanings.en: having a huge appetite for food, or an insatiable eagerness for an activity
meanings.zh: 贪婪的;狼吞虎咽的;如饥似渴的

examples: She's a voracious reader, finishing three audiobooks a week on her commute alone.
After the two-hour spin class, he had a voracious appetite and ordered enough takeout for three people.
The startup was voracious about growth, signing up new markets faster than support could keep up.
Her toddler has a voracious curiosity, taking apart the remote, the toaster, and once, alarmingly, the smoke detector.
The teenage boys demolished two entire pizzas with voracious speed, and their mother had already started ordering a third.
words.etymology: vorare(吞食) → 狼吞虎咽 → 贪婪

meanings.en: neatly skillful and quick in one's movements or actions

examples: The barista's deft hands turned out a perfect rosetta in the foam without her even looking down.
She handled the angry client call with a deft mix of empathy and firm boundaries.
With a few deft edits, he turned the clunky first draft into something the client actually wanted.
The tailor made a few deft stitches backstage, and the ripped hem was invisible by the time she walked out.
With a deft change of subject, he steered the toast away from the ex's name before anyone could wince.
words.etymology: 与 daft 同源,古英语 gedæfte(得当) → 手上得当 → 灵巧

meanings.en: looking unfriendly, threatening, or uninviting
meanings.zh: 令人生畏的;有压迫感的(注意非'禁止'之意)

examples: The interviewer's forbidding stare made even her rehearsed answers come out shaky.
Gray, forbidding clouds rolled in just as they reached the summit, and the group turned back.
Nobody on the team wanted to walk into the CEO's forbidding corner office uninvited.
The cliff looked forbidding even from the parking lot, its face streaked black with wet rock and no visible route up.
A forbidding silence settled over the Zoom call the second someone mentioned the missed revenue target.
words.etymology: forbid(禁止) → 一副拒人于外的样子 → 令人生畏

meanings.en: inspiring fear, respect, or admiration through being powerful or impressive
very difficult to deal with, overcome, or accomplish

examples: She built a formidable reputation as a negotiator long before she made partner.
His to-do list before the trip looked formidable: four deadlines, two flights, and a dentist appointment.
The debate team from the rival school was formidable, undefeated for three years running.
The new CFO walked into her first board meeting with a formidable command of the numbers that silenced the usual pushback.
Untangling the old codebase's tangled dependencies proved formidable, and the 'quick migration' stretched into a six-week project.
words.etymology: formido(恐惧) → 让人先怵三分 → 令人敬畏

meanings.en: the point at which a plan or project is realized or bears results

examples: After eighteen months of late-night coding sessions and three failed prototypes, her fitness app finally came to fruition last week.
The rooftop garden project only came to fruition once the landlord stopped stalling and approved the permit.
Ten years of rejection letters later, her debut novel finally came to fruition when a small press picked it up.
The mural the students designed in freshman year only came to fruition this spring, once the district approved the wall.
His dissertation on coral reef recovery came to fruition after four field seasons and two grant rejections in between.
words.etymology: 拉丁 frui(享用) → 到了能享用的时候 → 结果实、实现

meanings.en: consisting of diverse or dissimilar elements or parts
meanings.zh: 异质的;由不同种类组成的

examples: Our new product team is wonderfully heterogeneous — ex-bankers, a former chef, and two bootcamp grads all pitching features.
The dataset was so heterogeneous, mixing survey responses with raw sensor logs, that the model kept choking on it.
The jury pool turned out wonderfully heterogeneous — a retired plumber, two grad students, and a semi-retired opera singer.
Geologists were fascinated by the heterogeneous rock layer, a jumble of sediment types that suggested multiple ancient floods.
The apartment building's heterogeneous mix of tenants, students upstairs and retirees below, made the annual block party oddly charming.
words.etymology: heteros(不同) + genos(种类) → 种类不一 → 异质

meanings.en: hard to control, manage, or solve; stubbornly resistant to change
meanings.zh: 难驾驭的;难对付的;(问题)棘手难解的

examples: Traffic congestion downtown has become so intractable that the city just turned two lanes into a bus-only corridor.
My grandfather is intractable about doctor visits — no amount of pleading gets him past the clinic parking lot.
The bug proved intractable for weeks, resurfacing every time engineers thought they'd finally patched it.
Her chronic migraines had become intractable, unresponsive to every medication her neurologist tried over three years.
The dispute between marketing and engineering over the launch date turned intractable, with neither side willing to move the timeline.
words.etymology: in-(不) + trahere(拉) → 拉不动 → 难驾驭

meanings.en: (chemistry) the chemical process in which a substance combines with oxygen or loses electrons

examples: The lab report blamed oxidization for the corroded contacts, recommending a nitrogen-purged storage cabinet going forward.
Slicing the apple exposed it to air, and oxidization turned the flesh brown within minutes.
Years of harsh winters and road salt left the car's undercarriage eaten through by oxidization long before the engine gave out.
The sommelier explained that a little oxidization actually softened the tannins, which was why they'd decanted the bottle an hour early.
The bronze statue in the square had turned a soft green, decades of oxidization slowly replacing its original copper shine.
words.etymology: 希腊 oxys(酸、尖锐) → 酸的成因 → 氧化

meanings.en: (medicine) a noticeably rapid, strong, or irregular heartbeat, often due to anxiety, exertion, or a heart condition

examples: She went to the ER after two nights of palpitations, worried the extra espresso shots had finally caught up with her heart.
The cardiologist hooked him up to a 24-hour monitor to catch the palpitations that only seemed to strike after midnight.
She felt the first flutter of palpitations backstage, seconds before walking out to give the keynote to four hundred people.
He blamed the pre-workout supplement for the palpitations that kept him staring at the gym ceiling fan for ten minutes straight.
New mothers sometimes report palpitations in the weeks after delivery, which her OB said was usually just hormones settling down.
words.etymology: palpitare(急促跳动) ← palpare(轻拍) → 心悸

meanings.en: very steep; also, done with unwise haste or suddenness (distinct from the verb 'precipitate', which means to cause something to happen abruptly)
meanings.zh: 陡峭的;仓促的、鲁莽急促的(注意与动词 precipitate“促成,使骤然发生”相区分)

examples: The trail dropped off in a precipitous switchback that had two hikers turning back within the first mile.
Investors panicked at the precipitous 40% stock drop and started dumping shares before the earnings call even ended.
App downloads took a precipitous dive within days of the redesign, and the team rolled back the update by Friday morning.
The reservoir's water level had fallen so precipitously by August that the marina had to move its docks twice.
The mountain road narrowed into a precipitous stretch with no guardrail, and the bus driver slowed to a crawl.
words.etymology: prae-(向前) + caput(头) → 头朝前栽下 → 陡峭、仓促

meanings.en: shaky and likely to collapse or break; poorly constructed
meanings.zh: 摇摇欲坠的;不结实的;快散架的

examples: We climbed the rickety fire escape to the rooftop bar, half-convinced it would give way under all six of us.
The landlord still hasn't fixed the rickety banister, and I grip the wall every time I carry groceries upstairs.
The office chair had gone rickety years ago, one wheel wobbling every time he leaned back during a call.
We crossed the rickety suspension bridge one at a time, the whole thing swaying with every gust of wind.
The taco cart's rickety wheel finally gave out mid-block, sending napkins and hot sauce packets across the sidewalk.
words.etymology: rickets(佝偻病) → 骨头站不住 → 摇摇欲坠

meanings.en: to fall over, or cause something to fall over; to overthrow a government or leader
meanings.zh: 倒塌;使倒塌;推翻(政权、领导人)

examples: The toddler grabbed the tablecloth and toppled an entire tray of cupcakes onto the kitchen floor.
Leaked messages about the bribery scandal eventually toppled the mayor, who resigned within a week.
A gust of wind toppled the sandwich board outside the café, and it clattered across the sidewalk right as the lunch rush started.
Months of street protests finally toppled the regime, though the transition afterward proved just as chaotic.
He stacked the moving boxes one too high, and the whole tower toppled the second he let go.
words.etymology: tip(倾倒) 的反复形式 → 一下下歪到倒 → 倒塌

meanings.en: (economics) describing the theory that benefits given to businesses and the wealthy eventually spread to benefit everyone else
meanings.zh: (经济学)涓滴的;惠及富人后逐渐惠及大众的

examples: The senator defended the tax cuts with classic trickle-down logic: help corporations first, and jobs will follow for everyone else.
Economists still argue over whether trickle-down policy actually raised wages or just widened the gap between executives and workers.
City planners pitched the luxury towers with trickle-down logic, promising the construction jobs would eventually lift the whole neighborhood.
The CFO's foul mood had a trickle-down effect all week, and by Thursday even the interns were snapping at each other.
Critics of the trickle-down bonus structure pointed out that executives got seven figures while frontline staff hadn't seen a raise in three years.
words.etymology: trickle(细流滴落) + down → 一滴滴往下渗 → 涓滴效应

meanings.en: having a full, curvaceous figure; giving sensuous pleasure
meanings.zh: 丰满性感的;肉欲的,给人感官享受的

examples: The magazine cover praised her voluptuous curves, sparking the usual comment-section debate about body standards.
We sank into voluptuous silk cushions at the new lounge bar, the kind of seating that makes you never want to leave.
The classic car show's star was a 1959 model with voluptuous curves that made every phone camera come out.
The dessert menu described the chocolate torte in almost voluptuous terms — 'rich, dense, and utterly indulgent.'
The wedding dress had a voluptuous train of silk that took two bridesmaids to arrange before she walked in.
words.etymology: voluptas(快感) → 感官享受 → 丰满性感

meanings.en: the quality of using resources carelessly or extravagantly without a worthwhile result

examples: The sustainability audit called out the wastefulness of printing every internal memo when the whole office had monitors.
Investors questioned the wastefulness of the marketing budget after half of it went to a single unreleased ad campaign.
The wedding planner quietly noted the wastefulness of it all — half the buffet trays went straight into the dumpster by midnight.
A viral report exposed the wastefulness of online returns, showing pallets of barely-used clothes shipped straight to a landfill.
The city council debated the wastefulness of heating three empty floors of the old municipal building all winter.

meanings.en: the quality of being able to adjust to new conditions, environments, or requirements

examples: The interviewer kept probing for adaptability, asking how she'd handled three different reporting structures in one year.
Engineers praised the chip's adaptability, since the same architecture scaled from a smartwatch to a data-center server.
The restaurant's adaptability during the slow winter months, pivoting to a delivery-only menu, kept it afloat when three neighbors closed.
Biologists credited the species' adaptability for surviving the drought, since it could switch between three completely different food sources.
Her adaptability got her through four company reorgs in two years, each time landing on a different team without missing a beat.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + aptus(适合,同 ineptitude) → 能贴上去 → 适应性

meanings.en: a loud, confused noise or a vehement public outcry
meanings.zh: 喧闹声;(公众)强烈抗议,呼声

meanings.en: to demand or complain noisily and insistently

examples: The clamor from the protest outside city hall drowned out the council meeting's livestream audio.
Fans have been clamoring for a refund ever since the concert got cancelled twenty minutes before doors opened.
The clamor from the school cafeteria carried all the way to the principal's office by lunchtime.
Shareholders clamored for the CEO's resignation the moment the fraud allegations went public.
Employees have clamored for a four-day workweek ever since the pilot program's results leaked internally.
words.etymology: clamare(呼喊,同 declamation) → 众声呼喊 → 喧闹

meanings.en: to collect, compare, and combine texts, data, or documents in the correct order
meanings.zh: 整理;核对汇编;(将文件)整理排序

examples: Before the board meeting, I spent an hour collating everyone's quarterly numbers into one spreadsheet.
The office printer can collate and staple the handouts automatically, so nobody has to sort a hundred pages by hand.
The intern spent the afternoon collating survey responses from all twelve store locations into a single master file.
She collated three weeks of lab results by hand after the analysis software crashed and lost the automated report.
Before mailing invitations, they collated the RSVP cards by table number so the caterer could plan portions accurately.
words.etymology: com-(一起) + latus(带来) → 拿到一处比对 → 核对汇编

meanings.en: causing harm or damage

examples: Doomscrolling right before bed is detrimental to your sleep — my therapist has told me this three times now.
Skipping the code review step proved detrimental; the bug shipped straight to production and crashed checkout for an hour.
Nutritionists warned that the extreme diet was detrimental to her energy levels long before it showed up on the scale.
The rushed merger proved detrimental to morale, and half the acquired team quit within six months.
Years of price wars between the two chains turned out detrimental to both, and neither could recover the margin they'd cut.
words.etymology: de-(掉) + terere(磨) → 一点点磨损 → 有害

meanings.en: a real or imagined wrong causing resentment; a formal complaint
meanings.zh: 不满,委屈;(正式)申诉,投诉

examples: Employees filed a formal grievance after management quietly cut the remote-work stipend without any notice.
He's still nursing an old grievance about being passed over for the promotion two years ago.
The union filed a formal grievance after the warehouse skipped the mandatory safety briefing for the third week running.
A group of students submitted a joint grievance accusing the professor of grading essays inconsistently across sections.
Tenants banded together to file a grievance with the housing board after months of ignored noise complaints.
words.etymology: gravis(沉重) → 心里压着一块 → 不满、申诉

meanings.en: a modest view of one's own importance; lack of arrogance

examples: The CEO accepted the award with real humility, crediting the interns who'd caught the bug before launch.
Losing the pitch to a scrappier startup taught our whole team some much-needed humility.
He wrote the incident postmortem with real humility, owning the deploy mistake instead of blaming the on-call rotation.
A season-ending injury taught her more humility than any championship ever had, watching from the bench as her team advanced without her.
The professor's humility stood out at the conference; she credited her graduate students by name before presenting the findings as her own.
words.etymology: humus(泥土) → 低到尘土里 → 谦逊

meanings.en: (statistics/logic) based on or involving inference, drawing conclusions from evidence and reasoning rather than direct observation
meanings.zh: (统计学/逻辑学)推理的;推论的

examples: The paper relied on inferential statistics to estimate the effect across the population from just a 500-person sample.
The detective's case was purely inferential — no confession, no fingerprints, just a chain of circumstantial reasoning.
With the lab results still days away, the doctor made an inferential diagnosis based on symptoms and the patient's recent travel history.
The A/B test only ran for two days, so the inferential leap to 'this button color increases sales' felt shaky to the whole team.
The prosecution's entire case was inferential, built on phone records and timing rather than any direct witness.
words.etymology: in-(向) + ferre(带来) → 把结论带出来 → 推理的

meanings.en: a room or building providing basic medical care, especially in a school, workplace, or institution

examples: He was sent to the infirmary after fainting during the fire drill, and the nurse made him sit with an ice pack for an hour.
The boarding school's infirmary handled everything from sprained ankles to the flu outbreak that shut down half the dorms.
The camp infirmary saw a steady stream of bee stings and scraped knees every afternoon during free-swim hour.
Finals week always packed the campus infirmary with stressed-out students convinced their sore throat was strep.
The base infirmary treated everything from twisted ankles to homesickness disguised as stomachaches during the first week of training.
words.etymology: in-(不) + firmus(结实) → 收留身子不结实的人 → 医务室

meanings.en: showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise
meanings.zh: 一丝不苟的;极其细心的

examples: She kept a meticulous spreadsheet tracking every expense from the trip, down to the airport coffee.
The surgeon's notes were meticulous, timestamped to the minute for every step of the procedure.
The wedding planner kept a meticulous fifteen-page timeline, accounting for everything down to when the ice sculpture would start melting.
He's meticulous about sourdough, weighing every ingredient to the gram and logging the kitchen's humidity in a notebook.
The archivist was meticulous in labeling each photo negative, cross-referencing dates against decades-old newspaper clippings.
words.etymology: metus(害怕) → 怕出一点错 → 一丝不苟

meanings.en: having great variety; of many different kinds

examples: Running a food truck means juggling multifarious tasks — accounting, marketing, permits, and actual cooking, all before noon.
The app store is flooded with multifarious meditation apps, each promising the same calm in a slightly different color scheme.
A small-town mayor's multifarious duties range from approving the budget to personally unclogging the parade route's storm drains.
New parents juggle multifarious roles overnight — nurse, chef, referee, and sleep-deprived accountant, often all before 9 a.m.
The stage manager's multifarious job that night included fixing a zipper, cueing the lights, and calming a panicking understudy.
words.etymology: multi-(多) + -farius(种类) → 多种多样

meanings.en: to move or swing back and forth; to waver repeatedly between opinions or states
meanings.zh: (物理)摆动,振荡;(观点、情绪等)反复摇摆

examples: The ceiling fan's blade had bent slightly, so it oscillated with an annoying wobble all summer.
All week I oscillated between accepting the job offer and staying put, until the deadline finally forced my hand.
The stock oscillated wildly all week, swinging five percent in either direction on every earnings rumor.
Her manager oscillates between micromanaging every email and vanishing for two weeks without a single check-in.
The old grandfather clock in the hallway still oscillates steadily, ticking through renovations that replaced everything else in the house.
words.etymology: 拉丁 oscillum(悬着的小面具、秋千) → 来回荡 → 摆动

meanings.en: a solution or remedy claimed to solve all problems or difficulties

examples: Marketing keeps pitching the new CRM as a panacea, but it won't fix a sales team that never follows up on leads.
Intermittent fasting isn't a panacea for every health issue, no matter what the podcast ads claim.
City officials sold the new subway line as a panacea for congestion, though commuters on the east side still have no route at all.
The supplement's ads called it a panacea for fatigue, brain fog, and joint pain, which should have been the first red flag.
Leadership treated the new project-management tool like a panacea, as if switching software alone would fix a team that never talked to each other.
words.etymology: pan-(全部) + akos(药) → 包治百病 → 万灵药

meanings.en: a strong or habitual liking for something

examples: My roommate has a penchant for ordering dumplings at 1 a.m. no matter how full she claims to be.
The new hire has a penchant for interrupting meetings with unsolicited feedback on the deck's font choices.
My uncle has a penchant for buying tools he'll use exactly once, like the polenta stirrer still in its box.
She has a penchant for booking flights the night before, somehow always finding a deal nobody else can.
The new analyst has a penchant for reply-all, which means the whole department now knows about his lunch order.
words.etymology: 拉丁 pendere(倾斜、悬垂) → 心往那边偏 → 嗜好

meanings.en: to spread throughout something; to pervade every part

examples: The smell of the neighbor's cooking permeated the whole hallway by the time I got off the elevator.
A quiet anxiety about layoffs has permeated the office ever since the all-hands got rescheduled twice.
Wildfire smoke permeated the entire building for a week, seeping into carpets and curtains no amount of airing out could fix.
A quiet cynicism has permeated the newsroom since the third round of buyouts, and pitch meetings feel shorter every week.
That jingle from the gas station ad permeated my brain for three days straight, playing on loop during every meeting.
words.etymology: per-(穿过) + meare(通行) → 一路穿行 → 渗透

meanings.en: to prolong or extend something beyond its usual or desired length

examples: The landlord protracted the repair negotiations for two months, and we still don't have working heat.
Both sides protracted the merger talks so long that the smaller company ran out of cash before signing.
The custody battle protracted for nearly two years, draining both parents' savings long before a judge ever ruled.
Her visa renewal got protracted for months by a missing document nobody at the embassy could clearly explain.
The neighbors protracted their fence-line lawsuit so long that the disputed strip of grass grew waist-high before it settled.
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + trahere(拉,同 intractable) → 硬拉长 → 拖延

meanings.en: feeling or showing deep and solemn respect

examples: Visitors fall reverent and quiet the moment they step into the war memorial's main hall.
He talks about his old coding mentor in a reverent tone, like the guy invented Git himself.
The apprentice handled the antique typewriter with reverent care, cleaning each key with a cotton swab before ever pressing one.
The whole studio went reverent the moment the aging producer picked up his guitar, and nobody dared check a phone.
Even the interns turned reverent during the retiring engineer's final demo, watching in silence as he explained code he'd written twenty years ago.
words.etymology: revereri(敬畏,同 revere) → 虔诚

meanings.en: causing or likely to cause ruin; disastrous, often financially
meanings.zh: 毁灭性的;灾难性的(常指经济上)

examples: Taking out that second loan to cover the wedding turned out to be financially ruinous within a year.
A ruinous fire swept through the warehouse district, wiping out three small businesses overnight.
The ruinous legal fees from the custody battle ate through both of their savings accounts within eighteen months.
A ruinous typo in the merger contract cost the firm forty million dollars before anyone noticed the missing zero.
Ignoring the mold problem for two years proved ruinous, and the family ended up gutting the entire first floor.
words.etymology: ruere(倒塌) → 塌下来 → 毁灭性

meanings.en: (biology) the process by which a substance, such as a hormone or enzyme, is produced and released by a cell, gland, or organ

examples: The endocrinologist explained that insulin secretion drops sharply once beta cells in the pancreas start to fail.
The lab measured cortisol secretion at four points during the day to map the patient's stress hormone cycle.
The dermatologist linked her breakouts to overactive sebum secretion triggered by the new humidity in the office building.
Researchers tracked melatonin secretion from the pineal gland to explain why night-shift nurses struggled to fall asleep during the day.
The nutritionist explained that bile secretion from the liver spikes right after a fatty meal like the food-truck burrito he'd just eaten.
words.etymology: se-(分开) + cernere(分辨) → 分出来 → 分泌

meanings.en: (medicine/microbiology) the process of eliminating all microorganisms from equipment or a surface
(medicine) a surgical procedure that permanently prevents someone or an animal from reproducing

examples: The surgical team double-checked the autoclave log to confirm sterilization had reached the required temperature before the instruments went back into circulation.
The vet recommended sterilization for the shelter cats before adoption, both to control the population and prevent certain cancers.
The tattoo studio kept its sterilization log posted by the door after a customer's infection complaint went viral online.
New hires at the hospital spend their first shift shadowing sterilization protocols for every reusable instrument tray.
The city's low-cost sterilization clinic for stray dogs had a three-month waiting list by early spring.
words.etymology: sterilis(不育、贫瘠) → 让它长不出东西 → 灭菌

meanings.en: to supervise and manage an activity, place, or group of people

examples: The site engineer was hired specifically to superintend the bridge construction from foundation pour to final inspection.
She superintended the entire ballot-counting process, making sure every observer could see the tally sheets in real time.
The retired librarian now superintends the neighborhood book swap, making sure nobody hoards all the thrillers.
He was asked to superintend the office move, coordinating movers, IT, and forty confused employees in a single weekend.
The head chef superintends every plate that leaves the kitchen during the restaurant's Michelin inspection week.

relatedForms.zh: 监督人;主管;(美)学区总监

words.etymology: super-(在上) + tendere(留意) → 在上头盯着 → 监督

meanings.en: to overcome a difficulty or obstacle

examples: She surmounted every visa obstacle to finally start her master's program in Toronto this fall.
The startup surmounted its early funding setbacks and just closed a Series A round.
The prosthetic engineer had to surmount serious battery-life limits before the bionic hand could last a full workday.
Their mixed-doubles team surmounted a two-set deficit to win the club championship in a third-set tiebreak.
She surmounted her fear of public speaking by recording herself pitching the app idea every morning before work.
words.etymology: super-(越过) + mount(登) → 翻过去 → 克服

meanings.en: (finance/economics) the state of assigning a lower value to something, such as a currency, asset, or company, than its true worth

examples: Analysts pointed to the stock's undervaluation, trading at half its book value despite steady earnings growth.
Trading partners accused the central bank of deliberate currency undervaluation to keep exports artificially cheap.
The appraiser's undervaluation of the family home nearly cost them thousands when they tried to refinance last spring.
Investors flagged the biotech startup's undervaluation after its cancer-drug trial results leaked two days before the official announcement.
Employees argued the annual bonus formula relied on a systematic undervaluation of overtime hours logged during crunch season.

meanings.en: done by or affecting only one party; not mutual or agreed by all sides

examples: Management made a unilateral decision to cancel the holiday bonus — no vote, no warning.
The company issued a unilateral price hike on all subscriptions, and support was flooded with cancellation requests.
Without consulting the other co-founders, she made a unilateral call to pause the product launch just days before release.
The landlord's unilateral rent increase, taped to the lobby door on a Friday, broke at least two clauses in the lease.
He ended the partnership unilaterally over text, leaving his co-writer to find out from a group chat screenshot.
words.etymology: uni-(单一) + latus/later-(边) → 只有一边 → 单方面

meanings.en: not aware of what one is doing; unintentional

examples: The intern was an unwitting accomplice, forwarding the phishing email to half the marketing team.
I became the unwitting star of someone's TikTok after tripping over the dog on my morning run.
The barista became an unwitting meme after a regular filmed her perfectly timed eye-roll during the rush.
He was an unwitting test subject for the app's new algorithm, which quietly showed him triple the usual ads.
Her grandmother was an unwitting participant in the scam, reading out gift-card codes to a caller pretending to be tech support.
words.etymology: un- + wit(知晓) ← 古英语 witan → 不知情

meanings.en: to have an intense feeling of longing for something

examples: After three years in a cubicle, she yearned for the kind of freedom her freelancer friends kept posting about.
Stuck in traffic on the daily commute, I yearn for the tiny apartment near the office I keep talking myself out of.
By the third year of night shifts, he yearned for a single unbroken eight hours of sleep more than any raise.
She yearns for the quiet of her college dorm every time her toddler starts banging pots at six a.m.
After two years of remote work, she yearned for the ordinary chaos of a shared office kitchen and gossip by the coffee machine.
words.etymology: 古英语 georn(热切) → 心里发急 → 渴望

meanings.en: not showing proper respect; rude, especially toward someone older or of higher status

examples: Asking your manager's salary in the first team meeting is a pretty impertinent move, even at a 'flat' company.
The reporter's impertinent question about the CEO's divorce got her escorted out of the press conference.
Correcting the professor's grammar in front of the whole lecture hall was impertinent, even if he happened to be right.
The new intern's impertinent habit of replying-all with jokes annoyed half of upper management within a week.
Asking the bride's dress size out loud at the shower struck everyone as wildly impertinent, and the room went silent.
words.etymology: in-(不) + pertinere(相关) → 说不相干的 → 唐突无礼

meanings.en: impossible to stop or prevent; relentless in progress, unmoved by pleading
meanings.zh: 不可阻挡的;无法改变的,冷酷无情的

examples: The rent in this neighborhood has been on an inexorable climb since the new subway line opened.
Against the inexorable advance of the wildfire, the whole town evacuated within two hours.
The inexorable spread of the ransomware locked every hospital terminal within six hours despite IT's frantic patching.
Her promotion felt inexorable after two straight years of the highest sales numbers on the entire floor.
The glacier's inexorable retreat has exposed a valley floor no one alive has ever seen bare rock on.
words.etymology: in-(不) + exorare(求得动) → 怎么求都不松口 → 不可阻挡

meanings.en: the quality of being clever, original, and inventive in solving problems (contrast with 'ingenuousness', which means naive candor)
meanings.zh: 创造力;独创性,巧思(与 ingenuousness“天真率直”相区分)

examples: The engineers showed real ingenuity, rigging a backup cooling system out of spare drone parts during the outage.
Her ingenuity turned a cramped studio apartment into a functional home office, gym, and guest room.
The road crew's ingenuity turned three traffic cones and a shopping cart into a passable detour sign overnight.
The delivery driver's ingenuity got the fridge up three flights of stairs using nothing but furniture blankets and a hand truck.
Faced with a broken projector five minutes before the pitch, she improvised with such ingenuity that the investors never noticed.
words.etymology: ingenium(天生的才具) ← gignere(生) → 巧思

meanings.en: innocent or naive simplicity; artlessness and lack of guile (not to be confused with 'ingenuity', cleverness)
meanings.zh: 天真率直;单纯坦诚(易与 ingenuity“创造力”混淆,注意区分)

examples: There was an ingenuousness to the new grad's pitch — she genuinely believed every investor would say yes.
His ingenuousness at the negotiating table nearly cost the team the whole deal; he just told them our lowest price upfront.
His ingenuousness at the poker table was almost sweet — he'd grin every time he drew a good hand.
There was a certain ingenuousness in how she posted her salary publicly, assuming everyone would just be happy for her.
The rookie's ingenuousness showed when he thanked the opposing coach for 'such a fun, easy game' after getting blown out.
words.etymology: ingenuus(生而自由、天生如此) → 没学会遮掩 → 天真率直

meanings.en: showing an arrogant and contemptuous lack of respect, bolder than merely impertinent

examples: The waiter's insolent eye-roll when we asked for substitutions killed any chance of a decent tip.
He gave the coach an insolent shrug after being benched, which only guaranteed more bench time.
The new hire's insolent reply to the CEO's all-hands question — 'why does that matter?' — got him a stern email by lunch.
Her insolent tone with the flight attendant nearly got the whole family bumped from the overbooked connection.
He gave an insolent little smirk when the teacher returned his failed essay, as if the grade were beneath him.
words.etymology: in-(不) + solere(照惯例) → 不按规矩来 → 傲慢无礼

meanings.en: unwilling to change one's views or come to an agreement; uncompromising (about a person's stance, unlike 'inexorable', which describes an unstoppable process)
meanings.zh: 不妥协的;固执己见的(指人的立场,与 inexorable“不可阻挡的进程”相区分)

examples: The union stayed intransigent on healthcare benefits, and the strike dragged into its third week.
My uncle is intransigent about GPS — he still insists on printed maps for every road trip.
The HOA board stayed intransigent on the paint-color rule, even after half the street submitted a joint petition.
Negotiations stalled because the supplier was intransigent about the minimum order size, refusing to budge by even ten units.
She's intransigent about splitting the check exactly down to the cent, spreadsheet and all, every single dinner out.
words.etymology: in-(不) + transigere(谈拢) → 谈不拢 → 不妥协

meanings.en: lacking energy or vitality; pleasantly slow and relaxed
meanings.zh: 慵懒的;无精打采的,懒洋洋的

examples: We spent a languid Sunday afternoon on the balcony, too full from brunch to do anything but scroll our phones.
The heat made everyone languid by 3 p.m., and half the office was visibly fighting off a nap.
The cat stretched into a languid sprawl across the keyboard the moment the video call started.
Their honeymoon was ten languid days of hammocks, slow breakfasts, and phones left face-down in the villa.
By the fourth hour of the layover, everyone in the lounge had settled into the same languid, half-asleep slump.
words.etymology: languere(疲弱无力) → 慵懒

meanings.en: (of a tumor) cancerous and likely to spread; also, evil or harmful in intent
meanings.zh: (肿瘤)恶性的;(性质、意图)恶毒的,有害的

examples: The biopsy came back malignant, and she's starting chemo next week.
There's something malignant about the way that account spreads rumors just to farm engagement.
The radiologist circled the mass on the scan and used the word malignant before the patient had even sat down.
There was something malignant in how the ex kept 'accidentally' liking old photos just to needle his new girlfriend.
The compliance team flagged a malignant pattern in the trading algorithm, quietly siphoning fractions of a cent from every order.
