words.etymology: malus(坏) + gignere(生,同 malign) → 往坏里长 → 恶性

meanings.en: not direct or explicit in what is said; also, slanting rather than perpendicular
meanings.zh: 间接的,委婉的;倾斜的,斜的

examples: Her boss never says 'you're fired' outright — just an oblique comment about 'reassessing headcount' in Q3.
The photo, shot at an oblique angle from the balcony, made the whole street look like a miniature model.
Instead of rejecting the proposal outright, the client sent an oblique email about 'exploring other creative directions.'
The architect designed the skylight at an oblique angle so afternoon sun would never hit the desks directly.
Her mother's oblique questions about 'anyone new in your life lately' were really just fishing for wedding-planning updates.
words.etymology: 拉丁 obliquus(倾斜) → 不走直线 → 委婉、倾斜

meanings.en: not aware of or not noticing what is happening around one (contrast with 'oblique', indirect or slanting)
meanings.zh: 未察觉的;浑然不觉的(与 oblique“间接的/斜的”相区分)

examples: He was completely oblivious to the fact that he'd been on mute for the entire five-minute presentation.
She scrolled through videos, oblivious to the barista calling her name three times for a cold latte.
He walked straight into the glass door at the office, completely oblivious to the giant 'push' sticker at eye level.
She stayed oblivious to her own typos for the entire client email chain until someone finally flagged it in a reply-all.
Wearing noise-canceling headphones, he was oblivious to his roommate's frantic knocking about the flooding bathroom for a full ten minutes.
words.etymology: 拉丁 oblivisci(忘掉) → 全忘在脑后 → 浑然不觉

meanings.en: stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course of action

examples: The obstinate printer jammed for the fourth time this morning, and IT still won't replace it.
My dad is obstinate about never using ride-share apps, so we still drive him everywhere ourselves.
The toddler was obstinate about wearing the superhero cape to daycare, tantrum and all, every single morning that week.
Her obstinate refusal to update the ancient spreadsheet macro finally crashed the entire quarterly report on deadline day.
The negotiator stayed obstinate on the delivery deadline, unmoved by three separate pleas for a two-week extension.
words.etymology: ob-(顶着) + stare(站) → 站住不挪 → 固执

meanings.en: to make someone anxious, unsettled, or worried

examples: Nothing seemed to perturb her during the product launch, even when the live demo froze in front of forty investors.
He tried not to look perturbed when his manager casually mentioned 'restructuring' halfway through the sprint review.
The vet said the fireworks would perturb the dog for hours, so we closed every curtain in the apartment by six.
The sudden silence from her usually chatty group chat perturbed her more than any actual bad news would have.
He tried not to sound perturbed when the client canceled the contract mid-call, but his voice cracked on the last sentence.
words.etymology: per-(彻底) + turbare(搅乱) → 搅个底朝天 → 使不安

meanings.en: an instance of falling back into illness or a bad habit
to fall back into a previous illness or bad habit after improving

examples: Three months smoke-free, and one bad breakup made him relapse over a pack of cigarettes outside the bar.
Her physical therapist warned that skipping sessions could trigger a relapse before the knee had even finished healing.
He'd been off sugar for a month until the office birthday cake sent him straight into a relapse.
After a calm year, she relapsed into checking work email at 2 a.m. the moment the new project kicked off.
The rehab counselor said a single relapse doesn't erase eight months of sobriety, but it does reset the day count.
words.etymology: re-(再) + labi(滑倒) → 又滑了一跤 → 复发

meanings.en: admirably firm and determined, not changing one's mind

examples: After three rejected pitches, she stayed resolute about quitting her corporate job to freelance full-time.
The landlord was resolute — no pets, no exceptions — even after the tenant sent photos of the world's calmest cat.
He remained resolute about not checking work email on vacation, phone left in the hotel safe the whole week.
Despite the surgeon's warning, she stayed resolute about running the marathon just six weeks after the injury healed.
He remained resolute through four rounds of layoff rumors, refusing to update his resume until an official notice actually came.
words.etymology: re-(彻底) + solvere(解开) → 心结全解开了 → 坚决

meanings.en: occurring in sudden, brief, irregular bursts rather than continuously

examples: His productivity was spasmodic — three brilliant hours after midnight, then nothing useful until the next coffee.
The wifi in the mountain cabin gave off spasmodic bursts of signal, just enough to send one text before it cut out.
Her interest in the gym membership was spasmodic at best: two intense weeks in January, then radio silence until summer.
Her attention to the group project was spasmodic — a flurry of edits at midnight, then total silence for four days.
The old washing machine ran in spasmodic bursts, spinning hard for ten seconds before stalling out completely.
words.etymology: 希腊 spasmos(抽搐) ← span(拉扯) → 一阵一阵 → 断断续续

meanings.en: holding firmly to something; persistent in pursuing a goal despite difficulty
meanings.zh: 顽强的;坚持不懈的;紧握不放的

examples: The debt collector was tenacious, calling every single day for three weeks until the bill finally got paid.
She's tenacious about her morning run — typhoon, deadline, or hangover, she's still out the door by six.
Even after two rejections, he was tenacious enough to email the editor a third pitch with new data attached.
The toddler was tenacious about the locked cabinet, rattling the childproof latch for a solid twenty minutes straight.
Her tenacious follow-up emails, one a week for two months, finally got the vendor to issue the refund.
words.etymology: tenere(握住) → 抓住不放 → 顽强

meanings.en: sophisticated, refined, and courteous in a worldly, socially confident way
meanings.zh: 温文尔雅的;彬彬有礼的

examples: The new sommelier was so urbane that even a shattered vintage bottle turned into charming small talk with the table.
He showed up to the investor dinner in a perfectly tailored blazer, urbane and unbothered, like pitch decks were his native language.
Her urbane host manner made the awkward blind-date setup feel like an actual dinner party within minutes.
The retiring ambassador gave an urbane farewell toast that somehow made the awkward seating chart feel intentional.
Even fielding hostile questions from the board, the CFO stayed urbane, deflecting each one with a calm little joke.
words.etymology: urbs(城市) → 城里人的做派 → 温文尔雅

meanings.en: refraining from sex, or sexually pure and modest
(of style) simple and free from excessive ornamentation

examples: The reality show contestants signed a contract promising to stay chaste on camera — a rule nobody actually kept past week two.
After the divorce she chose a chaste, minimalist apartment: white walls, one plant, nothing that needed explaining to anyone.
Their whole courtship was oddly chaste, just long walks and voice notes, until the third month of dating.
Their pastor praised the couple for staying chaste until the wedding night, a detail the best man definitely didn't need to mention in his toast.
The convent's dress code required something almost aggressively chaste — ankle-length skirts, high necklines, no exceptions for summer heat.
words.etymology: 拉丁 castus(纯洁无瑕) → 贞洁

meanings.en: to search or research into something thoroughly

examples: She spent the whole flight delving into her ex's LinkedIn, cross-referencing every job change since 2019.
The new hire delved into six months of Slack history just to understand why the checkout bug kept reappearing.
Once the podcast delves into the company's early scandals, it's impossible to stop listening on the commute home.
The auditor delved into three years of expense reports before flagging a pattern of suspiciously round dinner receipts.
She delves into obscure true-crime forums every night instead of sleeping, chasing one more theory before bed.
words.etymology: 古英语 delfan(掘土) → 往深里挖 → 钻研

meanings.en: an act of attacking, plundering, or destroying something

examples: Years of corporate depredation had left the small town with a gutted factory and half its Main Street boarded up.
Marine biologists documented the depredations of illegal trawlers that had stripped the reef of fish in under a decade.
The old farmhouse showed the depredations of decades of neglect — rotted beams, a collapsed roof, weeds through the floorboards.
The report catalogued the depredations of the invasive beetle species, which had killed off entire pine forests within a decade.
Years of budget-cutting depredation left the public library with three working computers and a leaking roof.
words.etymology: de-(彻底) + praeda(猎物、战利品) → 当猎物扫荡 → 掠夺

meanings.en: not following a regular or predictable pattern; inconsistent
meanings.zh: 不稳定的;古怪的;飘忽不定的

examples: His Uber driving was so erratic — hard brakes, sudden lane changes — that she rated him two stars and tipped nothing.
The startup's revenue has been erratic all year, one great month followed by two that barely cover payroll.
Grandpa's texts have gotten erratic lately, sent at 3 a.m. and signed off with random emoji strings.
The stock's erratic swings after the earnings call left day traders scrambling to figure out what had actually gone wrong.
Her sleep schedule turned erratic the moment the new baby arrived, three-hour naps at completely random times of day.
words.etymology: errare(游荡、走错) → 到处乱走 → 飘忽不定

meanings.en: a minor fault or quirk in someone's character

examples: Sure, he alphabetizes his spice rack and refuses to send voice memos, but those foibles are part of why she loves him.
The performance review politely listed her foibles — chronic lateness, a weakness for reply-all — right under three glowing paragraphs.
Every roommate has a foible you learn to live with; hers was leaving one single dish unwashed by the sink, always.
Everyone at the office has learned to work around his one real foible: he can't start a meeting without a coffee refill first.
Among her many foibles, forgetting where she parked was the one that cost the most time every single week.
words.etymology: 古法语 feble(弱,即 feeble) → 弱的那一处 → 小毛病

meanings.en: lacking excitement or variety; boring and repetitive

examples: After the whirlwind of the wedding, the humdrum routine of grocery runs and dishwasher-loading felt almost like a relief.
He quit the humdrum accounting job to become a dive instructor and hasn't filed a spreadsheet since.
Most of parenting is humdrum — snacks, laundry, the same three songs on repeat — with a few unforgettable moments scattered in.
The internship turned out to be humdrum spreadsheet work, nothing like the exciting job description had promised.
Weekday mornings settled into a humdrum rhythm of alarms, cold coffee, and the same fifteen-minute commute.
words.etymology: hum(哼) 的叠韵重复,像一直哼同一个调 → 单调乏味

meanings.en: the quality of having many complex, interrelated parts; a complicated detail

examples: Nobody warned her about the intricacies of the visa paperwork until she was three stamps deep and still missing one form.
The watchmaker showed us the intricacy of the movement under a loupe — over two hundred parts smaller than a grain of rice.
Once you learn the intricacies of the tax code's freelance deductions, filing gets almost satisfying.
The chef walked us through the intricacy of the eight-course tasting menu, each plate timed to the minute.
New engineers spend their first month just learning the intricacies of the codebase's fifteen-year-old billing system.
words.etymology: in-(进入) + tricae(纠缠,同 extrication) → 缠成一团 → 错综复杂

meanings.en: the examination of one's own thoughts and feelings

examples: The therapy app pushed her toward more introspection than she expected, with a daily prompt she couldn't just swipe past.
A layoff has a way of forcing introspection — suddenly he was asking what he actually wanted from a career, not just a paycheck.
Her journal entries turned to introspection after the breakup, less 'what happened today' and more 'why do I keep doing this.'
Turning thirty pushed him into a bout of introspection he hadn't expected, mostly triggered by a single unflattering photo.
The retreat's silent mornings were built for introspection, though half the group just used the time to nap.
words.etymology: intro-(向内) + specere(看) → 往里看 → 内省

meanings.en: a long, eventful, or adventurous journey
meanings.zh: 漫长而充满曲折的旅程

examples: Getting the refund became a three-month odyssey through chatbots, hold music, and one supervisor who kept 'escalating' nothing.
Their post-graduation odyssey through six countries on a shoestring budget became the group chat's favorite story for years.
Moving apartments during a heatwave turned into a full odyssey — three flights of stairs, a broken elevator, and a U-Haul that showed up late.
Getting the visa approved turned into a bureaucratic odyssey involving four government offices and one notarized letter in the wrong language.
Their attempt to assemble the flat-pack crib became a two-hour odyssey ending with three leftover screws and a lot of muttering.
words.etymology: 荷马史诗中 Odysseus 十年归途 → 漫长曲折的旅程

meanings.en: not revealing one's thoughts or feelings readily; reserved
meanings.zh: 沉默寡言的;不愿吐露心声的

examples: He's oddly reticent about salary numbers, even with coworkers he trades everything else with.
She stayed reticent throughout the exit interview, giving one-word answers until HR finally stopped asking.
Normally reticent about his family, he opened up a little after his third drink at the reunion.
He stayed reticent about the diagnosis for weeks, only telling his sister after she noticed the hospital bracelet.
She's reticent online, no posts about her personal life, even though she'll happily talk your ear off in person.
words.etymology: re-(收回) + tacere(沉默) → 把话咽回去 → 沉默寡言

meanings.en: language intended to persuade or impress but lacking sincerity or substance
the art of effective or persuasive speaking or writing

examples: The candidate's campaign rhetoric about 'radical change' sounded great until reporters asked for a single concrete policy.
Her debate coach drilled classical rhetoric into her — ethos, pathos, logos — until arguing felt like architecture.
Stripped of the corporate rhetoric, the 'restructuring' memo just meant thirty people were getting laid off.
Strip away the marketing rhetoric about 'synergy' and the merger just meant three hundred people losing their jobs.
She studied rhetoric in grad school, analyzing how political speeches use repetition to make empty promises sound inevitable.
words.etymology: 希腊 rhētōr(演说家) → 演说术 → 华而不实的辞令

meanings.en: perceived by or affecting the mind without conscious awareness

examples: The ad agency swore the flashing logo wasn't subliminal messaging, just 'aggressive branding,' which somehow felt worse.
She never consciously noticed the background music at the mall, but its subliminal pull toward the food court worked every time.
Some fans insist the album has subliminal messages if you play the closing track backward — the band just laughs about it.
The app's notification sound was subtly annoying by design, a subliminal nudge that kept pulling him back to check it.
Marketers debated whether the flickering frame in the trailer counted as subliminal advertising or just a sloppy edit.
words.etymology: sub-(在下) + limen(门槛) → 意识门槛之下 → 潜意识的

meanings.en: to provide evidence to prove or support a claim

examples: The landlord couldn't substantiate the 'excessive wear' charge, so the deposit came back in full after one strongly worded email.
Her performance review cited 'communication issues' without a single example to substantiate it, so she asked HR for specifics in writing.
The influencer's before-and-after results were never substantiated by any actual lab testing, just a caption and good lighting.
The journalist refused to run the story until a second source could substantiate the whistleblower's claims about the factory conditions.
He couldn't substantiate his overtime hours without timestamped emails, so payroll only approved half of what he'd claimed.
words.etymology: sub-(在下) + stare(站立) → 底下立住了 → 证实

meanings.en: the highest point or peak of something, especially of success

examples: The band hit its zenith the summer their single played in every coffee shop and car window on the block.
By 2015, the mall was at its zenith — three bubble tea lines and a twenty-minute wait for the food court.
Her career reached its zenith with the promotion to creative director, right before the whole department got restructured.
The influencer's follower count hit its zenith right before the sponsorship scandal wiped out half her audience in a week.
Their startup reached its zenith at the funding announcement, with champagne in the office and a launch party that emptied the budget.
words.etymology: 阿拉伯 samt ar-ras(头顶的方向) → 天顶 → 顶点

meanings.en: to feel resentful envy about someone's success or possession; to give reluctantly

examples: I don't begrudge her the promotion — she answered emails at 11 p.m. for a year, she earned it.
He begrudged every dollar of the wedding budget, sighing audibly over the flower arrangements.
She begrudges her brother nothing except the fact that their parents still call him first with good news.
I don't begrudge him the corner office, honestly — he was first in and last out for two straight years.
She begrudged every hour spent proofreading her roommate's thesis, though she never actually said no to helping.
words.etymology: be-(使) + grudge(不情愿) → 心里过不去 → 嫉妒

meanings.en: to deliver or hand over formally, often to an unwelcome fate; to send goods for storage or sale
meanings.zh: 把…交付;把…打发(去某处/送人)

examples: After the third crash, the old laptop was consigned to a drawer, replaced without ceremony by a refurbished one.
The vintage coat was too small for her now, so she consigned it to a secondhand shop instead of the trash.
His first business plan got consigned to the back of a filing cabinet the moment the second, better idea showed up.
The rejected wedding dress design was consigned to a back rack, marked down twice before finally selling in March.
His unfinished novel got consigned to a desktop folder labeled 'someday,' which he hadn't opened in over a year.
words.etymology: com-(一并) + signum(印记) → 盖章交出去 → 交付

meanings.en: a future event or circumstance that is possible but unpredictable; something planned for as a precaution
meanings.zh: 意外情况;可能发生的事;应急预案

examples: The wedding planner had a rain contingency ready — a tent, folding chairs, and a playlist that didn't need an outlet.
Freelancers should keep three months of savings as a contingency, because clients ghost and invoices go 'lost' more than you'd think.
Every contract now includes a contingency clause for supply-chain delays, ever since the pandemic taught everyone that lesson the hard way.
The airline's contingency plan for the snowstorm meant three canceled flights and a hotel voucher nobody could actually redeem.
As a contingency against the server crashing during launch, the team kept a backup instance running quietly in a second region.
words.etymology: com-(一起) + tangere(触碰) → 恰好碰上 → 意外情况

meanings.en: in a state of disrepair or ruin, especially through age or neglect

examples: The listing photos made the cabin look rustic-chic, but in person it was just dilapidated — a caved-in porch and no working outlets.
They bought the dilapidated townhouse for a steal, then spent two years and every weekend fixing the roof.
A dilapidated bike sat chained to the same rack for so long that neighbors started calling it part of the scenery.
The dilapidated gym equipment in the building's basement hadn't been serviced since before the current tenants moved in.
They toured a dilapidated corner store with a caved-in ceiling, already imagining it as the coffee shop of their dreams.
words.etymology: dis-(散开) + lapis(石头) → 石头一块块散掉 → 破旧失修

meanings.en: to be a perfect or typical example of something

examples: The overflowing inbox and back-to-back Zoom calls epitomized what burnout culture looked like by 2026.
For a lot of commuters, that one photo of the flooded subway platform epitomized the whole disastrous morning.
Her tiny, plant-filled studio apartment pretty much epitomizes the 'city living on a budget' aesthetic everyone posts about.
The five-hour merger call that ended with no decision at all pretty much epitomized how the whole quarter went.
Her packed carry-on and three back-to-back layovers epitomized the exhausting reality behind those glossy travel-influencer photos.
words.etymology: epi-(在上) + temnein(切) → 切出一小块代表全体 → 集中体现

meanings.en: to strongly urge or encourage someone to do something

examples: The coach exhorted the team to keep pressing even at 3-0 down, and somehow they clawed back two goals.
Every wellness influencer on her feed exhorts followers to wake up at 5 a.m., journal, and cold-plunge before coffee.
His grandmother still exhorts him to call more often, usually right in the middle of him already calling her.
The CEO's all-hands email exhorted everyone to 'lean into the grind' just hours after announcing the layoffs.
Her personal trainer exhorts her to skip the elevator every single time, rain or shine, no exceptions.
words.etymology: ex-(出) + hortari(鼓动) → 把人推出去 → 力劝

meanings.en: to praise enthusiastically

examples: Every review extolled the ramen shop's broth, so of course the line was ninety minutes long by noon.
Grandpa still extols the virtues of his old flip phone, insisting it never once needed a software update.
The keynote spent twenty minutes extolling the new AI feature before anyone got to see it actually work.
The wedding toast extolled her patience for putting up with his terrible karaoke for six straight years.
Real-estate listings extol the 'charming character' of prewar apartments, which usually just means no closets and creaky floors.
words.etymology: ex-(向上) + tollere(举起) → 把人举高 → 颂扬

meanings.en: to have a noticeable, often restrictive or negative, effect on something; to encroach

examples: The new noise ordinance impinges on the night market's operating hours, and vendors are furious about the lost revenue.
Constant Slack pings from a different time zone kept impinging on what used to be an actual lunch break.
She resented how his moving schedule kept impinging on hers, every plan renegotiated around his last-minute shifts.
The new open floor plan impinges on everyone's focus time, with sales calls bleeding straight into the engineers' corner.
Her landlord's random inspection visits kept impinging on what little privacy the tiny studio already offered.
words.etymology: in-(向) + pangere(钉、撞) → 撞上去 → 侵犯

meanings.en: belonging naturally to something; essential and inherent

examples: She argued the painting's value was intrinsic — not the auction price, just the years of grief folded into every brushstroke.
Curiosity is intrinsic to how toddlers learn; you can't really schedule it into a lesson plan.
His manager kept pushing bonuses, but his motivation was intrinsic — he just liked solving the puzzle.
The coach argued that team trust was intrinsic to winning, no drill or scoreboard could manufacture it artificially.
For her, hiking has an intrinsic reward — no Strava badge required, just the quiet at the top of the trail.
words.etymology: intra-(内部) → 本来就在里面 → 内在固有

meanings.en: (chiefly British) a person who supervises students during an examination to prevent cheating

examples: The invigilator confiscated his phone the moment it buzzed on the desk during the final exam.
Two invigilators patrolled the hall, one checking ID cards while the other watched for wandering eyes.
The invigilator paced silently between the desks, pausing just long enough to make everyone paranoid about their own hands.
A nervous invigilator accidentally started the exam timer five minutes early, and half the hall didn't notice until it was too late.
Students grumbled that the new invigilator checked bags so thoroughly that the exam started ten minutes behind schedule.
words.etymology: in-(在旁) + vigilare(守夜警醒) → 在旁盯着 → 监考官

meanings.en: not able to be changed, reversed, or recovered; final
meanings.zh: 不可撤销的;不可挽回的

examples: Hitting 'delete account' came with a warning in red: this action is irrevocable, no recovery period, no second chances.
Signing the letter of intent felt irrevocable, even though the lawyer insisted they could still walk away before closing.
The damage to their friendship after the money dispute felt irrevocable, no matter how many times he apologized.
Clicking 'confirm purchase' on the nonrefundable flight felt irrevocable the second the confirmation email landed in his inbox.
The judge's ruling was irrevocable, and no amount of appeal filings could undo the custody arrangement now.
words.etymology: in-(不) + revocare(叫回来) → 叫不回来 → 不可撤销

meanings.en: deserving praise and commendation

examples: Cutting single-use plastic from the office kitchen was a laudable move, though everyone still microwaves fish at noon.
His laudable attempt to learn Mandarin from an app lasted exactly eleven days before the streak broke.
It's laudable that the startup offers unlimited PTO, though nobody on the team actually takes more than a week.
His laudable habit of tipping generously never wavered, even during the month he was between jobs himself.
The company's laudable parental-leave policy looked great in the recruiting deck, though almost no one senior actually used it.
words.etymology: laus/laud-(赞誉,同 eulogize 的另一半) → 值得称赞

meanings.en: a state of confusion or bewilderment caused by something complicated or hard to understand
(machine learning/NLP) a metric measuring how well a probability model predicts a sample, with lower values indicating better predictions
meanings.zh: (机器学习/自然语言处理)困惑度(评估语言模型的指标)

examples: She stared at the tax form in pure perplexity, unable to figure out which box applied to freelance income.
The new model cut perplexity almost in half on the validation set, which explained why its generated text suddenly read so much more fluently.
He stared at the IKEA instructions in total perplexity, convinced there was a missing step between panel four and five.
The new hire's perplexity over the company's three different Slack workspaces was obvious within her first hour.
The team fine-tuned the chatbot for another week after perplexity scores stalled just above their target on the benchmark set.
words.etymology: per-(彻底) + plectere(编织,同 implicate) → 缠成死结 → 困惑

meanings.en: sounding sad or mournful

examples: The dog let out a plaintive whine every time the suitcase came out of the closet, already bracing for the goodbye.
A plaintive violin note opened the film's trailer, and half the theater was already reaching for tissues.
Her voicemail sounded plaintive, not angry, just tired of asking him to call back.
The cat gave a plaintive meow at the closed pantry door every time the treat bag rustled somewhere else in the house.
His plaintive text — 'are we still on for tonight?' — sat unanswered for three hours before she finally replied.
words.etymology: plangere(捶胸恸哭) → 哀伤

meanings.en: to make or become less tight, tense, fast, or intense

examples: The climber slackened the rope just enough to let his partner adjust her footing on the ledge.
Demand for the product slackened sharply after the holiday rush, forcing the factory to cut a shift.
He slackened his pace for the last two miles of the marathon, worried he'd cramp before the finish line.
The dog walker slackened the leash the moment the puppy stopped pulling toward every single squirrel.
Foot traffic in the mall slackened noticeably once the anchor department store closed its doors for good.
words.etymology: 古英语 slæc(松弛) → 放松

meanings.en: comfort or consolation in a time of distress or sadness

examples: After the layoff, she found solace in a strict routine of morning runs and instant noodles at midnight.
He took solace in the fact that at least the breakup happened before they'd signed the apartment lease together.
Group chats became a real source of solace during the long, isolating months of the new job in a new city.
She found solace in baking sourdough every Sunday, the one ritual that survived three straight months of chaos at work.
He took solace in his houseplants after the divorce, something small and green that actually responded to being cared for.
words.etymology: 拉丁 solari(安慰) → 慰藉

meanings.en: to overcome or bring under control; to make less intense or quieter

examples: It took two roommates and a broom to subdue the raccoon that had wandered into the kitchen through the pet door.
The dim lighting and lo-fi playlist were clearly meant to subdue the after-work crowd into ordering another quiet round.
She tried to subdue her excitement about the job offer until the contract was actually signed.
It took the whole flight crew to subdue the passenger who wouldn't stop shouting at the gate agent over a delay.
She dimmed the string lights to subdue the harsh overhead glow before the guests arrived for dinner.
words.etymology: sub-(在下) + ducere(引导) → 压到下面 → 制服

meanings.en: showing strong, passionate feeling, often forceful or intense

examples: Her objection to the open-office redesign was vehement enough that the whole meeting went quiet for a second.
He's vehement about not answering work calls after 7 p.m., a boundary that took him three jobs to actually enforce.
The comment section turned vehement within minutes of the price-hike announcement, and the brand deleted the post by morning.
His vehement denial of the leaked memo only made the whole newsroom more certain that it was real.
She was vehement that the recipe needed real butter, not margarine, and refused to even taste-test the substitute.

meanings.en: to treat two distinct things as if they were one, blurring a difference that matters
meanings.zh: 把(不同的事物)混为一谈;混淆

meanings.en: to merge two or more texts, versions, or accounts into a single whole
meanings.zh: 把(文本、版本等)糅合为一体;合并

examples: The article conflates burnout with ordinary tiredness, so readers finish it believing a quiet weekend can undo a brutal year.
The reviewer conflated battery life with charging speed, and the comments spent three days untangling two numbers that measure nothing alike.
My manager keeps conflating being busy with being productive, which is why the calendar is full and the roadmap has not moved.
Don't conflate a friendly landlord with a fair lease — read the clause about the deposit before you sign anything.
The editor conflated three surviving manuscripts into one readable text, noting in the margins wherever the versions disagreed.
words.etymology: con-(一起) + flare(吹) → 吹到一起熔在一处 → 混为一谈

meanings.en: a large, organized collection of texts or recordings, gathered so that language or data can be studied at scale
meanings.zh: 语料库;(供研究的)文本、数据集合

meanings.en: the complete body of work produced by one writer, artist, or field
meanings.zh: (某人或某领域的)全部作品;文集

examples: The team trained the model on a corpus of thirty years of local newspapers, which is why it still writes like a 1998 city reporter.
Before signing off on the dictionary entry, she checked how often the phrase actually appeared in a corpus of spoken British English.
The startup's only real asset was a corpus of medical transcripts that nobody else had bothered to digitize.
His entire corpus fits on one shelf: two novels, a book of essays, and the letters his sister published after he died.
Critics who dismiss her early films clearly have not watched the full corpus, where the later ones quietly answer the first.
words.etymology: 拉丁 corpus(身体) → 文字的「全身」 → 文集、语料库

meanings.en: of an operation: either completing in full or having no effect at all, never leaving a half-finished state
meanings.zh: (计算机)原子性的,不可分割的(操作要么完整完成,要么完全不发生)

meanings.en: relating to atoms, or to nuclear energy and nuclear weapons
meanings.zh: 原子的;原子能的,核武器的

meanings.en: so small or basic that it is treated as a single unit and never broken down further
meanings.zh: 小到不可再分的,最小单元的

examples: Wrap the two database writes in a transaction so the whole thing is atomic — either both land or neither does.
The payment service retried the charge twice because the refund step was not atomic, and one customer got billed three times.
Her grandfather spent thirty years at the atomic weapons plant and would not say the word plutonium at the dinner table.
The lab's atomic clock drifts by less than a second every hundred million years, which the tour guide repeated three times.
Her note-taking system breaks every book into atomic ideas, one thought per card, filed by theme rather than by author.

relatedForms.zh: 以原子方式地,不可分割地

words.etymology: a-(不) + tomos(切开) → 不可再分 → 原子的、原子性的

meanings.en: accepted as the standard, official, or definitive form of something
meanings.zh: 标准的,规范的;公认权威的

meanings.en: belonging to the body of works accepted as major, or to the official version of a story
meanings.zh: 属于经典之列的;(情节)属于官方设定的

meanings.en: relating to church law, or to the books officially accepted as part of the Bible
meanings.zh: 教会法规的;(圣经)正典的

examples: Every product page ships a canonical URL, or Google will pick one of the six duplicates itself and pick wrong.
Store every phone number in one canonical format before you compare them, or the same customer shows up as four accounts.
Grandma's recipe card counts as the canonical version of the stew; every other cousin's attempt is a variation and everyone knows it.
Her reading project skips the canonical novels entirely and works through prize lists from countries she has never visited.
The seminar spent a whole week on why four gospels became canonical and dozens of other early texts did not.

relatedForms.zh: 按标准形式地;依正典地

words.etymology: 希腊 kanōn(量尺、准绳) → 标准 → 公认为标准的

meanings.en: a note printed at the bottom of a page that gives a source or an extra remark
a small detail or minor figure that the main story quickly leaves behind and forgets
meanings.zh: (比喻)无足轻重的小插曲,很快被遗忘的细节

meanings.en: to add footnotes to a text, or to back a statement up with a note giving its source
meanings.zh: 给...加脚注;为(说法)加注出处

examples: The claim looked solid until you chased the footnote and found it pointed at a blog post from 2009.
Half the fun of that biography is in the footnotes, where the author quietly demolishes three rival historians.
The contract's real terms hide in a footnote on page fourteen, printed in grey type nobody was meant to read.
The startup raised ninety million and folded within a year, now just a footnote in every talk about the bubble.
She footnotes every claim in her memos, which makes them twice as long and almost impossible to argue with.

meanings.en: not moving at all, or showing no energy and no willingness to act
meanings.zh: 一动不动的;死气沉沉的,无所作为的

meanings.en: chemically inactive; not reacting with other substances
meanings.zh: (化学)惰性的,不活泼的;不起反应的

examples: The cat lay inert on the warm radiator all afternoon, ignoring the doorbell, the vacuum, and finally the can opener.
The ethics committee has been inert for two years, meeting quarterly to postpone the same three items.
Three months after launch the app sat inert on ten thousand phones, opened once and never opened again.
The display case is flooded with an inert gas so the four-hundred-year-old manuscript cannot oxidize while tourists photograph it.
Ninety percent of the spray is inert ingredients; the label names none of them, which is exactly what the lawsuit is about.
words.etymology: in-(无) + ars(技艺、能力) → 无所施为 → 呆滞的、惰性的

meanings.en: a single piece of evidence that settles who is responsible, leaving nothing left to argue about

examples: The leaked pricing memo was the smoking gun: it logged the recall six months before anyone told the regulator.
Investigators spent eleven months on the case and never found a smoking gun, so the prosecutor quietly dropped two charges.
No smoking gun turned up in the audit, but a pattern of round-number invoices convinced the board to change accountants.
Her lawyer held up the timestamped badge scan like a smoking gun, and the courtroom went quiet for a full ten seconds.
Every fresh leak was billed as another smoking gun, and by the fourth one readers had stopped believing the phrase meant anything.
words.etymology: 枪口还在冒烟 → 刚开过枪的人就是凶手 → 铁证

meanings.en: conditions under which everyone competes by the same rules, with no one starting from a built-in advantage
meanings.zh: 公平竞争的环境;各方条件对等的局面

examples: European carriers lobbied for two years for a level playing field on state aid before the Gulf routes were reopened.
Blind auditions were meant to create a level playing field, and within a decade the orchestra's intake looked nothing like before.
Anyone calling the internship market a level playing field has never watched a partner's daughter skip the entire application process.
There is no level playing field in app-store search: the platform's own apps sit above the fold before anyone bids.
The ministry still invokes the level playing field it promised in 2019, though rural schools are sharing one laptop per class.

relatedForms.zh: 拉平差距,创造公平竞争的条件

words.etymology: 球场不倾斜 → 谁都不占坡度之利 → 公平竞争

meanings.en: competition in which rivals keep undercutting each other on wages, prices, or standards until everyone involved is worse off
meanings.zh: 逐底竞争;竞相压低工资、价格或标准以压过对手

examples: Once one platform waived its commission, the others followed within a month, and courier pay entered a race to the bottom.
Corporate tax rates have slid for a decade, and finance ministers privately admit the race to the bottom is now unstoppable.
Editors paying a cent a word are starting another race to the bottom, and the freelancers who can afford to quit already have.
Every airline shaved another inch off seat pitch, and passengers watched a decade-long race to the bottom play out in their knees.
The two supermarkets kept undercutting each other on milk until dairy farmers called it a race to the bottom and stopped supplying both.
collocations: start a race to the bottom
a race to the bottom in wages

meanings.en: a course of action that is hard to stop once begun and leads step by step to something far worse
meanings.zh: 滑坡;一开头就收不住、步步走向更坏结果的做法

meanings.en: the fallacy of arguing that one small concession must inevitably end in an extreme outcome
meanings.zh: (逻辑)滑坡谬误;断言小小一步必然导致极端后果的论证错误

examples: Letting the ministry vet a single broadcast licence is a slippery slope, and the next application will be judged by the same people.
Paying one supplier late to smooth cash flow is a slippery slope; by March you are choosing which invoices to ignore each week.
She started answering email at dinner and slid down the slippery slope her therapist had warned about; now she works every Sunday.
The coach called skipping one recovery day a slippery slope for a runner six weeks out from her first marathon.
Her opponent leapt from a parking fee to the collapse of small business, a textbook slippery slope the moderator named on the spot.

meanings.en: to force yourself to do or accept something unpleasant that you have been avoiding
meanings.zh: 咬紧牙关面对;硬着头皮去做(躲不掉的难事)

examples: After three winters of patching the roof, my parents finally bit the bullet and paid for a full replacement.
The startup bit the bullet and rewrote its billing system from scratch, losing two months of features to stop the nightly outages.
She kept postponing the dentist for a year, then bit the bullet and booked the root canal for a Monday morning.
I'm going to bite the bullet and tell my manager the deadline is impossible before the client hears it from someone else.
Every February she bites the bullet, opens the shoebox of receipts, and does her own taxes at the kitchen table.

meanings.en: official rules and paperwork so excessive that they delay or block getting anything done

examples: Opening the bakery took four months of red tape: three inspections, two permits, and a licence that arrived after the ovens did.
The grant itself was generous, but the red tape around reporting ate an entire staff position for the first year.
Getting my transcript recognized abroad meant six weeks of red tape, from notarized copies to a translator the ministry had approved.
Volunteers wanted to hand out surplus meals, but red tape over food-safety liability kept the trays in the freezer until they spoiled.
The mayor promised less red tape for small builders, then added a second review board six months later.
words.etymology: 旧时英国公文用红布带捆扎 → 繁琐的官僚手续

meanings.en: a warning or condition attached to a statement, limiting how far it holds
meanings.zh: 附带的告诫;限定条件;但书

examples: The doctor cleared him to start running again, with the caveat that he stop the moment his knee begins clicking.
Our landlord agreed to the dog, with one caveat: any scratched floorboard comes out of the deposit when we leave.
The benchmark looks impressive until you read the caveats buried in the footnotes about test hardware and warm-up runs.
Every glowing review of the restaurant carries the same caveat: book six weeks ahead or don't bother turning up.
The forecast comes with one large caveat: it assumes the port reopens in April, which nobody in shipping expects.
words.etymology: 拉丁 cavēre(警惕) → caveat(让他当心) → 附加的告诫

meanings.en: existing or holding power in reality, though not officially or legally recognized
meanings.zh: 事实上的;实际存在的(虽无法律地位)

meanings.en: in reality, whatever the official or legal position says
meanings.zh: 事实上;实际上(而非法律上)

examples: With the capital under siege, the port city has served as the de facto seat of government for eighteen months.
Her job title still says assistant, but she has been the de facto head of the department since March.
The spreadsheet nobody owns has become the de facto standard for tracking inventory, and two teams now refuse to use anything else.
The rule was never repealed, but with no inspectors left to enforce it, the ban is de facto over.
Nobody voted on it, but my flatmate is de facto in charge of the household budget, and the rest of us just transfer money.
words.etymology: 拉丁 de(出自) + facto(事实) → 事实上的(对 de jure)

meanings.en: following something disruptive, and as a result of it; takes a noun phrase, never a clause
meanings.zh: 紧随(重大或负面事件)之后,并因之而起;后接名词,不是中性的 after

examples: In the wake of the data breach, the company spent six months rebuilding a trust its ads had taken a decade to buy.
Three senior engineers quit in the wake of the reorg, and the on-call rota has been held together with volunteers ever since.
In the wake of a single viral complaint, the restaurant's booking page emptied out and the owner started answering the phone himself.
Insurance premiums across the valley tripled in the wake of last summer's fires, and half the older residents simply let their policies lapse.
Nobody at the ministry wanted the job in the wake of two resignations, so it went to the only deputy who hadn't testified.
collocations: in the wake of the scandal
in the wake of a crisis
in the wake of the pandemic
words.etymology: wake(船驶过后的尾流) → 重大事件过后的波及

meanings.en: sentence-initial connective that concedes the point just made and then turns against it
meanings.zh: 话虽如此;先认可上一句,再转向相反的一面(置于句首,后加逗号)

examples: The rollout slipped two weeks and the docs are still half-written. That said, nobody has filed a single bug since Friday.
Her portfolio is the strongest we've seen this year; that said, she has never shipped anything with more than four people on it.
The gym is overpriced and the showers are cold. That said, it is the only one open at five in the morning.
I still think we picked the wrong database. That said, the migration is done, and reopening the argument now would cost us a quarter.
Reviews called the new season slow and self-indulgent. That said, eleven million people watched the finale within a day of it dropping.
collocations: that said, it is worth noting
that said, none of this changes
that said, I would still argue
words.etymology: that having been said 的省略 → 话既已说过 → 话虽如此

meanings.en: not at all; emphatic negation — when it opens a clause the subject and verb invert
meanings.zh: 绝不是;远非如此(强调性否定,置于句首时主谓要倒装)

examples: By no means is the funding secure — the second tranche depends on a review nobody has scheduled yet.
By no means should you sign the lease before someone who has actually read clause 12 explains what the exit fee covers.
The prototype works, but it is by no means ready for anyone outside the team to touch without a walkthrough.
The new law by no means guarantees a refund; it only forces the airline to tell you within thirty days.
Only two of us objected, so the vote was by no means unanimous, whatever the minutes ended up recording.
words.etymology: means(手段、方法) → 用任何手段都不 → 绝不

meanings.en: in most cases but not all; 'usually', with the exceptions conceded rather than ignored
meanings.zh: 多半;十有八九(留有例外余地的 usually,可置句首或句中)

examples: More often than not, the bug turns out to be a stale cache, but the twenty minutes spent proving that still hurt.
Appeals against the parking fine succeed more often than not, which tells you how carefully the tickets were issued in the first place.
The senior nurses more often than not know the diagnosis before the scan comes back, though nobody writes that in the chart.
More often than not the cheaper flight wins, though anyone who has slept in Terminal 3 will argue the savings are imaginary.
Ask him for a deadline and more often than not you will get a question about scope instead of a date.
collocations: more often than not, the opposite is true
guess right more often than not
words.etymology: not 后省略了 often → 发生的次数多于不发生 → 多半

meanings.en: the estimating of an unknown value that lies between two known ones, so that a gap in a series is filled in
meanings.zh: 插值;内插(用已知点之间的推算值填补空缺)

meanings.en: a passage inserted into a text that was not in the original, typically added later by someone other than the author
meanings.zh: (文本中)插入的段落,窜入的文字

examples: The animation looked jerky until she turned on interpolation, and suddenly the ball arced between keyframes like it had weight.
Their dashboard fills gaps in the sensor feed by interpolation, which is fine until the gap is six hours wide.
Zooming past 400% exposes the interpolation: the software is inventing pixels that were never in the original photograph.
Most scholars treat the closing paragraph as a later interpolation, added by a copyist centuries after the author died.
He replaced the clumsy string concatenation with interpolation, and the log line finally became readable at three in the morning.

relatedForms.zh: 插值、内插;(在文本中)插入、窜改
内插得出的;后人插入的

words.etymology: inter-(之间) + polire(打磨、修饰) → 中间插入改动 → 插值;窜入

meanings.en: the fact of having happened only a short time ago, especially when that alone makes something feel more important than it is
meanings.zh: 新近性,近期性(尤指仅因发生得近而被高估的分量)

examples: The hiring panel's recency bias was obvious: everyone raved about the last candidate and forgot the strong one from Tuesday morning.
Retrospectives suffer from the recency effect — the team dissects last week's outage and never mentions the two quiet months before it.
The recommender overweights recency, so one late-night documentary binge buried six months of carefully cultivated taste.
Ranking search results by recency alone put a typo-ridden blog post above the specification it was misquoting.
Investors fall for recency bias every cycle, extrapolating three good quarters into a decade and calling the result a thesis.

meanings.en: of a data type or operation: supplied directly by the language or system and not built out of anything smaller
meanings.zh: (计算机)原生的,基本的(语言直接提供、无法再拆解的类型或操作)

meanings.en: belonging to an early stage of development, or crude and lacking the refinements now taken for granted
meanings.zh: 原始的,早期的;简陋的,粗糙的

meanings.en: a basic type or operation that a language or system provides as a building block for everything else
meanings.zh: (计算机)原语,基本类型;最小构件

examples: In JavaScript a string is a primitive value, so passing it around never gives two variables a handle on the same object.
Rewriting the parser around primitive types instead of wrapper classes cut the memory footprint of a single request nearly in half.
The lock is the only synchronization primitive the runtime exposes, so every queue in the codebase is built on top of it.
Their deployment process is still primitive — someone SSHes into the box at midnight and copies the files by hand.
The cabin was gloriously primitive: no wiring, no signal, and a wood stove that took three attempts to light.
words.etymology: primus(第一、最初) + -ive → 最初阶段的 → 原始的;最基本的

meanings.en: using exactly the same words as the original, with nothing changed, added, or left out
reproducing the original word for word, as a record or quotation does

examples: She repeated his apology verbatim in the group chat, and the tone that worked in person landed like a threat.
The intern copied the error message verbatim into the ticket, which is why the fix took twenty minutes instead of two days.
Reciting the terms of service verbatim did not impress the support agent, who had heard clause 14 quoted all morning.
The researcher insisted on a verbatim transcript, including every stray um, because the pauses were half of what she was studying.
His resignation email included a verbatim quote from the handbook, which made the whole thing feel drafted by a lawyer.
words.etymology: verbum(词) + -atim(逐一) → 逐字逐句 → 一字不差地

meanings.en: an obsessive preoccupation with someone or something that a person cannot let go of
meanings.zh: 执念;病态的迷恋;(心理学)固恋

meanings.en: the process of making something firm or permanent, as when a specimen is preserved for the microscope or nitrogen is locked into a compound
meanings.zh: 固定(作用);(标本的)固定处理;(氮的)固定

examples: Her fixation on the one-star review lasted three days, while the ninety-seven positive ones went completely unread.
The team's fixation on shipping by Friday meant nobody questioned whether the feature was something users had actually asked for.
After the breakup he developed a fixation with her Instagram stories, checking them at two in the morning like clockwork.
My therapist called it a childhood fixation: every argument with my boss somehow replays a dinner-table fight from 1998.
The lab ruined the sample because fixation ran twenty minutes too long and the cell membranes came out shredded under the microscope.

relatedForms.zh: 过度专注的;着魔般执着的

words.etymology: 拉丁 figere(钉住) → 固定 → 心理上钉住不放的执念

meanings.en: a small but secure position from which further progress can be made
meanings.zh: 立足点;(可据以发展的)稳固基础

meanings.en: a place on a rock or slope where a foot can be securely planted while climbing

examples: Three years after launching in Jakarta, the startup finally has a real foothold in Southeast Asia and is hiring locally.
Open-source drivers gave Linux its first foothold in the data center, and twenty years later it runs almost everything there.
She took the unpaid internship purely as a foothold, and within a year she was the one interviewing candidates.
Cheap prepaid plans let the carrier gain a foothold in rural markets that the big three had written off entirely.
Halfway up the wet granite she groped for a foothold, found nothing but moss, and shouted down for the rope.

meanings.en: returning to an earlier, less developed or less desirable state; moving backward rather than forward
of a tax or charge: taking a larger share of income from those who earn less, so the burden falls hardest at the bottom
meanings.zh: 累退的(收入越低实际负担越重,与 progressive 累进的相反)

meanings.en: relating to statistical regression, in which one variable is modelled as depending on others

examples: A flat sales tax on groceries is deeply regressive: the cashier ringing it up pays a bigger share than the owner.
Economists called the new toll regressive, since a nurse commuting from the suburbs pays the same five pounds as a banker.
Rolling back remote work felt regressive to everyone who had spent two years proving the office was never the point.
Under stress the four-year-old turned regressive overnight: back to the bottle, back to the crib, back to nobody sleeping.
Their regressive model predicts delivery dates from ticket counts, which works fine until someone files a hundred junk tickets.

relatedForms.zh: 倒退;退化;(统计)回归分析

words.etymology: re-(向后) + gradi(行走) → 往回走 → 倒退的

meanings.en: secret and dishonest; done in a way meant to escape notice
meanings.zh: 暗中的;不正当的;偷偷摸摸的

meanings.en: in sport, thrown or served with the hand kept below shoulder level
in a secret and dishonest manner

examples: Poaching the client list on his way out was an underhand move, and the whole industry heard about it within a week.
The landlord's underhand tactics, cutting the hot water and losing the paperwork, were designed to make tenants leave without a fight.
Nothing in the contract was illegal, but burying the auto-renewal in clause 34 struck the regulator as thoroughly underhand.
She serves underhand on purpose, and half the opposing team is still arguing about whether that counts as unsporting.
He got the promotion underhand, briefing against two colleagues in private meetings he later swore had never happened.

relatedForms.zh: 暗中的;不正当的(美式英语更常用,英式多用 underhand)

words.etymology: under(在下面) + hand(手) → 手压低不让人看见 → 暗中的

meanings.en: to make someone suffer something unpleasant — damage, pain, a penalty, or merely your own company
meanings.zh: 使遭受;把(痛苦、损害、惩罚)强加于

examples: The storm inflicted more damage on the pier in one night than a decade of budget meetings had managed to repair.
He seemed to enjoy inflicting the seating chart on people who had told him exactly who they could not sit beside.
The fine the regulator inflicted was small enough that the company wrote it off as a cost of doing business.
The coach inflicted a punishing set of sprints on anyone who arrived late, and word got round within a week.
Nobody counts the damage a rewrite inflicts on the people left keeping the old system alive in the meantime.
words.etymology: in-(在…上) + fligere(打击) → 把打击加在某人身上 → 使遭受

meanings.en: to take the worst of something bad, more of it than anyone else involved does
meanings.zh: 首当其冲;承受最重的一击

examples: Junior staff bore the brunt of the reorganization: three of the four cut roles sat below the manager line.
Coastal towns bear the brunt of every storm now, and their insurance premiums have doubled in six years.
The support team bears the brunt of each botched release, fielding complaints about decisions it was never consulted on.
Whoever answers the phone at a utility is bearing the brunt of a price rise they had no hand in setting.
She bore the brunt of the criticism at the hearing while the two executives who signed off stayed silent.
collocations: bear the brunt of the cuts
bear the brunt of the criticism

relatedForms.zh: 冲击的主力;最重的压力

words.headword: kick the can down the road

meanings.en: to postpone a hard decision, leaving the same problem for a later date and usually a worse one
meanings.zh: 拖延决策;把难题往后推

examples: Congress kicked the can down the road again, funding the agency for eleven weeks instead of settling the budget.
Every quarter we kick the can down the road on the migration, and every quarter the rewrite costs more.
Refinancing at a higher rate just kicks the can down the road; the principal is still sitting there in 2031.
The board kept kicking the can down the road on a successor, and then the CEO resigned with six weeks' notice.
Patching the roof a fourth time is kicking the can down the road, the inspector said, and the beams are already soft.
collocations: keep kicking the can down the road
just kicking the can down the road
words.etymology: 把罐子一路往前踢 → 问题永远在下一段路上

meanings.en: the easiest gains available, taken first because they cost the least effort for the most visible result
meanings.zh: 唾手可得的成果;最容易啃的那部分

examples: We spent the first sprint on low-hanging fruit and shipped four visible fixes before touching the architecture.
Cutting the unused software licences was low-hanging fruit; the hard part is the contract that runs until 2029.
Once the low-hanging fruit is gone, the savings target stops being a spreadsheet exercise and starts costing people jobs.
Every new consultant points at the same low-hanging fruit, which is why it has been picked over three times already.
Translating the help pages was low-hanging fruit next to localizing the checkout flow, so it went first.
words.etymology: 先摘够得着的果子 → 最省力的那份收益

meanings.en: to make a difference big enough to show up in the numbers that actually matter
meanings.zh: 产生实质影响;真正拉动指标

examples: The redesign looked sharper but did not move the needle: signups held flat for two straight quarters.
One podcast appearance moved the needle more than the entire quarter of ad spend, which nobody wanted to admit.
If a feature will not move the needle on retention, it goes to the bottom of the list no matter who asked.
Small refunds move the needle on churn far more than the loyalty program the company spent a year building.
They kept adding integrations, none of which moved the needle, until someone finally looked at the onboarding drop-off.
words.etymology: 仪表指针动了 → 才算真的有影响

meanings.en: to end something that is already running, deliberately and usually abruptly
meanings.zh: 叫停;终止(已在进行的事)

examples: Marketing pulled the plug on the campaign four days in, after the first billboard photo went around the wrong way.
Investors pulled the plug when the second pilot missed its numbers, and the office was cleared out by Friday.
Nobody wants to pull the plug on a project this visible, so it limps along consuming two engineers a quarter.
The venue pulled the plug at eleven sharp, mid-song, because the noise permit did not cover a minute more.
She pulled the plug on her own startup before the money ran out, which her board later called her smartest call.
words.etymology: 拔掉电源插头 → 正在跑的东西立刻停下

meanings.en: to approve something as a formality, without any real examination of it
meanings.zh: 走过场地批准;例行公事地放行

meanings.en: a person or body that approves whatever is put in front of them
meanings.zh: 只会盖章放行的人(或机构)

examples: The committee rubber-stamped the budget in nine minutes, including the line item that later triggered the audit.
Do not expect the ethics board to rubber-stamp a partnership that half the faculty has already objected to.
Approvals were rubber-stamped for eighteen months, which is how a supplier with no safety record got onto the list.
Shareholders complained that the board had become a rubber-stamp, meeting quarterly and querying nothing at all.
She refused to rubber-stamp the hire and asked for two references, which delayed the offer by a week.
words.etymology: 橡皮图章一按就过 → 不审查地批准

meanings.en: damaging someone's reputation by asserting something about them that is false

examples: The magazine pulled the profile within a day, conceding that two paragraphs were defamatory and could not be sourced.
Calling a competitor's product unsafe without evidence is defamatory, and the letter from their lawyers arrived by Tuesday.
He argued the post was opinion rather than defamatory fact, which is where most of these cases are actually decided.
The forum removed the thread after a defamatory claim about the surgeon spread to three other sites overnight.
A defamatory review can cost a small restaurant a season, and the correction never travels as far as the original.
words.etymology: dis-(四散) + fama(名声) → 把坏名声散出去

meanings.en: the traceable record of where something came from and whose hands it has passed through

examples: The gallery could not establish the vase's provenance beyond 1938, so the sale was quietly withdrawn.
Buyers now ask about provenance before price, because a clean ownership history is what makes a piece resellable.
Every ingredient on the menu lists its provenance, down to the name of the farm and the week it was picked.
The dataset shipped with no provenance at all, which made it useless for anything a regulator might later inspect.
A forged letter of provenance is easier to produce than a forged painting, which is why auction houses check both.
words.etymology: pro-(向前) + venire(来) → 从哪里来的

meanings.en: a strong feeling of dislike toward something, or an unwillingness to go near it

examples: Her aversion to open-plan offices was so strong that she took a pay cut for a job with a door she could close.
The fund manager's risk aversion cost the portfolio two years of gains, but it also spared clients the crash.
He developed a lasting aversion to oat milk after a barista scorched a whole jug of it in front of him.
Investors read the sudden aversion to chip stocks as a sign that the rate cut was no longer coming.
My nephew's aversion to anything green on his plate has turned every family dinner into a negotiation.
words.etymology: ab-(离开) + vertere(转) → 转身避开 → 厌恶

meanings.en: feeling or showing strong dislike for someone or something, or being fundamentally opposed to it
meanings.zh: 极其反感的;强烈抵触的

examples: The new principal was openly antipathetic to anything that smelled like standardized testing, and quietly shelved three district programs.
Critics called the studio's culture antipathetic to risk, which is why every summer release looked like the last one.
He was antipathetic toward the whole idea of networking events, yet somehow left with four business cards.
The committee proved antipathetic to the proposal long before the presenter reached his second slide.
Her father remained antipathetic to the marriage for a decade, then held the baby and forgot every objection.
words.etymology: anti-(反) + pathos(情感) → 情感相斥 → 反感的

meanings.en: done openly and without any attempt to hide it, usually of something bad
meanings.zh: 公然的,明目张胆的;毫不掩饰的

examples: The email was a blatant attempt to take credit for work the intern had done over three weekends.
Fans booed for a full minute after the referee ignored a blatant handball inside the box.
The listing's photos showed a blatant mismatch with the apartment we walked into on move-in day.
She called out his blatant disregard for the agenda, and the conference room went very quiet.
Regulators fined the bank for blatant advertising that promised returns nobody could actually earn.

meanings.en: pleasant, and easy to spend time with or in
meanings.zh: 令人愉快的;和蔼可亲的

meanings.en: willing to accept or go along with something
acceptable; satisfying what is required

examples: The hotel was nothing special, but the courtyard breakfast made it an unexpectedly agreeable place to spend a week.
Their new landlord turned out to be an agreeable man who fixed the boiler the same afternoon we called.
If everyone is agreeable to moving the deadline, I will send the client a revised schedule tonight.
She was agreeable to almost any restaurant, provided it was within walking distance of the office.
The terms looked agreeable on paper until our lawyer read the clause about automatic renewal.
words.etymology: ad-(朝向) + gratus(令人愉悦的) → 合心意的

meanings.en: deserving to be blamed for something that went wrong

examples: The report found the contractor blameworthy for skipping two inspections, but stopped short of recommending prosecution.
He is less blameworthy than the manager who signed off on the numbers without opening the spreadsheet.
Juries tend to find a distracted driver more blameworthy than one whose brakes simply failed.
She admitted she was blameworthy for the delay, then spent the weekend rebuilding the schedule anyway.
The ethics board called the omission blameworthy but not fraudulent, which saved his license and ended his career.

meanings.en: to act first in order to stop something from happening, or to make it irrelevant
meanings.zh: 先发制人地阻止;抢先一步化解

meanings.en: to take the place of a scheduled broadcast or a prior claim
meanings.zh: (节目)取代,占先播出;优先取得

examples: The company published its own audit on Friday to preempt the leak everyone knew was coming Monday.
She preempted the obvious objection by putting the cost breakdown on the very first slide.
Sending the apology before the story ran preempted a week of headlines the PR team had already drafted.
The city preempted a housing fight by rezoning the corridor while the developers were still hiring lawyers.
The emergency broadcast preempted the final ten minutes of the game, and the group chat has not forgiven it.
words.etymology: pre-(先) + emere(取,买) → 先取一步 → 抢先阻止

meanings.en: not easily noticed, because it does not stand out from what is around it
meanings.zh: 不显眼的;不引人注目的

examples: He chose an inconspicuous table near the kitchen so he could leave the interview without shaking twelve hands.
The bug lived in an inconspicuous helper function that nobody had opened since the original commit.
Her tattoo was deliberately inconspicuous, tucked where a rolled sleeve would hide it during client meetings.
The safe house looked inconspicuous from the road, which was the only feature the agency actually paid for.
A small, inconspicuous charge appeared on the statement every month until she finally called the bank.
words.etymology: in-(不) + con-(共) + specere(看) → 不被看到 → 不显眼

meanings.en: enjoying the company of other people and easy to be around
meanings.zh: 好交际的,合群的;友好随和的

examples: He is sociable in short bursts, then needs an entire quiet Sunday to recover from a birthday party.
The office moved to Friday lunches because the new hires were more sociable over food than over Slack.
Her grandmother stayed sociable well into her nineties, hosting card games that ran past midnight.
Border collies are sociable enough to greet strangers, but they will herd your guests toward the kitchen.
A sociable roommate sounded great until the third consecutive weeknight of strangers in the living room.
words.etymology: socius(同伴) + -able → 能与人为伴的 → 好交际的

meanings.en: produced or present in large quantities

examples: She took copious notes during the deposition, and three of them ended up deciding the case.
The recipe calls for copious amounts of butter, which is the only reason anyone finishes the tray.
His copious apologies did nothing to shorten the four hours we spent waiting at the gate.
The report includes copious detail about the outage but never says who approved the deploy.
Copious rain in April left the reservoir fuller than it had been in a decade.
words.etymology: copia(丰富,充裕) → 大量的

meanings.en: closed off from outside ideas and people, and uninterested in them
meanings.zh: 思想狭隘的;与外界隔绝的

meanings.en: belonging to or characteristic of an island

examples: The department had grown so insular that a good idea from another floor was treated as an accusation.
Living in the same six blocks for forty years made him insular in ways he could not hear in his own jokes.
Critics accused the festival of becoming insular, booking the same twelve bands the founders loved in college.
An insular engineering culture is how a company ends up shipping its fourth incompatible logging library.
The survey mapped insular species that exist nowhere but on three volcanic outcrops in the Pacific.
words.etymology: insula(岛) → 与外界隔绝 → 思想狭隘的

meanings.en: the belief that all human beings belong to one community, above nation or tribe
meanings.zh: 世界主义(视全人类为一个共同体的思想)

meanings.en: the quality of being at ease among many cultures; the international character of a place
meanings.zh: 国际化气息;见多识广的世界性

examples: The seminar traced cosmopolitanism from Diogenes calling himself a citizen of the world to today's climate treaties.
Critics argue that cosmopolitanism asks people to love humanity in general while neglecting the neighbors they actually have.
A wave of nationalist politics has made cosmopolitanism sound naive to voters who once found it obvious.
Her cosmopolitanism was learned in airport lounges, and it showed in how quickly she could read a room.
The city sells its cosmopolitanism in tourism ads, then argues about immigration at every council meeting.
words.etymology: kosmos(世界) + polites(公民) → 世界公民 → 世界主义

meanings.en: the act of stepping in to plead with someone on another person's behalf
meanings.zh: 代为说情;从中斡旋,调停

meanings.en: prayer offered on behalf of another person

examples: Only the ambassador's quiet intercession kept the two delegations at the table past midnight.
He got the internship through his aunt's intercession, and spent two years proving he deserved it anyway.
The prisoner's release came after months of intercession by a small human-rights group nobody had heard of.
Without the union's intercession, the schedule change would have gone through on a Friday afternoon email.
Her grandmother lit a candle every Sunday and asked for the saint's intercession on behalf of the family.
words.etymology: inter-(之间) + cedere(走) → 走到两者中间 → 说情

meanings.en: calm and casual about something that would normally cause concern
meanings.zh: 若无其事的;满不在乎的

examples: He was nonchalant about the missed flight until he learned the next one was thirty hours later.
She gave a nonchalant shrug that fooled everyone except the friend who had watched her rehearse it.
The goalkeeper's nonchalant clearance rolled straight to a striker who could not believe his luck.
His nonchalant tone on the call did not match the six drafts of the resignation letter on his desk.
Teenagers perfect a nonchalant walk past the very person they crossed the whole cafeteria to see.
words.etymology: non-(不) + calere(在意,发热) → 不上心 → 满不在乎

meanings.en: without money, food, or a home; extremely poor
completely lacking something, used with 'of'
meanings.zh: 全然缺乏的(与 of 连用)

examples: The fire left two dozen families destitute, sleeping in a school gym while the insurance calls went unanswered.
He died destitute in a rented room, twelve years after selling the patent that made someone else rich.
A single hospital bill can leave an uninsured household destitute within a month.
The charity was founded to house destitute veterans who had fallen through every other program.
The screenplay is destitute of a single line anyone would repeat on the way out of the theater.
words.etymology: de-(向下) + statuere(放置) → 被弃置一旁 → 一无所有

meanings.en: to calm someone down by giving them what they want
to give in to an aggressor's demands in the hope of avoiding conflict
meanings.zh: 姑息,绥靖(对侵略者让步)

meanings.en: to satisfy a hunger, thirst, or curiosity

examples: The airline offered vouchers to appease passengers who had spent the night on terminal floors.
He rewrote the announcement twice to appease a board that objected to the word restructuring.
Historians still argue whether the 1938 agreement appeased an aggressor or merely bought a year of rearmament.
Critics said the compromise appeased the loudest lobby while quietly taxing everyone who had not shown up.
A cold slice of pizza at two in the morning appeased his hunger enough to get him back to the draft.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + pax(和平) → 使趋于平和 → 安抚

meanings.en: acceptance of something without protest, often reluctant or merely passive

examples: The board took her silence as acquiescence, and the merger went to a vote before she could object.
Years of acquiescence to unpaid overtime ended the day the schedule appeared without a single day off.
His acquiescence came with a raised eyebrow that everyone in the room understood perfectly.
The treaty passed through tired acquiescence rather than any real agreement about what it would cost.
She mistook polite acquiescence for enthusiasm and booked the venue the same afternoon.
words.etymology: ad-(向) + quiescere(安静) → 静下来不反对 → 默许

meanings.en: morally offensive or disreputable, and best not looked at too closely
unpleasant to taste or smell

examples: The documentary dug up an unsavory chapter of the founder's career that the IPO prospectus had skipped.
He was fired for unsavory dealings with a supplier whose invoices nobody could match to a delivery.
The bar attracted an unsavory crowd after midnight, which the owner preferred to call atmosphere.
Her lawyer warned that the emails contained unsavory details that would look far worse read aloud.
An unsavory smell from the office fridge finally forced a company-wide amnesty on unlabeled containers.
words.etymology: un-(不) + sapor(味道) → 不合口味 → 令人反感的

meanings.en: not justified by the facts or the situation
meanings.zh: 无正当理由的;毫无根据的

examples: The audit found the layoffs were an unwarranted response to a single bad quarter.
She called the extra security screening unwarranted, and the airline eventually agreed in writing.
His confidence in the forecast was unwarranted, as anyone who had read the footnotes could have told him.
The court ruled the search unwarranted and threw out everything the officers had found in the trunk.
An unwarranted assumption about the file format cost the team three days of debugging.

meanings.en: unnecessary and rude, said of a remark or action nobody had any reason to make
meanings.zh: 唐突无礼的;多余而不必要的

examples: His comment about her accent was uncalled-for, and the room's silence made that clear before anyone spoke.
The review contained an uncalled-for jab at the author's earlier book that had nothing to do with this one.
She apologized for an uncalled-for email she had sent at midnight after reading the sales numbers.
Booing a nine-year-old at a school recital is uncalled-for no matter how flat the recorder sounded.
The coach called the tackle uncalled-for and pulled his own player off the field before the referee could.

meanings.en: refusing to change one's position or lower a standard, even under pressure
meanings.zh: 不妥协的,不让步的;(标准)严苛的

examples: The building inspector was uncompromising about the blocked fire exits, and the restaurant stayed shut for another three weeks.
Her uncompromising editing turned a bloated four-hundred-page draft into something a reader could finish on one flight.
He is uncompromising about sleep: no meetings before nine, no matter which time zone the client sits in.
The documentary takes an uncompromising look at how the factory treated its night shift, naming three managers on camera.
Investors called her uncompromising when she refused to soften the safety report days before the funding round closed.

meanings.en: happening in the mind without a person being aware of it
the part of the mind that shapes behaviour without being available to conscious thought

examples: Years in an open-plan office left her with a subconscious flinch whenever someone walked up behind her chair.
The designer admitted the logo's curve was a subconscious copy of a cereal box she stared at as a child.
He insists he picked the flight on price, but his subconscious was probably weighing the airline's crash record.
Therapists say the dream is the subconscious sorting through everything the commute gave you no time to process.
A subconscious habit of ending every email with an apology took her two years and one blunt mentor to notice.
words.etymology: sub-(在……之下) + conscious(有意识) → 意识层之下

meanings.en: deserving praise, especially for effort or principle rather than result

examples: Shipping the bug fix on Christmas Eve was commendable, but the on-call rota that forced it was not.
Her restraint was commendable: the client insulted the whole design team and she simply asked for the brief again.
The cafe's commendable decision to pay suppliers within a week cost it margin and won it every farmer in the valley.
It is commendable that he started learning Mandarin at fifty, though his colleagues still switch to English out of habit.
The report showed commendable honesty about the missed targets, naming the three decisions that caused them.
words.etymology: com-(加强) + mandare(托付) → 郑重推许

meanings.en: to be a living or physical expression of an idea, quality, or period
to include something as part of a document, law, or system

examples: The corner shop embodies everything the neighbourhood lost when the second chain supermarket opened.
She embodied the company's stated values so completely that HR started using her name in the onboarding deck.
The new charter embodies three of the demands the union spent two winters striking for.
That battered notebook embodies his whole method: no app, no backup, one pen, and nothing written twice.
The settlement embodies a clause that quietly caps every future claim at half the original figure.

meanings.en: complete confusion, the state of not understanding what is happening

examples: The new pricing page was met with such bewilderment that support tickets doubled in a single afternoon.
He stared at the ticket machine in bewilderment while a queue of commuters formed behind him.
Her bewilderment turned to anger once she realised the meeting had been moved without anyone telling her.
There was a moment of collective bewilderment when the keynote speaker opened with forty seconds of silence.
The exchange student described her first week of British small talk as three days of pure bewilderment.
words.etymology: be-(使) + wilder(迷失荒野) → 茫然不知所措

meanings.en: to reverse a decision, verdict, or result that had already been settled
meanings.zh: 推翻,撤销(判决、决定、结果)

meanings.en: to knock something over, or to remove a government or system by force

examples: The appeals court overturned the verdict after a lab technician admitted the samples had been mislabelled.
One late goal overturned a result that had looked settled since the twentieth minute.
Protesters overturned two parked scooters before the organisers regained control of the crowd.
The board overturned its own hiring freeze six weeks after announcing it, and explained nothing.
A single leaked memo was enough to overturn a government that had survived three no-confidence votes.

meanings.en: strongly disliking something, or unwilling to do it
meanings.zh: 反感的,厌恶的,不愿意的

examples: The fund is averse to anything without five years of audited accounts, which rules out most of the sector.
She is not averse to a nine-hour flight if the conference actually puts her in front of real buyers.
The older engineers here are averse to rewriting anything that has run without incident since 2009.
He seemed averse to putting a number on the estimate, which told the client more than a number would have.
Voters are famously averse to any tax that shows up on the bill with its own separate line.
words.etymology: a-(离开) + vertere(转) → 转身避开 → 反感

meanings.en: done before someone else can act, in order to stop them or reduce the damage

examples: The company issued a preemptive apology on Friday evening, hours before the newspaper published its investigation.
A preemptive email to the landlord about the slow leak saved him from being billed for the whole ceiling.
The startup's preemptive hiring of three rival engineers cost a fortune and gutted the competitor's roadmap.
She takes a preemptive painkiller before long flights, having learned what cabin pressure does to her jaw.
Regulators called the merger a preemptive move to buy a threat before it could grow into one.
words.etymology: prae-(先于) + emere(取得) → 抢先取得

meanings.en: to be a sign of something that will happen later, usually something bad

examples: The quiet resignation of the finance director foreshadowed a restructuring nobody was told about for months.
Two lines in the pilot episode foreshadow the betrayal that closes the season, and almost nobody catches them.
Falling ticket sales in March foreshadowed a summer the festival would not survive.
His habit of copying the whole leadership team on small complaints foreshadowed exactly how the project would end.
An unusually warm February foreshadowed a fire season that started six weeks earlier than the records suggested.
words.etymology: fore-(在前) + shadow(影子) → 事先投下影子
