meanings.en: praising powerful people insincerely in order to gain something from them

examples: The launch coverage was so sycophantic that two reporters refused to put their names on it.
His sycophantic replies to every post the chief executive wrote became a running joke on the team channel.
She could not sit through another sycophantic introduction praising a speaker who had done none of the work.
The memoir is sycophantic about the men who funded him and merciless about everyone who did not.
A sycophantic laugh at a genuinely bad joke told the room exactly who was hoping for the promotion.

meanings.en: to make someone like you by deliberate effort, usually for your own advantage
meanings.zh: 讨好,巴结(使自己受青睐)

examples: He tried to ingratiate himself with the hiring panel by quoting their own conference talks back at them.
She spent her first month ingratiating herself with the office manager, which turned out to be the smartest available move.
The new supplier ingratiated itself by fixing a problem it had not caused and never sending an invoice.
Ingratiating yourself with one loud stakeholder is a fast way to lose the other four.
His attempt to ingratiate himself with the neighbours involved homemade jam and a long conversation about bins.
words.etymology: in-(进入) + gratia(恩宠) → 挤进别人的好感

meanings.en: easy to notice, either because it stands out or because it is missing

examples: His absence from the all-hands was conspicuous enough that three people asked me about it separately.
The only conspicuous object in the whole flat was a nine-foot bookshelf holding eleven books.
She felt conspicuous in a suit at a party where everyone else had come straight from the beach.
The company's conspicuous silence about the data breach lasted four days and cost more than the breach itself.
A conspicuous red sticker on the folder meant legal had not cleared it for sending.
words.etymology: con-(完全) + specere(看) → 一眼就看得见

meanings.en: needing conscious effort, and visibly not yet automatic or fluent
meanings.zh: 费力的,吃力的(尚未自动化)

examples: Reading in a second language stays effortful until roughly the point where you stop translating in your head.
His effortful cheerfulness at the family dinner was more painful to watch than an argument would have been.
The first month on the new keyboard layout is effortful, and then one morning it simply is not.
Recovery was slow and effortful: twenty minutes on the bike, then a nap that swallowed the afternoon.
She writes in short effortful bursts of forty minutes, with the router unplugged and the phone in another room.

meanings.en: working hard and steadily, as a settled habit rather than a burst

examples: The most industrious person on the floor was also the one nobody thought to promote for four years.
Her industrious first term produced three papers, one of which nobody has cited since.
An industrious colony of ants had relocated the entire contents of the sugar jar overnight.
He is industrious in the way that worries people: no holidays, no hobbies, no obvious off switch.
The village looked industrious at six in the morning, with three bakeries already lit and trading.

meanings.en: the practice of severe self-discipline, giving up comfort and pleasure on principle

examples: His asceticism is selective: no alcohol, no sugar, no television, and a phone he checks two hundred times a day.
The retreat sells asceticism at four hundred euros a night, meals of rice and a room without a lock.
Silicon Valley rediscovers asceticism every few years, usually as fasting with an app attached to it.
Her grandmother's asceticism came from rationing rather than philosophy, and she never forgave anyone who wasted bread.
The order's asceticism extends to the building itself: stone floors, no heating, one narrow window per cell.
words.etymology: askein(操练) → 苦修自律 → 禁欲

meanings.en: the use of deception to cheat someone or to create a false impression

examples: The whole discount was trickery: the price had been raised on Monday and cut again on Friday.
It took a statistician twenty minutes to show that the chart's trickery lived entirely in the y-axis.
He calls it negotiation; the supplier who read the contract twice calls it trickery.
The film's best sequence uses no digital trickery at all, just a mirror and a very patient camera operator.
Voters forgive a bad policy faster than they forgive trickery about what the policy actually does.

meanings.en: going on at length without a clear point, and wandering off the subject
meanings.zh: (讲话、文章)冗长杂乱的,不着边际的

meanings.en: spreading out irregularly in many directions, said of a building or plant

examples: The rambling three-page email could have been a single sentence: the launch is delayed.
He gave a rambling answer about supply chains that never once mentioned the missing shipment.
Her rambling voicemail was oddly comforting, twelve minutes of nothing much at eleven at night.
They bought a rambling farmhouse with four staircases and no obvious front door.
A rambling wisteria had taken the whole south wall and most of the neighbour's gutter.

meanings.en: the act of claiming more importance, taste, or skill than you actually have
a claim or aspiration to a title, rank, or position

examples: The wine list had the pretension of a Michelin restaurant and the glassware of a village pub.
What saves the book is its complete absence of pretension: he explains the maths as if to a friend.
Her pretensions to the family business ended on the afternoon the will was read aloud.
There is a pretension in calling a two-person studio an agency, and clients notice it faster than you think.
The small kingdom's pretensions to naval power rested on four boats and a great deal of paperwork.
words.etymology: prae-(在前) + tendere(伸展) → 摆出姿态

meanings.en: put on to impress others, and recognisably not how the person really is
meanings.zh: 装腔作势的,做作的,不自然的

examples: His affected transatlantic accent survived exactly one trip home to Leeds and never came back.
The gallery talk was delivered in an affected whisper, as though the paintings might overhear.
She has an affected way of pausing before the word 'craft' that makes the whole studio wince.
Nothing about the restaurant is affected: paper menus, one wine, and a chef who eats with the staff.
Reviewers called the novel affected, and the author cheerfully agreed that plain prose bored him.

meanings.en: too willing to believe what you are told, and therefore easy to deceive

examples: The scheme worked because it targeted the credulous and the lonely, in roughly that order.
He is credulous about anything a doctor says on television and sceptical of every doctor he actually meets.
One credulous intern forwarded the phishing email to the entire finance team within four minutes.
The market was credulous enough to fund a company whose only real asset was a slide deck.
She was noticeably less credulous after the third contractor quoted half the going rate and then vanished.
words.etymology: credere(相信) → 太容易就相信

meanings.en: to make someone stop being friendly or supportive, usually without meaning to
meanings.zh: 使疏远,得罪,使产生隔阂

examples: The new commission structure alienated the three salespeople who had built the entire client list.
He alienated the neighbours over a hedge and spent the next decade parking two streets away.
Every attempt to broaden the show's audience alienated the viewers who had kept it alive.
She worried that moving abroad at fifteen would alienate her from cousins she only saw at weddings.
A single badly worded all-staff email can alienate people faster than a year of disappointing pay.
words.etymology: alienus(属于他人的) → 使变得像外人

meanings.en: a settled dissatisfaction with an authority, which quietly withdraws support from it
meanings.zh: 离心,不满(对当权者失去拥护)

examples: Disaffection in the warehouse showed up first in the rota, where suddenly nobody volunteered for anything.
The party mistook rural disaffection for apathy and lost forty seats in a single night.
Years of quiet disaffection ended with eleven resignations in the same fortnight.
Management measured engagement with a survey and missed the disaffection sitting in every exit interview.
The general's memoir traces the disaffection back to one broken promise about leave.
words.etymology: dis-(不再) + affect(情感依附) → 不再拥护

meanings.en: to free someone or something from a difficulty or from being physically trapped
meanings.zh: 使解脱,使摆脱(困境、纠缠)

examples: It took two lawyers and eight months to extricate her from a contract she had signed in one afternoon.
He extricated his sleeve from the escalator with the calm of a man this had happened to before.
The company is trying to extricate itself from a joint venture that now loses money in both currencies.
Firefighters extricated the driver through the rear window while traffic backed up for a mile behind them.
Extricating yourself from a group chat is a social problem rather than a technical one.
words.etymology: ex-(向外) + tricae(纠缠) → 从纠缠中脱身

meanings.en: an involvement or relationship that is complicated and hard to get out of
meanings.zh: 纠葛,牵连,难以摆脱的关系

meanings.en: a mass of things twisted together

examples: The firm's entanglement with a sanctioned bank surfaced in a footnote on page ninety of the annual report.
A brief romantic entanglement with a competitor's product manager ended two careers and one roadmap.
Divers spent an hour cutting the turtle free of an entanglement of fishing line and plastic rope.
He avoids political entanglements the way other people avoid gluten, loudly and not entirely consistently.
The cables behind the desk had grown into an entanglement nobody dared trace back to its source.
